utilization is taking place in the last quarter of the year.
2.7 Committee observes that in spite of its raising concerns over this trend of under
utilization of funds year after year, there does not seem to be any noticeable improvement
in this regard. Time and again the Committee has been advocating for higher allocation of
funds for this sector and this time the Committee is happy to note that the approved outlay
has seen a 32% hike over the last year’s Revised Estimate. The Committee reiterates its
concern and recommends to the Department to play a more pro-active role in identifying
the problems afflicting the utilization of funds in the Health Sector and initiate remedial
measures from the very beginning of the current financial year so that the old story of
revising estimates downwards and subsequent under utilization does not recur.
2.8 The Committee views with serious concern the under utilization of funds on account
of slow pace of expenditure on implementation of schemes like Pradhan Mantri Swasthya
Suraksha Yojana (PMSSY), Cancer, Mental Health, Capacity Building Project for Food and
Drugs, non-implementation of the recommendations of the Oversight Committee, New
Initiatives, and also non-finalizations of proposals relating to procurement of various
equipments, non-filling up of vacant posts, non-receipt of proposals from State Government/
Implementing Agencies etc. The Committee recommends the Department to keep the
activities of these schemes/institutions under constant monitoring so as to arrest this trend
of under utilization.
2.9 The pendency level of Utilization Certificates has been engaging the attention of the
Committee for the last few years. According to latest figures as on 1st March, 2008, there
were as many as 1318 Utilization Certificates in respect of Health Sector amounting to
Rs.677.61 crores for the grants released upto 2005-06. On a specific query regarding any
plans of the Department to reach a justifiable level of pendency, the Committee is given
to understand that a communication was sent by the Chief Controller of Accounts (CCA)
to all the States through Resident Commissioners on this issue giving full details of pending
UCs in respect of the Department of Health and Family Welfare. The Committee is
dismayed to note that in the name of efforts; only a letter has been issued. The Committee
feels that spirited efforts, which are apparently lacking, need to be made on priority basis
to clear the UCs which are pending for the last three decades or so. The Committee also

5
recommends to the Department to take up the case with concerned State Governments at
the highest level so as to assess whether the funds have been utilized properly or not.
2.10 In response to another specific query regarding audit of various Programmes/Bodies, the
Committee is given to understand that a fresh proposal will be submitted to take up the audit of
all centrally sponsored programmes, PSUs and autonomous bodies under the Department. As per
GFR 211 (1), the Grantee Bodies like autonomous bodies, PSU etc. receiving Grant-in-aid are to
be audited by Principal Accounts Office of the Ministry and C and AG and for this purpose a
provision is being incorporated in the Sanction. The Committee has been informed by the
Department that it has taken steps to strengthen its Internal Audit Wing also.
2.11 The Committee welcomes the proposal of the Department to introduce a provision in
the Sanction itself regarding audit of all centrally sponsored programmes, PSUs under the
Department and autonomous bodies which are receiving Grant-in-Aid. The Committee
recommends to the Department to expedite the same and intimate the progress made in
this regard.
2.12 The Committee is given to understand that the Department proposes to undertake the audit
of more centrally sponsored health programmes and PSUs and autonomous bodies during the
Financial Year 2008-09. Besides the names of Bodies/Programmes which would be covered
during 2008-09, the Committee would like to be informed about the centrally sponsored
health programmes, PSUs and autonomous bodies which were audited during 2007-08 along
with the adverse audit findings and the action taken by the Department thereon.
2.13 The Committee’s attention has been drawn by high level of pendency of Audit paras
contained in CAG Report and Internal Audit on matters relating to the Department. The
Committee is surprised to note that there are 62 pending Audit paras dating back from
CAG Report No.2 of 1998 to the latest CAG Report No. 20 of 2007 on the Performance Audit
of procurement of medicines and medical equipment. The Committee fails to understand the
reasons for such high level of pendency. The very fact that such a large number of Audit
paras remain to be reconciled indicates that internal financial management of the Ministry
is weak. The Committee would like to be apprised about the corrective measures taken in
the light of the pending Audit paras.
III. CENTRAL GOVERNMENT HEALTH SCHEME (CGHS)
3.1 CGHS, a welfare scheme of the Central Government, was started in 1954 and takes care
of the medical needs of the Central Government employees (serving and pensioners), sitting and
Ex-MPs, Judges of the Supreme Court/High Court (sitting and retired), Freedom Fighters (free of
cost), Ex-Governors, Ex-Vice Presidents of India, employees of the semi autonomous bodies/semi
Government Organisations, Accredited Journalists, serving and pensioner employees of a few
autonomous organisations in Delhi and the cities where CGHS is in operation. It provides medical
services-both inpatient and outpatient care including diagnostic and investigations at the level of
dispensaries, Central/State Government Hospitals, recognised private hospitals/diagnostic centres,
dispensaries/units under ISM and H, regional cancer centre, polyclinics to its beneficiaries. As per
the latest figures, there are 9.11 lakh CGHS cardholders and 33.01 lakh beneficiaries.
3.2 Plan allocation of Rs.50.00 crores and Non-Plan allocation of Rs.329.00 crores has been
made for CGHS for 2008-09. The Committee notes that Plan allocation for 2008-09 is at an
enhanced level when compared with provision of Rs.40.00 crores made for 2007-08. As per
the Outcome Budget (2008-09), against a Plan allocation of Rs.40.00.crores for 2007-08
under CGHS; expenditure reported upto 29.02.2008 is only Rs.19.08 crores. The Committee
is, however, surprised to note that in response to a specific query made by it, utilization of

6
Rs.32.16 crores was reported upto February, 2008. The Committee is unhappy with the
conflicting figures of utilization of Plan funds. Either the information published in the
Outcome Budget is incorrect or inaccurate status report has been furnished to the
Committee, that too on a specific query made by it. Both the positions compel the
Committee to conclude that there is a need for better management at the Department
level. The Committee apprehends that chances are there that major utilization under CGHS
has taken place during the last quarter of the year. If it is true, this indicates improper
handling of the funds. The trend of utilization of major chunk of funds during the last
quarter is not a healthy sign. The Committee would like to be apprised about utilization of
Plan and Non-Plan funds (quarter-wise) during 2007-08. In the light of last year’s experience
of utilization of funds, the Committee recommends that concerted efforts need to be made
for optimum and judicious utilization of enhanced allocation made for 2008-09.
3.3 The Committee has been given to understand that against a proposal for allocation of
Rs.453 crores submitted under Non-Plan in BE 2008-09, an allocation of Rs. 329 crores has been
made, which is lower when compared to provision of Rs. 368.00 crores in RE 2007-08. The
Committee has been given to understand that additional Non-Plan funds were meant for salary for
vacant posts likely to be filled up during the year and also for payments to the MSDs, local
chemists etc. The Committee, therefore, recommends that allocation of funds under Non-
Plan be enhanced adequately so that the services available to the CGHS beneficiaries are
not affected.
3.4 The computerization of CGHS dispensaries and offices in Delhi was taken up at an
expenditure of Rs.8.74 crores. The Committee was informed that as on 26.3.2008, 83
dispensaries in Delhi have been fully computerized and the process of computerization of
remaining 4 dispensaries was under way. The Committee would like to point out that
computerization process of CGHS dispensaries in Delhi could not be completed as scheduled.
Originally targeted to be completed by 2006-07, revised date of 17th August, 2007 could also
not be adhered to. By the end of financial year, 2007-08, 4 dispensaries in Delhi still
remained to be computerized. Computerization of CGHS dispensaries located in Mumbai,
Kolkata, Chennai, Hyderabad, Nagpur and Pune to be taken up in 2007-08 as scheduled, is
yet to start. The Committee can imagine the status of third phase slated to be completed
in 2008-09. The Committee, keeping in view the past experience in respect of Delhi
dispensaries, can only emphasize that all steps need to be taken to complete the
computerization of dispensaries outside Delhi at the earliest. Corrective measures based on
the problem areas noticed in the computerization of dispensaries in Delhi need to be taken.
3.5 The Committee is given to understand that the feedback received from the officials
regarding computerization is very encouraging while there has been a mixed reaction from the
beneficiaries. The Committee would like to point out that situation is some what different.
Problems are being faced both by the CGHS functionaries and beneficiaries. Technicians,
junior staff manning counters in dispensaries and attending doctors need to be fully trained.
Practical problems like internet and electricity failure have to be tackled by having an
alternative arrangement. These initial teething problems should not be allowed to be
prolonged. At present, beneficiaries which include senior citizens also are being made to
wait for hours at the dispensaries. Their ordeal starts right from the registration counter
and continues upto delivery of medicines. The Committee would appreciate if all the
measures including training, smooth running of computers with full connectivity, backup for
power failure are taken at the earliest and also closely monitored.
3.6 The Committee has been emphasizing for long for introduction of two shift system
in CGHS. The Committee does not appreciate the contention of the Ministry that a large

7
number of private hospitals and diagnostic centres have been empanelled under the CGHS
and in case of emergency, beneficiaries can go there for treatment and claim re-
imbursement later. The Committee would like to draw the attention of the Ministry once
again to the fact that idea behind having two shifts in CGGS dispensaries is the
inconvenience being faced by the CGHS beneficiaries, majority of them office goers in going
to the dispensaries in the morning hours. The Committee is disturbed by the element of
helplessness shown by the Ministry in their candid admission of staff side vehemently
opposing the move. In this era where the service providers like banks etc. are opting for
flexible timings to give their customers maximum possible services, at least the Ministry
could have come forward with a positive and proactive approach. The Committee would
reiterate its recommendation made last year for starting two shifts in a few dispensaries as
a test case. One must not forget that CGHS is a service oriented scheme, supposedly
providing health care mainly to our serving employees and pensioners. It is the
responsibility of the Ministry to make the CGHS employees understand and not to be
pressurized by them.
3.7 The Committee’s attention has also been drawn by the problems being faced by a very large
number of CGHS beneficiaries residing in Dwarka sub-city in Delhi. At present, these beneficiaries
have to travel 10-12 Kms. for medical treatment at the nearest dispensary located in Manglapuri,
Palam. For pathological tests they have to travel even further to Janakpuri Dispensary. The
Committee was informed that approval for opening of CGHS dispensary in Dwarka has been
received and work would start soon. The Committee recommends that construction of
dispensary in Dwarka where land is already available should start at the earliest. All
procedural formalities should be expedited and completion of project strictly monitored.
3.8 The Committee finds that in-principle approval for opening of new CGHS dispensaries
in Sector 82, Noida and Gurgaon was given by the Planning Commission way back on
14th March, 2006.  The Committee is surprised to note that even after two years, suitable
accommodation for housing the dispensary in Sector 82, Noida and Gurgaon could not be
managed. Secretary (Health) Government of Haryana is now being requested to allot a
building for CGHS Dispensary in Gurgaon. Proposal for housing the CGHS Dispensary in
Community Centre, Sector 82, Noida on rent-basis is under consideration. The Committee
strongly feels that the Ministry should pursue the two proposals in hand so that large
number of CGHS beneficiaries residing in these two areas do not continue to remain
deprived of health care any more.
3.9 The Committee notes that CGHS continues to suffer from manpower shortage. Against 84
sanctioned SAG posts, 74 posts are lying vacant. The latest figures supplied by the Department
show that 495 vacancies are there in the grade of GDMO alone. The Committee has been given
to understand that on the basis of CMSE 2006, 125 candidates had been offered appointment and
pre-appointment formalities for 175 candidates were under different stages of process. Based on
CMSE 2007 , dossiers of 176 candidates had been received and were being processed. As regards
vacancies in technical posts, after necessary approval, advertisement has been issued. Requisition
for stenographers and LDCs had been placed with SSC. Action for vacant promotional posts had
been initiated through DPCs. Further after a long but avoidable delay, the Department had finally
started implementing the SIU report. Accordingly, all surplus posts identified in cities outside Delhi
have been abolished and action for creation of posts has been initiated for obtaining approval of
the Ministry of Finance. The Committee recommends to the Department to take the issue on
priority with the Ministry of Finance to complete all the procedural formalities so that
necessary posts are created and subsequently filled up. The Committee would also like to
be apprised about the cadre strength created as a result of implementation of SIU report
and the efforts taken so far to fill up the vacant posts.

8
3.10 The Committee’s attention has also been drawn by a very large number of vacancies in
Group ‘C’ and ‘D’ categories. Out of 3022 category ‘C’ sanctioned posts, 568 posts were vacant,
with Delhi alone having the maximum vacancies of 292. Similarly, there were 550  vacant posts
against 2934 sanctioned Group ‘D’ posts, with Delhi having the maximum vacancies of 325.
Besides that, staff other than medical officers was being out sourced/engaged on contract basis in
Dehradun, Bhubaneswar, Ranchi, Chandigarh, Shillong and Bhopal. The Committee understands
that third party administrators for processing of claims and medical audit are also proposed
to be introduced. The Committee has been given to understand that as recommended by
SIU, Department of Expenditure, vacancies arising in Group ‘D’ posts are to be
progressively outsourced.
3.11 The Committee views with serious concern the growing number of vacancies in
different categories of posts in CGHS dispensaries. The Committee understands that all
surplus posts identified in cities outside Delhi have been abolished. It has also been
informed that the staff strength in the dispensaries is decided as per the workload. The
very fact that at the present juncture, no CGHS city can be stated to have full complement
of the staff strength as per the SID norms establishes that the existing dispensaries are not
functioning as envisaged. The Committee also strongly feels that outsourcing/hiring of staff
on contract-basis on a big scale is a remedy worse than the disease. The concept of public
private partnership cannot be applied across the board specially in a set-up meant for
providing health care. The Committee would like to have a status note on the sanctioned
posts and vacancies, category-wise and region-wise in CGHS dispensaries.
3.12 To a specific query of the Committee as to payment of consultation fees to other agencies
owing to new fulfillment of needs of various indenters by Medical Stores Organization (M.S.O.),
it was informed that M/S HSCC alone was paid Rs.9.03 crores towards consultancy fees. The
Committee recommends that all out efforts be made for reduction in the consultation fees
to 2% for procurement of drugs/medicines for CGHS as assured by the Ministry and the
Committee be informed accordingly.
3.13 The Committee notes that as there is no private hospital empanelled under CGHS for
treatment of cancer patients in Delhi only adhoc arrangements are in place. Accordingly, cancer
patients could get treatment from Apollo Hospital, New Delhi, Batra Hospital, New Delhi,
Dharamshila Cancer Hospital, Delhi and Rajiv Gandhi Cancer and Research Institute, Delhi upto
31st March, 2008. The Committee is happy to note that these  adhoc  arrangements would
continue until further orders. The Committee would, however, like to emphasize that
empanelment of these hospitals should be made on permanent basis, specially in view of
cancer patients undergoing prolonged and costly treatment. The Ministry has to play a
proactive role in such matters.
3.14 The Committee was informed that CGHS rules for various procedures, tests etc. in CGHS
empanelled private hospitals and diagnostic centres were fixed on the basis of lowest rates
quoted for a group of CGHS cities, depending on the classification of the cities for purposes of
City Compensatory Allowance. Subsequently, on objections being raised on clubbing of cities for
fixing of rates, it was decided to issue rate list for each CGHS city separately, based on the lowest
rates quoted by hospitals/diagnostic centres for that city. The Committee notes that under the
revised exercise, rates in respect of Bangalore, Chennai, Hyderabad, Jaipur, Kolkata,
Lucknow, Mumbai, Nagpur and Pune have been issued. The Committee hopes that rates for
the remaining cities would be issued at the earliest. The Committee would like to be
apprised about the level of difference in the rates for major hospitals/diagnostic centres in
the metro cities.

9
IV. SAFDARJUNG HOSPITAL AND V ARDHMAN MAHAVEER MEDICAL COLLEGE,
NEW DELHI
4.1 Safdarjung Hospital, established in 1942, is the largest of the three Central Government
Tertiary Care Multi-disciplinary Hospitals in Delhi with a pre-independence history. The Hospital has
total bed strength of 1531 including bassinets. The hospital presently has facilities in the 34 clinical
and 45 special clinics.
4.2 Plan allocation of Rs.51.00 crores for 2007-08 for the Hospital was raised to Rs.73.50
crores at the RE stage, keeping in view funds required for procurement of equipment, medicines
etc. and completion of ongoing projects. The Committee, however, notes that upto 29.02.2008
expenditure of only Rs.53.77 crores could be reported.
4.3 Against projected Plan requirement for the Safdarjung hospital (excluding VMMC) of
Rs.87.88 crores for the current year, allocation of Rs.50.00 crores has been made. The
Committee apprehends that the present allocation of funds to the Hospital might adversely
affect its services and in the process, the large number of patients. While cautioning the
Hospital to utilize its allocated funds judiciously and optimally, the Committee recommends
that it should be granted adequate funds to meet its functional requirements.
4.4 To a specific query on whether the Department proposes to work out a monitoring
mechanism in co-ordination with hospital authorities to ensure procurement of medical equipments
within the prescribed time limit and thereby result in reversing the trend of under utilization of
allocated funds, the Department came out with the often repeated rhetoric of ‘laid down
procedures’ that are to be followed. The Committee observes that procedures and rules are
made to streamline, strengthen and facilitate a process and not create hurdles and
bottlenecks. The Committee, therefore, recommends that effective coordination between the
Department and the Hospital authorities is required in this regard. If required, suitable
steps for improvement in the procedural aspect may be initiated so as to provide better
health care delivery system.
4.5 The Committee is happy to note that scheme of redevelopments of hospitals
including redevelopment of Safdarjung Hospital with the proposal to increase its bed
strength from 1531 to 3000 has finally been included in the approved schemes for the
Eleventh Plan. HSCC has submitted a final report on ‘Redevelopment Plan of Safdarjung
Hospital’ to the Department for consideration. The Department has started work for
engaging consultants for preparation of DPR for the detailed redevelopment plan. The
Committee would like to point out that ‘in-principle’ approval by the Planning Commission
has already taken considerable time. The Committee therefore, urges the Department to
make wholehearted efforts to expedite the procedural formalities at the earliest. The
redevelopment plan is required to be started without any further delay, keeping in view the
ever-increasing patient load on the Safdarjung Hospital. The Committee recommends that
scarcity of funds and lack of coordination should not come in the way of its timely
completion and the Department should make every conceivable effort in this regard.
4.6 The Committee has been monitoring the progress made in the projects relating to
establishment of Renal Transplantation Unit in the Department of Surgery/Urology and Invitro
Fertilization (IVF) clinic in Obs. and Gynae Department for the last two-three years. As per the
latest information furnished by the Department:—
“The space has been identified and funds allocated. Rs.98.48 lakhs for the purpose have
been placed at the disposal of CPWD for the renovation work. Equipments are under
process of procurement and likely to be completely procured within next quarter of
2008-09. Two Surgeons, one Pathologist and 15 Nurses have already under-gone training

10
in Renal Transplant at AIIMS. As regards IVF Unit, a proposal has been submitted by the
HOD, Obs. and Gynae for approval in principle.”
4.7 The Committee expresses its serious concern on the slow progress made with regard
to setting up of Renal Transplantation Unit. Status of the project for IVF unit is more
discouraging as ‘in-principle’ approval is yet to come. The Committee can only emphasize
that the Renal Transplantation Unit should be made functional by the year end by closely
monitoring the progress of the same. Procedural formalities with regard to IVF unit also
need to be completed at the earliest.
4.8 The Committee’s attention has been drawn by a large number of vacancies in
different categories of posts in Safdarjung Hospital. Out of the total sanctioned staff
strength of 4781, there were 1054 vacant posts in different categories as on July, 2007. The
Committee has been given to understand that workload of the Hospital has progressively
increased manifold in the past few years. The doctor-patient ratio has inversely grown, there
is an acute need of more doctors per patient and related infrastructure including sub-staff.
In such a scenario, with the redevelopment project of Safdarjung Hospital likely to take off
at the earliest, additional staff strength of all the categories would be required. The
Committee, accordingly, recommends that the Department in co-ordination with hospital
authorities should chalk out an action-plan for acquiring the required manpower.
V. DR. RAM MANOHAR LOHIA HOSPITAL, NEW DELHI
5.1 Dr. Ram Manohar Lohia Hospital is one of the main public tertiary level hospitals in New
Delhi which was set up in 1954. Over the years, RML Hospital has grown to become a 1000-bed
hospital providing services in almost all major specialities and many super-specialties. Chosen by
the WHO to be developed as a model health promoting hospital, the first of its kind in India, RML
Hospital caters to two-lakh emergency patients and l2-lakh outdoor patients annually. The hospital
had been actively involved in information education communication activities. It had conducted
various training programme of HIV/AIDS, Hospital Waste Management, Leptospirosis, etc. It is
actively participating in National Programmes like Blindness Control, Leprosy, Family Welfare,
Immunizations, and Drug De-Addiction Programmes. It is a designated hospital for training of
Dengue and AIDS by WHO.
5.2 The Committee notes that an approved outlay of Rs.36.00 crores (including PGIMER) was
revised to Rs. 71.95 crores in 2007-08. However, upto 29.02.2008, expenditure reported is only
Rs. 56.60 crores. The Committee is constrained to note that inspite of an assurance that
each Central Institute will have a separate monitoring Committee, given by the Secretary,
H
 and FW before the Committee last year, no action seems to have been taken. The
Committee, therefore, reiterates that a proper monitoring mechanism needs to be put in
place so as to arrest this trend of sub-optimal utilization of the funds.
5.3 The Committee has been observing that a number of projects-big and small,
envisaged for strengthening and augmenting the existing services in the premier Hospital,
continue to remain in the implementation status with very little progress being made. The
Committee has been constrained to point out that the year 2007-08 was also no exception.
Funds allocated remained under-utilized with the following three major projects running
behind schedule:—
• Strengthening of Accidents and Emergency Department and setting up of Trauma Care
Centre.
• Setting up of PGIMER at Dr. Ram Manohar Lohia Hospital.
• Upgradation of School of Nursing into College of Nursing.

11
All these projects were to be completed in 2007-08 only. The Committee notes that
academic session for PG courses in Medicine, Paediatrics and Anesthesia is to begin in 2008-
09. While welcoming the starting of PGIMER at Dr. RML hospital, the Committee would
appreciate if the PGI becomes fully operational running all the courses with the required
infrastructure and regular staff in place. The Committee apprehends that there is little
chance of Trauma Care Centre becoming operational in 2008-09 with appointment of 178
additional staff yet to be made and process of purchase of equipment and consumable going
on. The Committee also finds that not much progress seems to have been made in the
upgradation of School of Nursing into College of Nursing. The target remains the same in
2008-09 also as in the previous year.
VI. ALL INDIA INSTITUTE OF MEDICAL SCIENCES (AIIMS)
6.1 AIIMS was established in 1956 as an institution of national importance. It continues to be
a leader in the field of medical education, research and patient-care in keeping with the mandate
of the Parliament.
6.2 Against annual requirement of Rs.500.00 crores, Plan allocation of Rs.200.00 crores was
made for AIIMS, out of which only Rs.160.00 crores were provided by the Planning Commission/
Ministry of Finance at the RE stage in 2007-08. Again, against a projected requirement of
Rs.733.00 crores of Grant-in-Aids in 2008-09 only Rs.452.00 crores have been allocated out of
which the Plan component is Rs.162.00 crores and Non-Plan component is Rs.290.00 crores. The
Committee was informed that the allocated funds would not be sufficient for maintaining
the infrastructure and patient care services of the Institute. The Committee feels that the
decrease in Non-plan from Rs.310.00 crores in 2007-08 to Rs.290.00 crores is surely going
to affect the patient care services offered by the Institute. The Committee apprehends
return of the ‘user charges regime’ in AIIMS because consumables are the only negotiable
component of the Non-Plan budget as salary and bills have to be paid any way.
6.3 The Committee notes that approved outlay for AIIMS for the Eleventh Plan is Rs.1461.00
crores which is more than double of the T enth Plan allocation of Rs.631.12 crores. The Committee
finds that the Institute could not keep pace with the enhanced provision being made in the last
three years of the Tenth Plan period. The Committee has been informed that full utilization of Plan
funds during 2002-03 (Rs.105.00 crores) and 2003-04 (Rs.105.00 crores) the first two years of
the Tenth Plan was made possible only by diversion of Plan allocation to Non-plan to the tune of
Rs.61.45 crores and Rs.32.25 crores for 2002-03 and 2003-04 respectively. During the next two
years of the Tenth Plan, i.e. 2004-05 and 2005-06 Plan funds remained under utilized. For the last
year of the Tenth Plan, out of Plan provision of Rs.205.86 crores, expenditure reported
was Rs.160.00 crores, with Rs.30.00 crores being released as late as on 15.03.2007 and
Rs.30.33 crores on 31.03.2007.
6.4 The Committee is constrained to observe that enhanced outlay for the Eleventh Plan
period does not seem to have any visible impact. Plan provision of Rs.200.00 crores for
2007-08 not only remains at the same level as in the previous Plan period but has also been
brought down to Rs.160.00 crores at the RE stage with actual expenditure reported up to
29.02.2008 being only Rs.113.33 crores. The Committee is not able to comprehend the
reasons for under-utilization of funds duly allocated for specific purposes. Failure on the
part of a premier institute like AIIMS to utilize the funds as targeted indicates that
problem areas continue to persist both in the co-ordination between the administrative
Ministry and the Institute and its functioning.
6.5 The Committee in its last year’s report had called for making conscious effort to break the
deadlock between the premier institute of the country and the administrative Ministry which had

12
affected the quality of services of the Institute badly. The Committee has been informed that on
17.03.2008, Minister of Health and Family Welfare along with officials of the Ministry had a one
to one dialogue with the heads of all the Departments of the Institute to try and find out the areas
to be focused in the days to come regarding creation of adequate manpower and allocation of
resources. The Committee hopes that position would improve now.
6.6 The Committee has been given to understand that the Centre for Dental Research at the
Institute has become fully functional in February, 2008. The Committee hopes that all the necessary
posts created for the centre have been filled up. The Committee notes that EFC has been submitted
for the project of Surgical Block with an estimate of Rs.42.00 crore to be commissioned by
2009-10. The Committee would emphasize that procedural formalities for the centre should
be expedited so as to complete it by the targeted date.
6.7 The Committee also takes note of major new initiatives for which plans were under
preparation during 2007-08 as listed below:—
➢ Construction of new PC Block.
➢ Advance facilities for Paediatrics (Medical) and (Surgery).
➢ Advance facilities for Geriatrics.
➢ Facility for Family Medicine and Public Health.
6.8 The Committee finds that another set of new projects has been listed to be taken
during 2008-09. The Committee strongly feels that new initiatives should be taken up with
priority being fixed for the most needed ones. The Committee would appreciate if these
initiatives do not continue to be on paper during 2008-09. The Committee recommends that
funds provided for the AIIMS in the Eleventh Plan show both optimum and judicious
utilization as per the action plan with additional provision as and when required. The
Committee is of the view that an effective monitoring mechanism to be effected by all
concerned both at the institute and the Ministry level needs to be in place for the purpose
at the earliest.

training grounds for the doctors and that too at highly subsidized rates involving precious
tax payers’ money. The Committee is of the view that this brain drain is on two counts -
higher studies and lucrative assignments. At the same time, the Committee is also of the
opinion that some policy or enactment should be made so that tendency of leaving the
Institute by doctors/nurses can be minimized. This could be in the form of a monetary bond
or post qualification compulsory service. The Committee strongly feels that urgent steps are
required to be taken so as to ensure an ideal working environment for our young talented
doctors along with all the incentives comparable to those enjoyed by private sector doctors
to the extent possible. The Committee would like to be apprised of the steps taken in this
regard which should not be only AIIMS specific but should also cover all the Government
medical institutions.
6.12 The Committee is given to understand that the Valiathan Committee had submitted its
report on the functioning of AIIMS more than a year ago. The Committee is surprised to note
that only follow up action taken so far is a meeting held under the Chairmanship of Secretary
(Health and Family Welfare) with Director, AIIMS on the 1st March, 2008. The Committee was
informed that the matter was now under Government’s consideration. The Committee is not
happy with the undue delay in the implementation of Valiathan Committee recommendations.
Any further delay would simply negate the very purpose of setting up such a Committee, that
too at the directive of the Prime Minister. The Committee, therefore, urges upon the
Department to expedite the implementation of the Valiathan Committee Report.
6.13 The Committee in its last year’s Report had expressed its reservation to the casual approach
adopted by the Department to its earlier recommendation of setting up of a Burns Unit in AIIMS.
The Secretary, during the course of deposing before the Committee informed that the proposal for
setting up the same in the JPNA Trauma Centre, AIIMS could not be placed before the Standing
Finance Committee of the Institute on the 31st March, 2008, as scheduled and the same will be
done on the 17th April, 2008. The Committee can only hope that the Burns Unit, duly
approved, will be made operational by the targeted date.

VIII. NORTH EASTERN INDIRA GANDHI REGIONAL INSTITUTE OF HEALTH AND
MEDICAL SCIENCES (NEIGRIHMS), SHILLONG
8.1 The main objective of the Institute is to provide advanced specialized health care to
the people of the North Eastern Region including those of Sikkim, to serve as a regional
referral services centre and to promote a programme of health manpower development and
training in identified fields of super-specialization. The Institute is fully funded by the Government
of India.
8.2 Though originally slated for completion in March, 2005, at a cost of Rs.422.60 crores, the
project has been delayed time and again due to various reasons. In view of the slippages, the
Institute (500 bedded hospital) is likely to be fully operational by 2008-09.
8.3 The Committee has been monitoring the progress being made, specially in the procurement
of equipments required for operationalizing various Departments and recruitment of manpower. The
Committee notes that like in previous years, allocated funds remained under-utilized in 2007-08
also. Provision of Rs.75.00 crores at the beginning of the year had to be brought down to
Rs.42.00 crores at the RE stage and by 29.2.2008 expenditure reported was only Rs.30.00 crores.
The Committee has, however, been informed that all the major equipments required for
operationalizing various Departments have already been procured and installation is going on at
present. The Institute has been operationalized as 365 bedded hospital as of March, 2008.
8.4 The Committee also observes that the Institute is successfully running a Nursing College
since 2006 with 50 seats capacity. Now, the third batch is being admitted to the Nursing College.
The process of expanding the Nursing College by increasing the number of seats to 100 is going
on at present and already SFC Note has been circulated for the purpose. MBBS and PG courses
are slated to be started during this year. Approvals are being obtained from various Government
Bodies/Departments for the same.
8.5 The Committee is happy to note that considerable progress has been made in
operationalization of NEIGRIHMS during 2007-08. The Committee is, however, perturbed to
note that no improvement could be made so far as manpower required for the Institute is
concerned. Like 2006-07, position remained unchanged during 2007-08 also. The Committee
has been informed that a total of 95 faculty members, including 31 senior faculty, 28 senior
residents and 36 junior residents have joined so far. For senior faculty positions, 31 out of 79 posts
are already filled in. To overcome the difficulty faced in attracting qualified faculty for
operationalizing various speciality and super-speciality Departments in the institute, the Ministry has
invited eminent institutes of India to collaborate with NEIGRIHMS and operationalize the
departments. The Institute has already entered into an understanding with NIMHANS for
operationalizing the Department of Neurology and Neuro-Surgery by transferring and operating the
faculty posts from NIMHANS. The Institute has also entered into MoA with Dr. Cherian’s Frontier
Lifeline, International Institute of Cardiology, Cardio-Thoracic and V ascular Surgery for outsourcing
the services of the Departments of Cardiology and Cardiothoracic Surgery. Efforts are on to clinch
similar agreements with other eminent institutes including CMC-Vellore, CMC-Ludhiana, Amrita
Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS), Kochi and efforts are on to take the expertise of other GoI
institutes like AIIMS, PGIMER.

17
8.6 The Committee would like to point out that efforts made by the Department for
getting the teaching/specialists faculty posted/deputed fr om Armed Forces Medical Services
have not been successful due to shortage of senior faculty in the AFMS cadre also. The
Committee would again emphasize that it does not have much faith in the collaboration
measures reported to be made with Institutions like NIMHANS and Dr. Cherian’s Frontier
Lifeline. The Committee is not aware how far the efforts for clinching similar agreements
with CMC-Vellore, CMC-Ludhiana, Amrita Institute of Medical Sciences, Kochi, AIIMS and
PGIMER would prove to be successful. The Committee fails to comprehend how the
Departments of Neurology, Neuro-Surgery and Cardiology could be made operational at the
Institute located at Shillong by hiring the services of faculty of NIMHANS located at the
other corner of the country. Same would be the position with the proposed tie-up with other
Institutes. The Committee would also like to point out that the Department must be fully
aware about the shortage of faculty at these premier Institutes also. The Committee
strongly feels that such stop-gap arrangements, even if made, cannot make the Institute
fully functional. Target of making 500 bedded hospital and teaching Institute at Shillong is
thus likely to remain on paper only for considerable time. The Committee reiterates that
the Department has to make all conceivable efforts for having permanent faculty at the
Institute. Special incentives and extra facilities have to be worked out for attracting the
required manpower to the Institute. Collaboration with leading Institutes/public-private
partnership can be feasible for limited number of posts and period only. The Committee
would also like to be apprised about the present status of phase-I of filling up of 725 posts
and phase-II of filling up of 794 posts.

XII. IMPROVEMENT OF NURSING SERVICES
12.1 During the Tenth Plan, a provision of Rs.102.00 crores was made for Development of
Nursing Services. The Committee has been emphasizing the urgent need for expansion and
strengthening of Nursing Services in the country. The Committee notes that enhanced allocation of
Rs.280.65 crores for Development of Nursing Services for Eleventh Plan can be considered a step
in the right direction. Another encouraging sign is a new initiative proposed for the Eleventh Plan

21
is provision of Rs.2900.00 crores for upgradation/strengthening of Nursing Services. Provision of
Rs.18.00 crores and Rs.198.00 crores has accordingly been made under these two components for
2008-09.
12.2 The Committee takes note of reported utilization of Rs.12.40 crores upto 29.02.2008 against
a provision of Rs15.00 crores with likely expenditure of Rs.1.80 crores during March, 2008.
However, the Committee is surprised to observe unsatisfactory level of achievement under
the quantifiable deliverables/physical outputs set for 2007-08. The first target set was
training of 8000 nursing personnel through 48 identified Nursing Institutions. By the end
of the year, no progress seems to have been made from the details made available to the
Committee. Proposal for conducting 78 courses for training of 2340 nurses was under
process. Training of additional 1600 nurses depended upon proposals to be received from the
Institutions. The Committee has been informed that out of 30 institutions, funds could be
released for strengthening of 23 institutions. Status of these institutions is, however, not-
known. The Committee would also like to point out that projects like upgradation of RAK
College of Nursing into Centre of Excellence, upgradation of School of Nursing into College
of Nursing at Dr. R.M.L. Hospital, Safdarjung Hospital and Lady Harding Medical College
and establishing a College of Nursing in JIPMER, Puducherry have been there for the last
few years with no evidence of progress being made. Only exception is College of Nursing
at Lady Harding Medical College reported to have started functioning in 2007. The
Committee hopes that required manpower and infrastructure has been made available there.
12.3 As per the Outcome Budget (2008-09), College of Nursing at Dr. Ram Manohar Lohia
Hospital will start functioning from the session, 2008. The Committee is not very hopeful as
upgradation of School of Nursing at Dr. R.M.L. Hospital has also been listed as one of the
targets to be achieved during 2008-09. The Committee would like to reiterate that all these
projects need to be closely monitored so as to ensure their completion within the time
schedule without any cost escalation in the original estimate. The Department should not
be a mere spectator, it should devise some mechanism for proper utilization of the funds
and its repeated contention that the utilization/grants of funds depends upon receipt of
SOE/UCs is not acceptable to the Committee. The Department has to play a more proactive
role in co-ordination with the hospital/college authorities. The problem areas, wherever
noticed, need to be removed at the earliest.
12.4 The Committee is not aware about the existence of any Monitoring Committee for
such projects. The Committee is of the view that such a mechanism will prove to be very
useful, especially in view of Rs.198.00 crores allocated for strengthening/upgradation of
Nursing Services . This provision is proposed to be utilized during 2008-09 for establishment of
12 Centres of Excellence, opening of 73 ANM Schools, and 69 GNM Schools, strengthening of
20 State Nursing Councils and establishment of 6 Colleges of Nursing. The Committee welcomes
the enhancement in the assistance to be provided to Nursing Institutions from Rs.10.00
lakhs to Rs.25.00 lakhs. Such a move was overdue. The Committee, however, wonders
whether any exercise has been initiated for identification of locations of all the proposed
Centres/Schools/Colleges so far. The Committee would appreciate if implementation of all
these projects is carried out in a time-bound manner. The Committee is not aware about
any assessment/review made recently about the (training both pre and in-service)
programmes for Nurses and also functioning of Training Institutions for Nurses. The
Committee is of the view that such an exercise is necessary for strengthening the Nursing
Services which is a very crucial component of health care.
12.5 The Committee is happy to note that the National Awards for Nurses, given as a
mark of highest recognition for the meritorious services of the nurses and nursing
profession in the country, that continued up to 1989, have been revived and named as the

22
National Florence Nightingale Award from 2007 with the consent of the President of
India. 17 Nursing personnel have been awarded with this prestigious award during the year
2007.
12.6 On a clarification sought by the Committee, it was given to understand that there is no Live
Register of Nurses. Out of 9.28 lakh nurses registered with various State Nursing Councils, only
40% are active. There is a proposal with the Indian Nursing Council to conduct census on working
Nursing Personnel in India on experimental basis. Pilot study was done in this regard in one of
the districts in Tamil Nadu. Similar study in another four districts in different States is under
consideration. The Committee recommends that a suitable mechanism should be evolved for
maintaining a live register of nurses so as to enable the Department for formulating
appropriate policy pertaining to nurses.
12.7 Committee takes note of the Bajaj Committee recommendation that against a projected
requirement of 10.43 lakh nurses by 2012, only 6.84 lakh would be available. The Committee is
given to understand that the Department has come up with the following proposal to bridge the
gap:—
• Establishment of Auxiliary Nurse Midwifery (ANM) and General Nursing and Midwifery
(GNM) schools in those districts which are not having both these training programmes.
• Establishment of post graduation nursing (M.Sc Nursing) institutions.
• Renewal of registration once in every 5 years linked with continuing education.
• Establishment of Regional Institute of Excellence with the objective of improving the
standard on all India basis and provide opportunity to access high quality Nursing
Education through out the country.
• Strengthening of State Nursing Councils.
• Strengthening of Nursing Cells at the state level.
The Committee recommends that the Department should make all out efforts
including effective co-ordination and close monitoring so that all the proposals for
strengthening of nursing education are implemented properly and desired results are
achieved for getting adequate number of qualified and trained nursing personnel.
12.8 Committee’s attention has been drawn by media reports about increasing trend of nurses
leaving the country for abroad for rendering their services noticed in the recent years. On a
specific query in this regard, the Committee has been given to understand that the Indian Nursing
Council is proposing to study the trend in consultation with Foreign Nursing Councils.
12.9 The Committee also takes note of incentives like nursing allowance, uniform allowance,
construction of Nurses Residential Complex and grant of two additional increments for acquiring
higher qualification. In addition, National Awards for Nurses has been revived since 2007 as mark
of highest recognition for the meritorious services of the nurses and nursing profession in the
country. While appreciating the initiatives, the Committee would like to point out that out
of total nursing strength of 3015 in Central Government Hospitals in Delhi, only 795
nursing personnel have been provided with accommodation. If such unsatisfactory conditions
are in Delhi, the Committee can well imagine the conditions in State Government Hospitals.
The Committee strongly feels that residential facilities for Nurses need to be augmented at
the earliest. The Committee recommends to the Department to formulate a comprehensive
policy to stop exodus of nurses as also to offer more incentives so as to make the
profession more attractive for arresting this trend.

XIV . RASHTRIYA AROGYA NIDHI
14.1 R ashtriya Arogya Nidhi was set up under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare in 1997
to provide financial assistance to patients living below poverty line, who are suffering from major
life threatening diseases to receive medical treatment in Government Hospitals. Under the scheme
of Rashtriya Arogya Nidhi, grants-in-aid is also provided to State Governments for setting up State
Illness Assistance Funds. Such funds have been set up by the Governments of Andhra Pradesh,
Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Goa, Gujarat, Himachal Pradesh, Madhya Pardesh, Jharkhand, Maharashtra,
Mizoram, Rajasthan, Sikkim, Tamil Nadu, Tripura, West Bengal, Uttarakhand, Haryana, Punjab,
NCT of Delhi and Puducherry. Other States/Union Territories have been requested to set up the
fund, as soon as possible.
14.2 In order to provide immediate financial assistance to the extent of Rs.50,000/-per case, to
critically ill, poor patients who are living below the poverty line and undergoing treatment, the
Medical Superintendents of Dr. Ram Manohar Lohia Hospital, Safdarjung Hospital, Smt. Sucheta
Kriplani Hospital, All India Institute of Medical Sciences New Delhi, PGIMER Chandigarh, JIPMER
Pondicherry, NIMHANS Bangalore, CNCI Kolkata, Sanjay Gandhi Post Graduate Institute of
Medical Lucknow, and CIP Ranchi have been provided with a revolving fund of Rs.10-20 lakhs.
The revolving fund is replenished after its utilization. For cases requiring financial assistance above
Rs.50000/- per case, the applications are processed in the Department of Health and Family Welfare
through a Technical Committee headed by Director General, Health Services before being
considered for approval by a duly constituted Managing Committee with Minister of Health and
Family Welfare as the Chairman. During the year 2006-07, financial assistance to the tune of
Rs. 305.35 lakhs was given directly to 234 patients under Rashtriya Arogya Nidhi.
14.3 The Committee observes that even after more than a decade of setting up of the
Fund with 50% of the contribution made by the State/UT to be provided by Central
Government, there are still several States/UTs which have not set up the State Illness

24
Assistance Fund. Every State/UTs should have such a fund. The Committee would appreciate
if this matter is taken up at the highest level in all such States/UTs.
14.4 The Committee feels that in order to facilitate easy access to quality health care to
the poor and downtrodden strata of our society, the limit of Rs.50,000 under immediate
financial assistance fund, per case, for which funds are placed at the disposal of Medical
Superintendents of above hospitals, need to be enhanced realistically for treatment of
dreaded diseases like AIDS, Cancer etc. Some of the major States like U.P., Assam,
Karnataka, Kerala and Jammu and Kashmir do not have such a fund. With only a very few
major hospitals located in metros having extended facility under the fund, people of such
States/UTs are being deprived of medical care for no fault of theirs. From the details of
funds released to States/UTs during 2005-08, it is very clear that such States are having
negligible funds at their disposal. The Committee wonders about the adequacy of such State
Funds. The Committee is of the view that with the increasing rate of inflation and also
increasing number of patients suffering from major diseases, an assessment of the
Rashtriya Arogya Nidhi should be made at the earliest. Necessary changes may be made
thereafter. The facility of financial assistance should be extended to more hospitals so as
to cover the geographical limits of the country. The Committee also recommends to the
Department to give wide publicity to the scheme specially in the hospital campuses to
generate awareness so that the same can be utilized by the needy and poor patients.
XV. NATIONAL URBAN HEALTH MISSION (NUHM)
15.1 As per 2001 census, 28.6 crores people live in urban areas, out of which 3.26 crores live
in slum areas of the cities/towns having a population of 1 lakh and above, which is expected to
reach 5.01 crores by 2007-08, thus putting greater strain on urban health infrastructure which
already has serious deficiencies. For urban poor, access to Urban Health facilities is severely
restricted due to their being ‘crowded out’ because of the inadequacy of the public health delivery
system; lack of economic resources inhibits/restricts their access to private facilities and lack of
standards and norms for urban health delivery, illegal status, poor environmental condition, over
crowding and environmental pollution makes the urban poor more vulnerable and worse off than
his rural counterpart. During 2008-09, it is proposed to launch the National Urban Health Mission
(NUHM) to address primarily health needs of these segments of population. This will complement
the activities undertaken by NRHM in rural areas. The Programme will be on Public-Private
Partnership mode.
15.2 All Cities with population above 1 lakh and State Capitals would be covered under it. 430
cities with a population of 22 crores with focus on 6.25 crores slum population would benefit.
Duration of the Mission is Eleventh Plan (2008-2012). Urban Poor families living in listed and
unlisted slums, un-authorized colonies and all other vulnerable population such as homeless, rag-
pickers, street children, rickshaw pullers, construction and brick kiln workers, sex workers and
any other temporary migrants would be identified by the Urban Local Body (ULB) concerned or
any other State specific mechanism and shall be issued a photo Family Health Card. Though, no
person would be denied service in the public health facilities, marginalized urban families identified
under the scheme would receive service on concession terms under National Urban Health Mission
(NUHM). Synergies are envisioned with Jawaharlal Nehru Urban Renewal Mission (JNNURM),
SJSRY , Integrated Child Development Scheme (ICDS) Swarna Jayanti Sharkari Rozgar Yojana
(SJSRY), etc. and with the ongoing National Health Programmes for maximizing benefits.
15.3 The Committee notes that the programme has been assigned an approved outlay of
Rs. 4495.00 crores during the Eleventh Plan out of which Rs.50.00 crores are earmarked for
2008-09.

25
15.4 The Committee observes that NUHM is one of the most ambitious Projects after
National Rural Health Mission (NRHM). Objectives of the Mission are laudable and are
according to the requirements of the present scenario. The Committee cautions the
Department to take all necessary steps so that the problems afflicting the implementation
of NRHM like those related to ground level healthcare functionaries, availability of doctors,
paramedics and infrastructure do not recur and interfere in the implementation of this
parallel scheme meant for urban areas. For achieving the targets proposed under mission,
the Department should do proper homework and work out modalities for their
implementation. The Department should start coordinating with the States right from the
beginning of the project. The Committee would like to be apprised about the progress made
in this regard.
XVI. NATIONAL AIDS CONTROL PROGRAMME (NACP)
16.1 The AIDS epidemic has emerged as one of the communicable diseases of immediate
concern. Based on the estimated prevalence rate of 0.36% (0.27% - 0.47%) it is presumed that
there are 2 to 3.1 million HIV infected persons in the country. Adult HIV prevalence is greater than
1 in Manipur (1.68%), Nagaland (1.27%) and Andhra Pradesh (1.06%). Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka,
Maharashtra and Tamil Nadu contribute 63% of the HIV infected persons in the country. Around
39% of the infections are in women and 3.8% in children. Out of the reported AIDS cases in 2007
(Jan-Oct 2007), 87.4% of the infections were transmitted through the sexual route and peri-natal
transmission accounted for 4.7% of infections. 1.8% and 1.7% of infections were acquired through
injecting drug use and contaminated blood and blood products respectively. The HIV prevalence
among high risk groups continues to be nearly 6 to 8 times greater than that among the general
population.
16.2 The National AIDS Control Programme accounts for about 9% of our national health
budget. NACO is scaling up its programmes through Targeted Interventions (TI) for High Risk
Groups, strategizing comprehensive Information, Education and Communication (lEC) packages for
specific segments and scaling up of the service delivery component.
16.3 The Committee was informed that the States of Tamil Nadu and Maharashtra have shown
a decline over a period of time and have recorded less than 1 % HIV prevalence in ANC clinic
attendees. There is decline in the HIV prevalence among ANC clinic attendees in most of the high
burden states, reflecting the impact of interventions. Similar trends are seen in Female Sex Workers
also. However, there are indications of increase in HIV prevalence among ANC population in some
of the low prevalence States. New pockets of HIV infection among ID users have been detected
in States like West Bengal, Punjab, Orissa and Tamil Nadu. The dual mode of transmission has been
observed in North Eastern States. Based on HIV/AIDS prevalence, 156 districts have been classified
in Category ‘A’ and 39 districts in Category ‘B’, which are focus of the programme interventions.
16.4 Currently, there are 571 SACS-funded TIs for FSWs/MSMs/IDUs with a coverage of 42%
and 165 TIs covering bridge populations (migrants/truckers), resulting in a total of 736 TIs. In
addition, by March 2008, it is expected to put in place 284 new TIs. During 2008-09 there will
be a scale up of 53% of core TIs which will ensure 85% coverage as per the present estimates
for core population. The scale up for Non-core TIs will be 58% during 2008-09 which would entail
the setting up of 308 TIs for Commercial sex workers and MSMs, 46 for Injecting Drug Users,
100 for Migrants and 106 for the Truckers totaling 506 interventions.
16.5 The Committee is constrained to note that against a Plan provision of Rs.815.00
crores which was increased to Rs.953.89 cror es at the RE stage during 2007-08 for NACP,
expenditure reported upto 13th March, 2008 was only Rs.767.34 crores. The Committee
observes that optimum utilization has not been achieved in any of the components of

26

16.9 The Committee in its last year’s report  had recommended to the Department to take some
initiative towards starting the second line of treatment so that the sufferings of patients, who have
been receiving Anti-Retroviral Treatment (ART) under the National AIDS Control Programme and
have become drug resistant, can be lessened to some extent. The Committee is given to understand
that NACO has developed a regulatory framework to implement the 2nd line treatment of drug
resistant PLHAs. A Technical Resource Group (TRG) on ART was set up in 2006 at NACO. The
TRG recommended that upfront introduction of second line treatment would be counter productive
as there are several operational issues that need to be addressed in the first instance namely,
training of doctors on second line treatment; establishing laboratories for viral load estimation which
is central to facilitate second line therapy; developing technical and operational guidelines for
providing second line treatment and clinical diagnosis and monitoring tools. The TRG further
recommended that above protocols must be in place before the rollout as drug resistance to second
line therapy has no further recourse and therefore great care needs to be taken to ensure that
patients, to the extent possible, are delayed being put on second line therapy. Complete adherence
to the second line is a must in order to prevent progression of the disease. The necessary
preparatory activities for roll out have now been done such as preparation of technical documents,
monitoring tools and handouts, counselling mat erial, job aids and patient education material. A team
of doctors from two centres was sent to Bangkok for hands-on experience on second line ART.
Drugs for second line ART are being supplied by Clinton Foundation which has an agreement with
UNIT AID, an international non-profit organization which raises funds by collecting tax on airlines
for funding HIV/AIDS treatment. As per regulatory mechanism developed, the patient selection for
second line will be done by a special panel of experts constituted by NACO. A SACEP (S tate AIDS
Clinical Expert Panel) has been established at state level. The panel consists of ART centre in
charge, another expert from outside the centre and programme person from the SACs. The panel
will meet periodically to review the records of patients failing on first line and decide on second
line drugs for these patients. The panel shall ensure that a very strict adherence protocol is
maintained for patients on second line ART and shall monitor them closely for adverse effects.
Hence, the second line roll out has been done at two sites initially-GHTM, Chennai and JJ Hospital,
Mumbai on a pilot basis and it shall be expanded later to other centres based on the experience
gained. The patients will be followed up very strictly and home visit shall also be made in case
of default to treatment. At NACO, the data from both centres is being collected about patient
evaluated for second line, tested for viral load and actually initiated on second line at these two
centres.
16.10 The Committee is happy to note that though delayed, the Department has taken the
desired step towards starting the second line of treatment to lessen the sufferings of drug
resistant patients. The Committee would like to recommend to the Department to put in
place an effective mechanism so that no patient in need of second line ART is deprived of
it.

Counselling Services in Colleges, Work Place stress Management and Suicide prevention services),
Spill over of Tenth Plan schemes of modernization of existing State run mental hospitals and
upgradation of psychiatric wings of Government medical colleges/general hospitals, setting up of
Regional Institutes of Mental Health and Neurosciences on the pattern of NIMHANS by upgrading
8 identified mental health hospitals/institutes, IEC/NGO Participation, Research and Training and
Monitoring and Evaluation.

National Urban Health Mission for optimizing the results. It is proposed to provide grants to a
particular State as per the number of districts/institutes to be funded and the grants would be
released to the State Health Society along with the schemes and guidelines for NMHP. State Nodal
Officer representing the programme in the State Health Society would get the grants released for
various districts and institutions. At the district level, the programme officer would represent the
programme in the District Health Society and facilitate operationalisation of DMHP. It has been
proposed that active participation of credible and community based organizations would be listed
at the State and District level.

XX. NATIONAL PROGRAMME FOR PREVENTION AND CONTROL OF DIABETES,
CARDIOV ASCULAR DISEASES STROKE (NPDCS)
20.1 India is experiencing a rapid health transition, with large and rising burdens of chronic Non-
Communicable Diseases especially Cardiovascular Diseases (CVD), Diabetes Mellitus, Cancer,
Stroke and Chronic Lung Diseases. It is estimated that in 2005 NCDs accounted for 5,466,000
(53%) of all deaths (10,362,000). Considering the fact that Non-Communicable diseases are
surpassing the burden of communicable diseases in the country and the existing health system is
mainly focused on communicable diseases, the National Programme on Prevention and Control of
Diabetes, Cardiovascular Diseases and Stroke was envisaged.
20.2 The pilot programme for prevention and control of cardiovascular diseases, diabetes and
stroke, has been planned with the objectives of providing effective promotion, prevention and
control strategies to provide an integrated action plan for these chronic diseases. The pilot
programme was launched on 4th January, 2008 in 7 St ates with one district each namely Assam
(district-Kamrup), Punjab (district-Jalandhar), Rajasthan (district-Bhilwara), Karnataka (district-
Shimoga), Tamilnadu (district-Kancheepuram), Kerala (Thiruvanathapuram) and Andhra Pradesh
(Nellore {tentatively}). Financial outlay for the pilot phase is Rs.5 crores.
20.3 Programme interventions have been grouped into three components i.e. Health Promotion
for the General Population, Disease Prevention for the High Risk Population and Assessment of
Prevalence of Risk Factors. At the state level, a State Non-Communicable Disease Cell with a nodal
officer will be established. The programme will be run through the District NCD Cell Society set
up under the NRHM. A nodal officer will be assisted by 2 contractual consultants with
competencies to manage two separate units of Health Promotion and Health Prevention/Surveillance
aspects which will constitute the District NCD Cell.
20.4 The Committee is happy to note that the pilot phase of the programme has finally
taken off during 2007-08. The Committee observes that the following targets have been set for
2008-09:—
➢ District Health promotion programme in 50 districts.
➢ Establishment of 20 Dedicated units of CVD/ Diabetes/Stroke Prevention Centers.
➢ Establishment of State NCD cells are proposed to be established at all States and UTs
and also Central level.

35
➢ Setting up of National Institute for Non-Communicable Diseases (NINCD) and Health
Promotion council of India.
20.5 The Committee notes that out of an approved outlay of Rs.1660.50 crores for the
Eleventh Five Y ear Plan, only Rs.30.00 crores have been earmarked for 2008-09. This, when
taken into account along with last year’s utilization of Rs.4.42 crores, leaves behind a
whopping amount of Rs.1625.50 crores for the last three years of the plan. The Committee
is given to understand that a steering Committee has been established to review and
expedite the Programme. A meeting of the States participating in the pilot project was held
on 17th October, 2007. Appreciating this initiative, the Committee recommends to the
Department to carry forward the  p rogramme vigorously during the remaining period of the
Plan so that the set targets are achieved with the optimum utilization of funds available for
the programme.
XXI. MEDICAL EDUCATION
21.1 The State Governments have the main responsibility for providing proper public health care
delivery system and also setting up of teaching institutions in the medical as well as para medical
spheres. The Central Government is involved in regulating the standards of medical and para
medical education. Under the Indian Medical Council Act, 1956, regulations have been framed
containing norms for setting up of new medical colleges and also prescribing the medical
curriculum. In the context of severe shortage of manpower resources in the country, the
Government is in the process of updating these regulations so as to increase the seat capacity of
medical students and to improve the standards of the institutions including the medical curriculum,
provide relaxation in regulations for encouraging promotion of new colleges in hilly areas in various
deficient States and facilitate public-private partnership in setting up of these colleges.
21.2 The Committee is informed that out of an yearly requirement of about 60,000 MBBS
doctors only about 32,000 are passing out of the Medical Institutions. Further only about 3500 post
graduate level seats are available to them, which is a big gap.
21.3 Committee takes note of the following initiatives of the Department regarding the reforms
in medical education particularly in the under served areas and high focus States under the NRHM
as well as the North Eastern States:—
➢ Compulsory rural posting for doctors for one year for availing PG admission.
➢ To enhance PG seats and establish new PG Disciplines, Central funding to be given to
State Government Medical Colleges.
➢ MCI regulation under modification.
(i) UG medical educational regulation
(ii) PG medical educational regulation
(iii) Starting of new medical college
(iv) Minimum qualification of medical teachers education
➢ Relaxation of MCI norms in setting up medical colleges in NE States and high focus
States under NRHM.
➢ Allowing corporate entities to set up Medical Colleges.
➢ Allowing public private partnerships with Government/District Hospitals.

36
➢ Allowing private promoters to have land in 2 pieces within 10 Kms. of each other.
➢ Recognition of foreign PG Degrees.
➢ Up-dating UG and PG Curriculum.
21.4 The Committee is aware that keeping in view the shortage of doctors and existing
medical institutions not being adequate enough, MCI norms for opening of colleges/increase
of seats need to be reviewed. The Committee, however, feels that this exercise should be
undertaken with extreme caution so that objective of imparting quality medical education
remains intact. Relaxing norms by allowing private promoters to have land in two pieces
within 10 Kms. of each other and allowing corporate entities to setup medical colleges are
initiatives which should be implemented after examining all pros and cons. The Committee
is of the opinion that in the exercise of relaxation of existing norms, assessment of those
experts having the experience of this field should be given due weightage.
21.5 The Committee also takes note of the suggestion of the Department to MCI for
relaxing the age of retirement of staff of Private Medical Educational Institutes from 65 to
70 years, subject to their physical ability, in order to fill-up the acute shortage of teaching
staff in that sector. Secretary, Department of Health and Family Welfare has also informed
the Committee that a Cabinet Note has been prepared for increasing the age of retirement
to 65 years in Government Medical Educational Institutes. Committee is also given to
understand that PG degrees of USA, UK, Australia, New Zealand and Canada have been
recognized and for other countries like Germany and France the matter is under
consideration. The idea is that they can come and settle here or they can come as visiting
faculties. The Committee welcomes these steps.
21.6 The Comm ittee has been informed that on a request of the Indian Ambassador in China, a
14 Member delegation visited China during 3rd June- 16th June, 2007 to assess the standard of
medical education available for Indian students in China. As per the report of the delegation, the
medical curriculum, medium of instruction, examination system and standard of medical education
imparted in China is different from the one prescribed in India. The Committee had a strong
apprehension that this would have a bearing on the quality of Indian healthcare when the doctors
educated in China practice medicine after their return to India. On being asked as to whether
any mechanism was in place to check this, the Secretary, Department of Health and Family
Welfare stated that at present there is no mechanism to prevent Indian students from going
abroad to study. The Committee is of the view that the Department needs to devise an
effective mechanism, which could include legislation, so that Indian medical students can be
prevented from going to such places whose educational system does not match with ours.
The Committee would like to be informed about the steps taken by the Department in this
regard.
21.7 On a specific query, the Committee is given to understand that at present there are 271
medical colleges in the country, out of which MBBS degree of 79 medical colleges are yet to be
recognized and 192 medical colleges in the country are already recognized under IMC Act 1956
and included in the First Schedule to the Act. There are 27 medical colleges where the first batch
of MBBS students has appeared for final examination but are yet to be recognized. Out of these
27 medical colleges, Medical Council of India has sent its recommendations to the Central
Government for recognition of MBBS degree in respect of 9 medical colleges, which is under
consideration of the Ministry. The Committee is anguished to note that the fate of so many
students of the remaining 18 medical colleges, who have already appeared in their final
examination, remains undecided. The Committee is of the view that the students should not
suffer due to such technicalities and bureaucratic hurdles. A decision without any further

37
delay may be taken in the matter. A Status Note on such colleges may also be submitted
to the Committee.
21.8 The Committee notes that the National Knowledge Commission has submitted a number of
recommendations with respect to areas of improvement in medical education in India, as indicated
below:—
• System of regulation of medical education by MCI is neither adequate nor appropriate.
A standing committee within the structure of the Independent Regulatory Authority for
Higher Education (IRAHE) may be constituted. MCI should function only as a
professional association with power to conduct nationwide exams and to give licenses
to prospective doctors.
• There should be only one All India Common Entrance Test including both Government
and Private medical colleges.
• An independent and standardized National Exit Exam immediately after the University
Exam to serve also as a postgraduate entrance exam.
• Continuing medical Education should be revamped based on distance learning. Research
centers should be set up at medical colleges with Central Assistance.
• Five regional centers for teacher training/faculty development should be set up.
• A list of priority sites for establishing medical colleges should be made by Central
Government for taking necessary follow up action.
• One institution should be identified in each State that can serve as a Centre of
excellence and role model for the other institutions of the State.
• Every district hospital should have an attached nursing school.
• A three tiered structure consisting of a one year diploma course, a three year B.Sc.
course and a three year Master’s Course may be introduced.
21.9 The Committee opines that if implemented, the recommendations of the Commission would
be a milestone in improving the standards and quality of medical education in India. The Committee
recommends that action may be initiated in this regard and Committee apprised accordingly.

22.4 The Committee has been receiving a large number of representations, particularly from the
GDMO cadre regarding very bleak chances of their career progression. The Committee is given to
understand that SAG level promotions to the GDMOs in Central Health Services is not at par with
other All India services. On a specific query regarding this, the Committee was informed by the

40
Secretary that the Department is aware that in GDMO cadre there are doctors who have PG
degrees and in many cases they are working as specialists also, but still they are not on the fast
track of career progression like specialists. The reason cited by the Secretary for this was that
while they are offered GDMO post after selection by UPSC on the basis of their MBBS degree,
they apply for PG courses and seek joining time till they complete their PG degree, which is usually
granted to them. But after two years they still join as GDMO and not as specialists. The Committee
is informed that the Department is looking into the demands of such GDMOs positively. As regards
their demand for enhancing the age of superannuation to 62 years, the Committee was assured that
the Department is going to take the issue to the Cabinet very soon. The Committee is further given
to understand that the recommendation of the Fifth Pay Commission that SAG level positions in
All India service should be 17% of total cadre strength could not be implemented. The Department
had initiated for up gradation of these posts and creation of extra posts at SAG and HAG level
to plug the gap arising due to Fifth Pay Commission recommendations. However, due to a stay in
a court case no fresh appointment could be made in SAG. Further, now the Sixth Pay Commission
has recommended that if additional posts are to be created to fulfill any gap, these should be
created in such a manner that they are filled up by direct recruitment. Further the Department has
expressed its practical difficulty in identifying supervisory level posts in approximately 40
participating units under Central Health Services so as to justify higher level of promotions. The
Committee is informed that due to this practical difficulty, they are moving for a proposal for one
time in-situ promotion which means that though they will be at dispensary level, they will get one
time promotional benefit of SAG grade.
22.5 The Committee views with serious concern the grave injustice done to the GDMO
cadre for no fault of theirs. Inspite of their being eligible for specialist post, continuance
of such doctors in GDMO cadre is indeed against all principles of natural justice. Non-
implementation of Fifth Pay Commission recommendation of SAG level positions in All
India Service to be 17% of total cadre has created another hurdle in their career
progression. The Committee finds that Sixth Pay Commission’s recommendation of filling
up the additional posts to be created for fulfilling any gap, by direct recruitment, will make
the position of GDMOs very vulnerable. The Committee is of the firm opinion that the
Department should take up this issue immediately with the Ministry of Finance. Every
attempt should be made to remove the grave injustice done to the GDMO cadre so that this
sub-cadre of professionals gets due recognition and morale boost like others in All India
Services.

PART-B
NATIONAL RURAL HEALTH MISSION (NRHM)
AND FAMILY WELFARE PROGRAMMES
1. The National Rural Health Mission was operationalised in April 2005 throughout the country.
The Mission covers the rural areas of the entire country with special focus on 18 States viz.
8 Empowered Action Group States (Bihar, Jharkhand, M.P., Chhattisgarh, U.P., Uttarakhand, Orissa
and Rajasthan) 8 North-East States, Himachal Pradesh and Jammu and Kashmir. The main objective
under the Mission is to provide universal access to equitable, affordable and quality healthcare
delivery, especially to the poor and the vulnerable sections of the society, bridge gaps in healthcare,
facilitate decentralized planning in the health sector, ensure population stabilization, gender balance
and bring about inter-sectoral convergence. The NRHM also provides an overarching umbrella to
the existing programmes of Health and Family Welfare including RCH-II, V ector Borne Disease
Control Programme, TB, Leprosy, NPCB and the Integrated Disease Surveillance Project.
Mainstreaming of AYUSH is also one of the strategies under the Mission.

below:
➢ Reducing Maternal Mortality Ratio (MMR) to 1 per 1000 live births.
➢ Reducing Infant Mortality Rate (IMR) to 28 per 1000 live Births against the target of
30 per 1000 live berth fixed under NRHM.
➢ Reducing Total Fertility Rate to 2.1.
➢ Raising the sex ratio for age group 0-6 to 935 by 2011-12 and 950 by 2016-17.
➢ Providing clean drinking water for all by 2009 and ensuring no slip-backs.
➢ Reducing malnutrition among children of age group 0-3 to half its present level.
➢ Reducing anemia among women and girls by 50%.
