III. INFRASTRUCTURE STRENTHENING
3.1 NRHM aims at strengthening of Primary Health Infrastructure and improving effective
service delivery across the country. Sub-centers, Primary Healthcare Centers and Community
Health Centres are the three pillars on which rural infrastructure is built upon. As on March. 2007,
there are 1,45,272 Sub-Centers, 22,370 PHCs and 4045 CHCs in the country. There is a shortfall
of 20,855 Sub-Centres, 6491 PHCs and 2525 CHCs in the country based on the 2001 population
norms. The Committee has been constantly drawing the attention of the Department to the uneven
spread of these centres across the country with prominent gaps in the High Focus States. The
Committee finds that there is no marked improvement in this regard.
The Committee has been expressing its serious concern on the continuance of lack of rural
health infrastructure, especially in the High Focus States where the need is the most. On being
asked to identify the problem areas, the Committee has been informed that health infrastructure and
allocation of health workers under NRHM is planned on the population, workload and distance
norms. Shortages on the basis of 2001 population are quantified as the difference between the
required number of facilities/providers as per the norms and those that are functioning or in
position. This method of determining norms and shortage does not take into account the varying
epidemiological, geographical and socio-demographic patterns across the different States!
Communities and between rural and urban areas within States. The actual availability of different
types of providers or the extent of private/voluntary sector involvement in health care delivery at
the community level is also not taken into account. The Committee notes that against the backdrop
of these very visible deficiencies, norms for setting up of the Sub-Centres and PHCs have been
modified by the Steering Committee of the Planning Commission. These norms to be adopted
during the Eleventh Plan have been duly approved by the Planning Commission also. The
Committee has been given to understand that population-centric norms are replaced with
flexible norms comprising habitation-based needs, community based needs and disease-pattern
based needs.
3.2 The Committee welcomes the modification in the criteria for assessing the
requirement of health infrastructure in the country. In a vast country like ours, rigid
norms based on population only and made uniformly applicable were perhaps not proving to
be justified and not based on ground realities. The Committee is also of the view that
change in the norms for health infrastructure proposed by the Planning Commission was
called for. The Committee is, however, not aware whether any preparatory exercise has been
initiated for conducting surveys as per the revised norms. The Committee is afraid that if
this issue is allowed to linger on for long, the very objective of NRHM of bridging gaps in
the health care will continue to be a distant dream. The Committee, accordingly, impresses
upon the Department to initiate action at the earliest.

ASHA
3.11 One of the most important strategic interventions under the National Rural Health Mission
is ASHA—a social health activist. ASHA is envisaged as a trained woman community health
volunteer who will reinforce community action for universal immunization, safe delivery, new born
care, prevention of water borne disease and communicable disease, improved nutrition and
promotion of household toilets. She is required to inform, interact, mobilize and facilitate improved
access to preventive and promotive healthcare and also provide basic curative care through her
drug kits. She will assist in formulation of village health plan by the Village Health and Sanitation
Committee. ASHA will also promote awareness and usage of ISM. The requirement for ASHA is
one per thousand population with relaxation to this norm depending upon the workload and terrain.
ASHA is envisaged to be a primary resident of the village who would be selected by the Gram
Sabha following an intense community mobilization process. She will be fully accountable to the
Panchayats. ASHA has been a major intervention for the ten high focus States namely Uttar
Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Bihar, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Orissa, Rajasthan, Assam
and Jammu and Kashmir.

51
3.12 Capacity building of ASHA is critical in enhancing her effectiveness as a link between the
community and the health facility. The initial orientation training is for a period of 23 days spread
in 5 rounds over a period of 12 months and followed by periodic re-training for about 2 days once
every alternate month, apart from the on-the-job training she would be getting. Training modules
for this purpose have been developed based on a thematic approach and States have also
constituted district and block training teams for this purpose. The Department has informed the
Committee, during its discussion on demand for grants, that selection of 5,87,512 ASHA has been
completed, 4,90,000 ASHA have completed their first round training and 2,18,339 ASHA have been
provided with drug kits.
The Committee is happy to note the progress made by the Department on the ASHA
initiative under NRHM. It is also happy to note that 86.41% ASHA have been trained in
their first module post induction training till 12th March, 2008. The Committee observes
that ASHAs have to undergo three more rounds of training. So far, only 27% ASHAs have
undergone 2nd round of training. The Committee is of the view that every effort needs to
be made to ensure that second round of training of all the ASHAs is completed at the
earliest.
The Committee has its apprehensions regarding the effectivity of ASHA as a multi-
purpose social health activist, as envisaged under the NRHM. The Committee observes that
job responsibilities of ASHA are manifold as indicated below :—
– awareness generation- Health, RCH, HIV/AIDS.
– advising newly married couples for their special needs.
– guiding pregnant women for availing of institutional facilities for Ante-Natal,
Natal and Post-Natal needs.
– counselling on nutrition, pregnancy, breast-feeding, immunization and family
planning.
– establishing link with PHCs, private providers and others for service requirement
of beneficiaries.
– mobilising parents for child survival interventions.
– promoting basic sanitization.
– provision of non-clinical spacing contraceptives.
– surveillance of communicable diseases.
3.13 ASHA is also the primary provider for National Health Programme. She is the Depot
Holder for health commodities like Vitamin A, Impregnated bed nets, ORS etc. She is also
supposed to handle treatment of minor ailments. Another  major task assigned to ASHA is
to provide escort services for women seeking delivery services at institutions, requiring
emergency care and MTP services, women and men for clinical contraception services and
VCTC. The Committee has been given to understand that States have also taken up the
training of ASHAs on diagnosis of malaria cases. For being eligible for ASHA, a woman has
to be 25 to 35 years of age, married, resident of the village, acceptable to the village and
community and proficient in reading and writing. The Committee fails to understand as to
how a single woman, who is a simple villager can take care of one thousand population by
performing such wide-ranging tasks. Situation becomes more complex and well away from
ground realities, when one finds that only remuneration payable to ASHA is for providing
Escort Services. Instances of Escort Services may not be very frequent some times. The
Committee strongly feels that ASHA is supposed to play a very challenging role.

52
3.14 The Committee is of the view that with the passage of time, the number of
responsibilities of ASHA will itself become a challenge for her to cope up with. This will not
only reflect in the quality of her work and performance but ultimately fail in fulfilling the
very objectives with which the initiative was initially conceptualized. As the initiative is still
in the early stages, the Committee suggests that the Department should review the
responsibilities entrusted to the ASHA. Committee’s attention has been drawn by the
findings of Common Review Mission which conducted appraisal of NRHM in November,
2007,16 months after NRHM got final Cabinet approval in July, 2006. Appraisal was based
on one-two districts in A.P., Assam, Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Orissa, M.P., Gujarat, J&K,
Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu, Tripura, U.P. and West Bengal. The Committee notes that
performance assessment of ASHA has led to mixed findings in different States. Non-
payment against activities/conflicts regarding compensation money and lack of role clarity
between ASHAs and AWWs are two major  problem ar eas identified. The Committee
apprehends that situation may worsen with more complexities arising in future. The
Committee is, therefore, of the view that role of ASHA needs to be reassessed and
reformulated.

would also be a good idea if two-three performing and non-performing districts in each State
are taken together for making an comparative analysis. Incorporation of surprise visits will
make the assessment more realistic.
IV. NATIONAL VECTOR BORNE DISEASE CONTROL PROGRAMME (NVBDCP)

guidance and for monitoring and evaluation of programme implementation in respect of prevention
and control of the vector borne diseases. The States are responsible for planning, implementation

allocation of funds for control of a major disease does not seem to make any sense if year
after year same constraints seem to persist. The Committee once again tries to impress
upon the Department to take immediate steps for removal of bottlenecks in the successful
implementation of Malaria Control Programme. The Committee would like to mention
that under the National Vector Borne Disease Control Programme, major component is

55
Malaria Control having the maximum allocation of Rs. 351.68 crore out of a provision of
Rs. 440.03 crores for the entire programme in 2008-09. Therefore, it is in the fitness of
things that concerted efforts are also made for optimum and judicious utilisation of
allocated funds.
4.4 As per the information furnished in the Outcome Budget, the annual incidence of Malaria
currently is around 1.80 million cases and about 80% of malaria cases and deaths are reported
from the N.E. States, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, Orissa, Andhra Pradesh,
Maharashtra, Gujarat, Rajasthan, West Bengal and Karnataka. During 2007 (till November), the
impact indicator Annual Parasite Incidence (API) i.e., the number of malaria cases per year per
1000 population, stood at 0.89 per thousand population. The fact that comes to the notice of the
Committee is that the number of Pf-positive cases has been steady between 40-50 per cent over
the last four years and during 2007, the number of Pf-positive cases that were reported till
December is more than 50%. Not only this, in many pockets in the highly endemic States, the
disease has developed resistance to Chloroquine—the chief malarial drug.

the NE States and Assam, Andhra Pradesh, Orissa and West Bengal for the year 2007 is given below:

The Committee is alarmed by the trend of Pf cases reported from these States.
Committee’s attention has also been drawn to quantum jump of number of malaria deaths
reported in the country. In 2006, 1639 deaths were reported against 963 deaths occurring
in 2005. By November, 2007, this figure has already reached 807. The Committee has every
reason to apprehend that actual figures of deaths may be higher than what is officially
recorded. Reason being there is no mechanism at present to independently verify the field
level figures for any State.
4.6 The Committee has been persistently drawing the attention of the Department to the
urgent need for implementation of all malaria control measures in Malaria endemic States
of NE Region, Orissa and West Bengal. The Committee is well aware that NE States
together contribute 4% of the country’s population, 12% of malaria cases, 18% of Pf cases
and 54% of the total malaria related deaths reported in the country during 2006. Figures
must have remained unchanged in 2007 also. Another  cause of concern is increasing trend

56
of resistance to conventional anti-malarial drug Chloroquine noticed in NE States. The
Committee notes that Global Fund supported Intensified Malaria Control Project in NE
States being implemented since July, 2005 with a contribution of US $ 30 million for the
first two years of the project also seems to have failed to have the desired impact.
4.7 The Committee notes that increased supervision and monitoring is one of the main
strategies adopted for effective control of malaria. The latest figures made available to the
Committee reveal continuance of shortage of surveillance and supervisory staff in NE
States. In Assam, the biggest State of NE Region, against the sanctioned posts of 694 Health
Supervisor (Male) only 570 were in position, against 343 Health Supervisor (Female), there
were 316 and only 1647 MPW(M) against 3080 sanctioned posts. What is more disturbing is
that while Tripura failed to furnish the data, Meghalaya and Nagaland have provided
incomplete information. The primary role of MPW (M) and MPW(F) is door to door
surveillance and detection of communicable diseases and it’s reporting. The fact that these
functionaries play a vital role in disease detection and surveillance cannot be ignored. By
not appointing these functionaries, the States leave a big gap at the field-level disease
surveillance, detection and treatment. This vital issue needs to be pursued at the highest
level in the concerned States. The other strategy adopted is use of Rapid Diagnostic Kits
by ASHAs. The Committee does not have high expectation from this initiative as firstly
required number of ASHAs have to be in place in malaria endemic States and even if they
are there, they would be over-burdened with the various tasks already assigned to them.
The Committee fails to comprehend the continuance of such a discouraging situation inspite
of special dispensation for NE States. The Committee can only reiterate that there is need
for drastic measures and extensive monitoring under the supervision of State Nodal
Officers.
Kala-azar
4.8 Kala-azar is a slow progressing indigenous the disease caused by protozoan parasite
leishmania donovani and spread by its vector—the Sandfly. The National Health Policy (2002) has
set the goal for elimination of Kala-azar from the country by 2010. An amount of Rs.20.86 crores
was earmarked in 2007-08 for combating the disease and which has been enhanced to Rs. 29.51
crores in 2008-09. Kala-azar is endemic in 33 districts in Bihar, 4 districts in Jharkhand, 5 districts
of Uttar Pradesh and 11 districts of West Bengal (total 53 districts) besides sporadically occurring
in a few other areas.
4.9 The Committee has been observing increasing trend of Kala-azar cases. In 2006, 39178
cases and 187 deaths were reported with 162 deaths occurring in Bihar alone. Position seems to
have worsened further in 2007. Upto November, 2007, already 35,638 cases with 158 deaths have
been reported. State-wise figures upto May, 2007 indicate that out of 79 deaths reported till then,
64 deaths have occurred in Bihar. While the Committee would not dispute the Department’s stand
that intensive surveillance has led to reporting of increased number of cases, the fact remains that
treatment compliance of Kala-azar cases detected is far from satisfactory in view of alarming rate
of deaths being reported. A number of initiatives undertaken for Kala-azar elimination seem to have
made no impact with ground reality continuing to be as discouraging as before. The Committee
understands that 200 villages of 9 districts reporting large number of Kala-azar cases have been
selected for focused interventions. The Committee strongly feels that effective surveillance,
timely treatment and compliance of treatment regimens in all PHCs would lead to better
reports in 2008. The Committee is of the view that only if intensive monitoring at all levels
is carried out, the goal of elimination of Kala-azar by 2010 can be made achievable.
Situation so far has not been very encouraging. All the quantifiable objectives listed in the
Action Plan for 2008-09 need to be closely monitored on monthly basis.

57
Japanese Encephalitis
4.10 Japanese Encephalitis (JE) is a viral disease with a tendency of seasonal outbreaks. JE has
been reported repeatedly from 15 States out of which, Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Haryana, Karnataka,
Kerala, Maharashtra, Manipur, Tamil Nadu, Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal have been reporting
repeated outbreaks. There is no specific anti-viral drug for JE and cases are managed
symptomatically. Efforts have been directed to provide technical support and strengthen capabilities
of State through training to tackle this disease. A vaccination programme for children between 1
and 15 years of age under the Universal Immunization Programme, using single dose live attenuated
SA-14-l4-2 vaccine has been launched in 2006. In 2006, 11 districts in 4 States were covered
which was expanded to 28 districts in 10 States during 2007. A total of 93.08 lakhs children were
vaccinated against the target of 105.31 lakhs children achieving 88.39% coverage. As per the
Annual Report, 2007-08, the vaccination campaign has so far been completed in Assam (89%),
Haryana (86%), West Bengal (61%) and in 7 districts of Uttar Pradesh (99.7%).
The Committee is dismayed to note that despite various methods adopted by the
Department over the past year to contain the disease, the number of cases reported to be
suffering from JE/ AES has shown an increase over the previous year figures. The fact is
even more disturbing that though the Department claims to have completed 99.97%
immunization in the past year in 7 worst affected districts in Uttar Pradesh, the situation
there has worsened with 2675 cases and 577 deaths in 2007 (till December) over the 2006
figures of 2320 cases and 528 deaths. The Committee fails to comprehend as to why inspite
of a number of preventive measures taken by the Central Government in co-ordination with
the State Government of Uttar Pradesh, the JE/AES related cases and deaths continue to
be high in the State. The Committee apprehends that the actual figures would increase the
tally much further. The Committee would like to take the opportunity to state that though
the data for Assam has not been made available by the Department, going by the fact sheet
of 2006, it is apprehensive that the situation in Assam would also show a similar trend as
that of U.P.
4.11 The Committee would like to draw the attention of the Department to the fact that
the year 2006 had reported a visible impact of preventive measures initiated by registering
a declining trend when compared with 2005 figures. Quantum jump in the first three
quarter of 2007 calls for a serious review with special focus on Assam and U.P., the two
main endemic States. The Committee would impress upon the Department that analysis of
epidemiological and entomological data for epidemic outbreak prediction and timely remedial
measures is required to be carried out on an urgent basis.
The Committee feels that perhaps the precautionary methods adopted by the
Department have not percolated properly to the affected population because of which the
disease has once again registered an increase. The Committee adds that lax monitoring of
the disease by the Central as well as the State Government could aggravate the situation
further unless it is dealt with a sense of urgency. It suggests the Department to undertake
on-the-spot review of the situation as to the possible causes for upsurge in the reported
cases. The Committee urges the Department to step-up the ongoing IEC activities in the
endemic States so that the desired objective is reached soon.
Dengue/Dengue Haemorrhagic Fever/Chikungunya
4.12 Dengue/Dengue Haemorrhagic Fever is an acute viral infection transmitted by Aedes aegypti
mosquitoes that breed in man-made containers in which water stagnates for more than a week.
Dengue is endemic in 18 States/UTs with the population of about 450 million at risk. During 2005,
there were outbreaks in many parts of the country reporting 11985 cases and 157 deaths in 2005.

58
Year 2006 has also reported 12,317 cases and 184 deaths. In 2007 up to November 4574 cases
and 59 deaths have been reported.
4.13 Chikungunya is a debilitating, viral illness spread by the bite of infected mosquitoes. The
disease resemble dengue fever and is characterized by severe, sometimes persistent, joint pain
(arthritis) as well as fever and rash. Chikungunya fever has re-emerged in 16 States in the country
during 2006 in epidemic form after about three decades. The reported number of suspected
Chikungunya fever cases in the country in 2006 was 1.39 million. 15961 samples were tested out
of which 2001 were found positive for Chikungunya. During the year 2007 upto November, 56355
suspected Chikungunya fever cases have been reported. 7482 samples were tested, out of which
1876 were confirmed cases.
4.14 The overall strategies for prevention and control of Chikungunya are same as in Dengue
such as symptomatic management of cases, reduction of breeding sources, personal protection
and intensive IEC and capacity building. The Committee notes that against an allocation of
Rs.2.50 crores during 2007-08, the allocation for 2008-09 has been enhanced to Rs.14.59 crores.
The Committee has been given to understand that Dengue and Chikungunya are outbreak prone
viral diseases which require adequate IEC activities, capacity building, strengthening of sentinel and
Apex Laboratories and supply of diagnostic test kits.
4.15 Several steps were reported to have been taken during the last year to tackle Dengue and
Chikungunya, which include:
• Regional monitoring and identification of 13 Apex Referral Laboratories for advanced
diagnosis and regular surveillance of Dengue and Chikungunya fever cases and 110
sentinel surveillance hospitals for pro-active surveillance.
• States advised for intensive IEC activities through print, electronic media, Inter-personal
communication, outdoor publicity as well as Inter-sectoral collaboration with civil
society organizations (NGOs/CBOs/Self-Help Groups), Panchayati Raj Institutions
(PRIs), for taking community based measures.
The Committee also notes that an emergency package of Rs.21.60 crores was sanctioned
to the affected States for items like Fogging Machines, Pyrethrum Extract, Temephos and
Insecticide-treated bed nets and IEC activity.
4.16 State-wise analysis of suspected Chikungunya cases and number of confirmed cases during
2006 and 2007 reveals a very disturbing trend about the spread of this disease. In 2006, maximum
number of confirmed cases were reported from Maharashtra (804) followed by Karnataka (298)
and Gujarat (225). In contrast, Kerala reported the highest number of confirmed cases of 909 while
there are 347 confirmed cases occurring in West Bengal in 2007 uptil November. Another cause
of serious concern is overall increase in total number of confirmed Chikungunya cases from 2001
in 2006 to 1876 in 2007 (upto November).
4.17 Incidence of Chikungunya cases in the country during 2006 and 2007 has led the
Committee to the conclusion that various initiatives taken by the Department have so far
failed to yield any desired results. The Committee strongly feels that with the enhanced
allocation of Rs. 14.59 crore in 2008-09 for Dengue and Chikungunya, effective measures
are required to be undertaken in the affected States. Mere circulation of detailed guidelines
and advisories for prevention and control of these diseases to all affected States would not
serve any purpose. What is required is to identify the affected districts and go for regular
fever surveillance in such endemic areas to detect an unusual trend. The Committee is of
the view that if this analysis of ground reality is followed by IEC activities and
strengthening of apex Referral Institutions for diagnosis and treatment, number of Dengue/

59
Chikungunya cases would show a declining trend. The Committee apprehends that unless
adequate remedial measures are taken, sporadic outburst of these diseases would continue
to be reported from different States every year.
V. NATIONAL T.B. CONTROL PROGRAMME
5.1 T.B is a major health problem in India. India accounts for 1/5th of the global incidence of
T.B. cases. As per the latest estimates, there are approximately 18 lakh new cases every year in
the country. Two persons die from T.B. in India every three minutes, more than 1000 people every
day, and almost 3,70,000 every year.
5.2 To control this major health problem of the country, Revised National TB Control Programme
is being implemented. Phase-II of the project (period October, 2005 to September, 2011) has
a total outlay of Rs.1,156 crores which includes credit from World Bank of Rs.756 crores and
commodity assistance of anti-TB drugs from DFID through WHO for Rs. 287 crores with balance
of Rs.191 crores being given by GoI. In addition, Rs.385.5 crores through GFATM and USAID
have also been provided. Phase-II of RNTCP is a step towards achieving the TB related Millennium
Development Goal (MDG) targets. DOTS remain the core strategy. The Department has informed
that the total allocation under the Programme during 2007-08 was to the tune of Rs.267 crores
with expenditure of Rs.237.20 crores reported upto 29th February, 2008.
5.3 The Committee notes that around 4,03,917 patients have been put on treatment during 2nd
quarter of 2007 saving around 65,000 lives. More than 1,20,000 patients are being put on DOTS
every month. One of the major initiatives taken is the involvement of 2421 NGOs and 15,900
private practitioners working under the programme under Government approved NGO/ PP
Guidelines. Over 240 medical colleges are participating in the programme. Besides that, all the 16
centrally owned ESI Hospitals, Zonal Railway Hospitals, Coal, Steel and Mines Health Facilities,
Port Trust Hospitals, CGHS Hospitals and 150 Corporate Hospitals, BHEL, NTPC, Ranchi Armed
Forces Hospital are involved in RNTCP.
5.4 The Committee appreciates the successful implementation of RNTCP Phase-I and
ongoing Phase-II. Several initiatives/interventions taken at different levels and variety of
implementing agencies have contributed to the increasing population coverage and 85%
cure rate. However, India still contributes 20% of TB cases reported in the world. Out of
8.8 million cases per annum, 1.8 million cases are from India alone. New complex off shoots
of TB also keep on emerging, the most visible being worsening HIV epidemic increasing the
number of TB cases. The Committee notes that HIV is the most potent risk factor for
progression of TB infection to disease form. HIV-TB patients detected in 2005 were 12,062,
13,614 in 2006 and 18,559 in 2007. The Committee is aware that increase in number of
co-infected (HIV-TB) patients being detected over the last three years is a result of
innovative and co-ordinated measures taken by the Department. But the other dimension
of this trend is increasing complexities involved in the treatment of such cases. The
Committee hopes that the National Framework formulated by RNTCP and NACP for joint
TB/HIV collaborative activities will lead to better and effective control of this emerging
problem area.
5.5 The Committee observes that the other major challenge to TB control in the country
is increasing number of MDR- TB cases. The Committee is aware that such cases are bound
to increase the magnitude and severity of TB epidemic and pose a major threat to TB
control. The Committee in its earlier Report has pointed out that 7% defaulters in a year
is quite a significant number of cases remaining untreated or half-treated. With a single
TB patient infecting 10-15 persons in a year, rate of infection is bound to increase. The
Committee would like to point out that formulation of guidelines for management of MDR

60
TB cases and publication thereof will not prove to be sufficient enough. The Committee had
given a simple suggestion for identifying the defaulter TB patients from the records being
maintained at centres/ hospitals with the help of NGOs/Social Workers and Private
Practitioners. Intention of the Committee was to identify such cases at the first default
stage itself. The Committee finds that under a new initiative a total of 50 MDR- TB patients
were to be registered for treatment in Gujarat and Maharashtra during 2007-08 to be
doubled every year subsequently and ultimately in the entire country. While welcoming this
initiative, the Committee would also like to point out that cost of MDR- TB treatment is
300 times more than non-MDR TB. The Committee can only say that preventive measures
will be both cost-effective and helpful for the patients. The Committee is of the firm
opinion that through effective IEC activities and alertness of health workers regular intake
of medicines can be easily monitored. The Committee, therefore, suggests that monitoring
of TB patients the most vital aspect, should not be ignored at any cost.
5.6 The Committee is disappointed to note that in spite of repeated cautioning by it
regarding the issue of unspent balances being carried forward to the next year there has
been no improvement in the situation. Despite various measures like training of

the Routine Programme Evaluations be carried out by the States (2 districts per quarter) and the

suggest proper utilisation of the funds allocated under the scheme. In reply to the above

to utilization of funds and activities undertaken by the NGOs. The Committee would like the

utilization of funds and activities undertaken by the NGOs. The Committee would also like
to suggest here some measures for increasing advocacy, communication and social
mobilisation. It recommends that the Department should sit with the Private Print and
Media sector and should work out modalities as to how they can be involved in the IEC
activities for the programme.
5.8 Reacting to a query on the status of research by the Tuberculosis Research Centre, Chennai
that is currently involved in the designing stage of a new TB drug the Department has informed
that Johnson & Johnson pharmaceuticals approached Tuberculosis Research Centre, Chennai (TRC)
with the protocol for the multi-centric trial for A Phase II, placebo-controlled, double blind,
randomized trial to evaluate the anti-bacterial activity, safety and tolerability of TMC 207 in subjects
with sputum smear positive pulmonary infection with multi-drug resistant Mycobacterium
tuberculosis (MDR-TB). After extensive discussions with senior researchers at TRC followed by
the members of 35th Scientific Advisory Committee (SAC) of TRC in Nov 2007 as well as by a
Sub-Committee constituted by the SAC, the protocol now is ready to be presented to the
Institutional Ethics Committee (lEC) TRC in the month of March, 2008. In the meantime, the Drug
Controller of GoI has given clearance for the trial. It is likely to start in the month of May, 2008.
The Committee is happy to note that the pharma company Johnson & Johnson has
undertaken the responsibility for developing a drug for treatment of patients with Multi-
Drug Resistant TB. The Committee has been given to understand that the cost of treatment
of MDR- TB patients is very high. The Committee feels that the issue of cost effectiveness
of the drug needs to be examined simply because patients in India are generally poor and
lack means to afford the drugs. Under the circumstances, the affordability of the drug could
be construed as a blessing for the poor and downtrodden.
5.9 Committee’s attention has also been drawn by Studies like Social Assessment Study,
Institutional Assessment Study in respect of TB Control measures undertaken so far. The
Committee would like to point out that TB infection is no more confined to poor and
marginalise section of the society. Growing number of patients now belong to middle class
and also affluent population. There is an urgent need for making an analysis of basic
factors behind this emerging situation which can ultimately reach to alarming proportions.
The Committee hopes that with the availability of both funds and manpower, the
Department will take up such an exercise at the earliest.
VI. NATIONAL LEPROSY ERADICATION PROGRAMME (NLEP)
6.1 National Leprosy Eradication Programme was launched with the objective of eliminating
Leprosy i.e. achieving prevalence rate of <1case/l0,000 population from the country. National level

62
elimination of Leprosy has been achieved since 31 December 2005 when the prevalence rate came
down to 0.95 or less than 1/10,000 population. 0.83 lakh cases were on record as on 1st April
2007 giving a Prevalence rate (PR) of 0.72 per 10,000 population. 31 States/ UTs have achieved
the level of elimination i.e. PR less than 1/10,000 population. 80% of districts and 75% of blocks
across the country have also achieved elimination. Four States, namely Bihar, Chhattisgarh,
Jharkhand and West Bengal having PR between 1 and 2 per 10,000 population with Chhattisgarh
having more than 2 per 10,000 population are yet to achieve elimination status.
6.2 The budget allocation was Rs.40.00 crores in 2007-08. As the States had unspent balances
with them, the BE 2007-08 was reduced to Rs.27.12 crores at RE stage. Expenditure reported upto
29.02.08 is only Rs.21.57 crore. Allocation of Rs.45.00 crore has been made for 2008-09. The
increased provision is meant for incentive to be given to leprosy affected persons undergoing re-
constructive surgery and institutions performing re-constructive surgery and performance based
incentive to ASHA in S tates with high leprosy burden such as Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Jharkhand,
Chhattisgarh and West Bengal.
The Committee in its 22nd Report, had voiced its serious concern for
under-utilisation of allocated funds in 2006-07 due to unspent balances in majority of
the States. The Committee takes note of detailed analysis of actual expenditure pattern in
2006-07 carried out by the Department. The Committee is surprised to observe that even
this detailed analysis indicates provisional figures of 77.59% of utilisation of allocated funds
by the States. The Committee’s concern is further deepened by the fact that the two major
States Bihar and Jharkhand could utilize only 33.9% and 30% of the allocated funds during
the year 2006-07. Creation of confusion due to merger of the leprosy society with the State
Health Society under NRHM has been cited as the main reason for this position. The
Committee has been given to understand that a number of measures like review of
programme performance and expenditure pattern in the quarterly review meetings of
district Leprosy Officers streamlining of procurement procedure and monitoring at the
central level were initiated during 2007-08. The Committee also notes that more focus was
given on implementation of Action Plan during annual meeting and quarterly review
meetings of State Programme Officers. Not only this the States were also instructed to
prepare a month-wise Action Plan of IEC and Training from July, 2007 onwards and
submitting the monthly implementation reports of these activities. The Committee is,
however, constrained to observe that these elaborate measures initiated by the Department
failed to make any visible impact as the ground realities continue to remain unchanged.
Drastic reduction of allocated funds had to be made at RE stage in 2007-08 with even that
provision remaining under-utilised upto 29.02.08.
6.3 The Committee is apprehensive that an enhanced allocation during 2008-09 may also
face similar outcomes. The Committee feels that though the plan of action under the
programme is well prepared, monitoring the timely and proper utilization of funds needs to
be taken on a more serious note. Mere advisories to State Implementing Agencies will not
serve the purpose. It, therefore, recommends that the Department take up the issue with
the State Programme Officers especially of Bihar and Jharkhand in an emphatic manner
during its quarterly review meetings.

24,145 cases, Bihar 14,300 cases, Maharashtra 9,516 cases and West Bengal 9803 cases. The
Committee observes that the approximate number of leprosy affected persons with grade-II

VII. NATIONAL PROGRAMME FOR CONTROL OF BLINDNESS
7.1 The National Programme for Control of Blindness was launched in the year 1976 as a 100%
Centrally-Sponsored scheme with the goal to reduce the prevalence of blindness from 1.4% to
0.3%. As per Survey in 2001-02, prevalence of blindness is estimated to be 1.1%. Target for the
Tenth Plan to reduce prevalence of blindness to 0.8% by 2007 could not be reached but the
prevalence rate of blindness has reduced to 1%.
7.2 Plan allocation of Rs.140.00 crores provided in 2007-08 was enhanced to Rs.171.87 crore
at RE stage. Enhanced allocation of Rs.250.00 crores has been made for 2008-09. The Committee
observes that upto 29.2.2008, utilization of Rs.120.62 crore has been reported.
7.3 The Committee has been given to understand that following new initiatives are proposed to
be taken with the enhanced provision of Rs.250.00 crores in 2008-09:—
1. Construction of dedicated Eye Wings and Eye OTs in District Hospitals in North-Eastern
States, Bihar, Jharkhand, J and K, Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand and few other States
where dedicated Operation Theaters are not available as per demand.
2. Appointment of the following Manpower:

64
1. Ophthalmic Surgeons In New Districts in District Hospitals.
2. Ophthalmic Assistants
3. Ophthalmic Assistants In PHCs/Vision Centers, where they are not available.
4. Eye Donation Counsellors In Eye Banks under Government Sector and NGO Sector
3. Grant-in-aid to NGOs for management of other Eye diseases other than Cataract like
Diabetic Retinopathy, Glaucoma Management, Laser Techniques, Corneal
Transplantation, Vitreo-retinal Surgery, Treatment of childhood blindness etc. of Rs.750
per case for Cataract/IOL Implantation Surgery and Rs.I000 per case of other major
Eye Diseases as described above.
4. Development of Mobile Ophthalmic Units in NE States, Hilly States & difficult terrains
for diagnosis and medical management of eye diseases.
5. Involvement of Private Practitioners in Sub District, Blocks and Village Level.
6. Maintenance of Ophthalmic Equipments supplied to Regional Institutes of
Ophthalmology, Medical Colleges, District/Sub-District Hospitals, PHCs/Vision Centres.
The Committee endorses the new initiatives that the Department has proposed for initiating
during the Eleventh Five Year Plan under NPCB. The Committee feels that such measures with
focused attention on NE States and also in the States of Bihar, Jharkhand, J and K, Himachal
Pradesh and Uttarakhand would surely go a long way in paving way for accessible eye-care for
the people in those regions where presently there is dearth of proper eye-care facilities.
7.4 The Committee is, however, surprised to find that implementation of new initiatives
depends on the approval of EFC Memo by the Ministry of Finance and CCEA. Till then, the
funds allocated for 2008-09 will continue to be utilized as per the existing scheme approved
for the Tenth Plan. The Committee is not happy with this state-of-affairs. Second year of
Eleventh Plan has already started and by the time approval of the competent authority is
finally received, the year 2008-09 would be nearing its end. The Committee would like to
point out that some of the new initiatives like construction of dedicated Eye Wings/Eye OTs
in District Hospitals, appointment of manpower, development of mobile Ophthalmic Units in
NE States will have to undergo a number of procedural formalities before their actually
taking off. The Committee accordingly recommends that concerted efforts need to be made
for getting the formal approval at the earliest. The Committee would appreciate if
simultaneously preparatory activities are also started.
7.5 As per the existing scheme under the Programme, the NGOs perform cataract operations
directly under the supervision of Respective District Blindness Control Societies, which function
under the State Blindness Control Society at the State level. To a query regarding the monitoring of
the working of 881 NGOs hospitals with eye-care facilities spread over in different parts of the
country, the Committee has been informed that working of NGO hospitals with eye care facilities
participating under NPCB are being monitored by the respective District Blindness Control Societies
directly. However, during State level meetings organized under the programme, NGOs’ hospitals are
also invited and the work done by them is reviewed. In addition, general guidelines for pre-operative,
operative and post-operative precautions for eye surgery have been circulated to all States from time
to time and last time these were circulated in the year 2007-08 to avoid eye mishaps.
The Committee has been taking note of instances of malfunctioning of Eye Camps
reported in the Media in the different States. The Committee feels that monitoring of Eye
Camps is being exclusively done by the District Blindness Control Societies. Department’s

65
role starts as and when reports regarding malfunctioning of Eye Camps held in States are
brought to the notice of the Ministry. Corrective measures are accordingly taken by the
Ministry. The Committee, however, feels that the Department needs to be more pro-active
in such cases. One corrective measure which can be initiated by the Department without
any special efforts involved is to review the performance of such Eye Camps in the State
level meetings, with required follow-up action taken on the reported incidents of
malfunctioning of Eye Camps. The Committee is also of the view that follow-up treatment
after Eye Camps should be made mandatory and strictly enforced. District hospital
authorities also need to be involved in the conducting of such Eye Camps by introduction
of compulsory, pre-checks in Eye Camps before start of Eye surgery and other treatment.
The Committee would like to add here that the Department should also devise some method
of surprise inspection of such eye camps organized by the NGOs to facilitate cataract
operations. This, the Committee feels, would ensure stricter compliance by all the concerned
entities and help reduce eyes mishaps. The Committee notes that the process for
independent evaluation of NPCB including evaluation of work being done by NGOs has been
initiated. The Committee would appreciate if this exercise is expedited so that corrective
measures are taken at the earliest.
7.6 It had come to the notice of the Committee that collection rate of eyes donated remained
discouraging inspite of IEC activities. The Committee notes that during 2004-05, number of eyes
donated was 23,553, followed by 28,007 in 2005-06 and 30,034 in 2006-07, with States like Goa,
H.P., Uttarakhand, Arunachal Pradesh, Manipur, Mizoram, Nagaland, Sikkim, showing nil
performance. The Department has informed that at present, as per information available, about
30,000 donated eyes are collected annually in the country against the requirement of at least 80,000
to 1,00,000 of corneas per year for transplantation purpose.
7.7 The Department has informed that in order to encourage eye donation among masses, IEC
activities are being intensified under the programme. The major focus towards this direction is
organization of National Eye Donation Fortnight from 25th August to 7th September every year.
During the fortnight, intensified publicity through all available media is given to step up eye
donation campaign and persuade people to donate eyes after death. The focus of the fortnight has
been shifted from “Pledging of Eyes” to “Actual Collection of Eyes” by launching “Hospital
Retrievable Programme” in major hospitals with various specialties, teaching hospitals attached to
medical colleges and large multi-specialty hospitals in Government and Non-Government Sector,
Army, Railways, ESI and Industrial Establishments of the Country. In addition to this, the message
for eye donation is being propagated through various print and electronic media.
The Committee is not convinced that the IEC activities are being carried out as
intensely as is stated by the Department. The Committee has been given to understand that
out of the total allocated budget under National Programme for Control of Blindness,
around 7% has been spent on IEC, which according to the Committee, is quite a sizable
amount. The Committee strongly feels that public awareness about the noble cause of eye
donation for blind persons continues to be very low. The Committee is of the view that a
review of IEC activities on this aspect need to be made in consultation with all the stake
holders, specially reputed Eye Hospitals/NGOs doing commendable work in this area and
also both Government and private ad agencies. The Committee would also like to emphasise
that the functioning of Eye Banks in the country requires to be reviewed in view of reported
lack of logistic support for timely collection of eyes by the Eye Banks. Steps also need to
be taken for increasing the number of Eye Banks in the country.
7.8 The Department has informed the Committee that the Rapid Survey on Avoidable Blindness
was conducted in randomly selected 16 districts of 15 States (including two Districts from Uttar

66
Pradesh). The study was carried out by the Department of Community Ophthalmology, Dr.R.P.
Centre for Ophthalmic Sciences, AIIMS, New Delhi. The three disturbing findings of said survey
are as follows:—
• Performance of States of Orissa (Ganjam district) and West Bengal (Malda district)
needs to be augmented so that the gains of the technological revolution in eye care can
be effectively harnessed across the country.
• Cataract remains the single largest cause of blindness, low vision and one eye blindness
in India if the data of the 16 districts are pooled together.
• The prevalence of blindness in general population is 1%.
7.9 The Committee’s attention has also been drawn to the findings of a survey on Rapid
Assessment of TRACHOMA cases done in the district in States of Haryana, Gujarat, U.P.,
Uttarakhand, Punjab and Rajashtan. Findings of this survey were that against the popular perception
of there being no transmission of trachoma cases in India, all districts showed active cases.
The Committee notes with disappointment that the target to bring prevalence of
blindness to 0.8% by 2007 has not been reached. The Department has informed that as per
the report of Rapid Survey on Avoidable Blindness (2007), the prevalence of blindness has
come down to 1% and that Cataract remains the single largest cause of blindness, low
vision and one eye blindness in India. The Committee also infers from the above study that
the prevalence of blindness due to Trachoma also continues to be there. It is a well known
fact that blindness is a bane of nature. The Committee believes that most of the people in
smaller towns and rural areas are not aware of the symptoms of the above ailments, and
the methods to manage eye care, their eye-care service seeking behaviour pattern do not
change. The Committee exhorts the Department to take all possible necessary steps to
devise IEC activities in local media and television channels so that awareness among the
people is increased. The Committee believes a lot of cases of blindness can be checked by
such a measure and would in the long run help to achieve the targeted goals under the
programme.

ROUTINE IMMUNISATION PROGRAMME
9.14 The Committee has been observing the trend of under-utilization of allocated funds
under this programme. For 2006-07 against an allocation of Rs.345.00 crore, utilization of only
Rs.228.83 crores could be made. In 2007-08, position was very unsatisfactory. Allocation of
Rs.317.00 crore had to be reduced to Rs.260.00 crore and expenditure reported upto 29.02.08 is
only Rs.171.88 crores. Delayed procurement procedure has been cited as the main factor for
reduced allocation and utilization thereof during 2007-08. The Committee observes that an enhanced
allocation of Rs.615.00 crores has been kept for 2008-09 as it is proposed to use Hepatitis-B
Combo-vaccine (DPT+Hepatitis) from 2008-09.
9.15 The Committee has been observing that State specific problems specially in the low
performing States continue to persist. Shortage of Health Workers, lack of awareness and
laxity in monitoring and supervision of the programme are some of the problems being
noticed in such States. Reported coverage of different vaccines under the Routine
Immunization Programme confirms the Committee’s apprehensions that in some of the
States like Arunachal Pradesh, Bihar, Jharkhand, Manipur, position is very unsatisfactory.
The Committee would like to point out that the steps taken for strengthening the Routine
Immunization Programme like recruitment of health workers, regular reviews at all levels
and catch up rounds in poor performing States do not seem to have yielded the desired
results. The Committee can only say that catch-up rounds in poor performance States with
the districts identified before hand is the most important step for effective reduction in the
number of un-immunized and partially immunized children. Entire focus of the
implementing agencies should be on this alone.
9.16 The Committee understands that the three pioneer institutes namely Central
Research Institute (CRI), Kasauli in Himachal Pradesh, Pasteur Institute of India (PTI),
Koonoor, Tamil Nadu and the BCG Vaccine Laboratory (BCGVL) in Chennai, Tamil Nadu
have been directed to stop vaccine production. The Committee strongly feels that these
vaccine production units should not be converted to only testing laboratories. The

withdraw the order without delay.

affect the completion of construction and developmental activities undertaken by them and
in the process the institutions. (Para 2.3)
The Committee notes that the overall allocation for the health sector (outside
NRHM) has been on the higher side. Still, the Committee is constrained to note that the
Department has failed to project its budgetary requirements in an effective way for the
simple reason that the utilization of funds during the Tenth Plan is far from satisfactory
which is evident from the fact that the sanctioned BE for 2005-06 and 2006-07 was
Rs.4253.84 crore and Rs.3564.95 crore, respectively, which was reduced to Rs.4096.25 crore

to illustrate that the Department’s record in utilization of the allocated funds is below par.
The Committee would, therefore, recommend the Department to first ensure optimum and
judicious utilization of the funds allocated instead of highlighting the reduced budgetary
allocation. The Committee also recommends to the Department to take substantive steps so
that the stumbling blocks in the utilization of sanctioned funds for 2008-09 for a crucial
sector like health, are removed. (Para 2.4)

Committee would like to be apprised about utilization of Plan and Non-Plan funds (quarter-
wise) during 2007-08. In the light of last year’s experience of utilization of funds, the
Committee recommends that concerted efforts need to be made for optimum and judicious
utilization of enhanced allocation made for 2008-09. (Para 3.2)
The Committee, therefore, recommends that allocation of funds under Non-Plan be
enhanced adequately so that the services available to the CGHS beneficiaries are not
affected. (Para 3.3)
The computerization of CGHS dispensaries and offices in Delhi was taken up at an
expenditure of Rs.8.74 crores. The Committee was informed that as on 26.3.08, 83
dispensaries in Delhi have been fully computerized and the process of computerization of
remaining 4 dispensaries was under way. The Committee would like to point out that
computerization process of CGHS dispensaries in Delhi could not be completed as scheduled.
Originally targeted to be completed by 2006-07, revised date of 17th  August, 2007 could also
not be adhered to. By the end of financial year, 2007-08, 4 dispensaries in Delhi still
remained to be computerized. Computerization of CGHS dispensaries located in Mumbai,
Kolkata, Chennai, Hyderabad, Nagpur and Pune to be taken up in 2007-08 as scheduled is
yet to start. The Committee can imagine the status of third phase slated to be completed
in 2008-09. The Committee, keeping in view the past experience in respect of Delhi
dispensaries, can only emphasize that all steps need to be taken to complete the
computerization of dispensaries outside Delhi at the earliest. Corrective measures based on
the problem areas noticed in the computerization of dispensaries in Delhi need to be taken.
(Para 3.4)
The Committee would like to point out that situation is some what different.
Problems are being faced both by the CGHS functionaries and beneficiaries. Technicians,
Junior staff manning counters in dispensaries and attending doctors need to be fully
trained. Practical problems like internet and electricity failure have to be tackled by having
an alternative arrangement. These initial teething problems should not be allowed to be
prolonged. At present, beneficiaries which include senior citizens also are being made to
wait for hours at the dispensaries. Their ordeal starts right from the registration counter
and continues upto delivery of medicines. The Committee would appreciate if all the
measures including training, smooth running of computers with full connectivity, backup for
power failure are taken at the earliest and also closely monitored. (Para 3.5)
The Committee has been emphasizing for long for introduction of two shift system
in CGHS. The Committee does not appreciate the contention of the Ministry that a large
number of private hospitals and diagnostic centres have been empanelled under the CGHS
and in case of emergency, beneficiaries can go there for treatment and claim re-

75
imbursement later. The Committee would like to draw the attention of the Ministry once
again to the fact that idea behind having two shifts in CGGS dispensaries is the
inconvenience being faced by the CGHS beneficiaries, majority of them office goers in going
to the dispensaries in the morning hours. The Committee is disturbed by the element of
helplessness shown by the Ministry in their candid admission of staff side vehemently
opposing the move. In this era where the service providers like banks etc. are opting for
flexible timings to give their customers maximum possible services, at least the Ministry
could have come forward with a positive and proactive approach. The Committee would
reiterate its recommendation made last year for starting two shifts in a few dispensaries as
a test case. One must not forget that CGHS is a service oriented scheme, supposedly
providing health care mainly to our serving employees and pensioners. It is the
responsibility of the Ministry to make the CGHS employees understand and not to be
pressurized by them. (Para 3.6)
The Committee recommends that construction of dispensary in Dwarka where land
is already available should start at the earliest. All procedural formalities should be
expedited and completion of project strictly monitored. (Para 3.7)
The Committee is surprised to note that even after two years, suitable
accommodation for housing the dispensary in Sector 82, Noida and Gurgaon could not be
managed. Secretary (Health) Government of Haryana is now being requested to allot a
building for CGHS Dispensary in Gurgaon. Proposal for housing the CGHS Dispensary in
Community Centre, Sector 82, Noida on rent-basis is under consideration. The Committee
strongly feels that the Ministry should pursue the two proposals in hand so that large
number of CGHS beneficiaries residing in these two areas do not continue to remain
deprived of health care any more. (Para 3.8)
The Committee recommends to the Department to take the issue on priority with the
Ministry of Finance to complete all the procedural formalities, so that necessary posts are
created and subsequently filled up. The Committee would also like to be apprised about the
cadre strength created as a result of implementation of SIU report and the efforts taken
so far to fill up the vacant posts. (Para 3.9)
The Committee understands that third party administrators for processing of claims
and medical audit are also proposed to be introduced. The Committee has been given to
understand that as recommended by SIU, Department of Expenditure, vacancies arising in
Group ‘D’ posts are to be progressively outsourced. (Para 3.10)
The Committee views with serious concern the growing number of vacancies in
different categories of posts in CGHS dispensaries. The Committee understands that all
surplus posts identified in cities outside Delhi have been abolished. It has also been
informed that the staff strength in the dispensaries is decided as per the workload. The
very fact that at the present juncture, no CGHS city can be stated to have full complement
of the staff strength as per the SIU norms establishes that the existing dispensaries are not
functioning as envisaged. The Committee also strongly feels that outsourcing /hiring of staff
on contract-basis on a big scale is a remedy worse then the disease. The concept of public
private partnership cannot be applied across the board specially in a set-up meant for
providing health care. The Committee would like to have a status note on the sanctioned
posts and vacancies category-wise and region-wise in CGHS dispensaries. (Para 3.11)
The Committee recommends that all out efforts be made for reduction in the
consultation fees to 2 per cent for procurement of drugs/medicines for CGHS as assured by
the Ministry and the Committee be informed accordingly. (Para 3.12)

76
The Committee is happy to note that these adhoc arrangements would continue until
further orders. The Committee would, however, like to emphasize that empanelment of
these hospitals on permanent basis should be made, specially in view of cancer patients
undergoing prolonged and costly treatment. The Ministry has to playa proactive role in such
matters. (Para 3.13)
The Committee notes that under the revised exercise, rates in respect of Bangalore,
Chennai, Hyderabad, Jaipur, Kolkata, Lucknow, Mumbai, Nagpur and Pune have been
issued. The Committee hopes that rates for the remaining cities would be issued at the
earliest. The Committee would like to be apprised about the level of difference in the rates
for major hospitals/diagnostic centres in the metro cities. (Para 3.14)
IV. SAFDARJUNG HOSPITAL AND V ARDHMAN MAHAVEER MEDICAL COLLEGE,
NEW DELHI
The Committee, however, notes that upto 29.02.2008 expenditure of only
Rs.53.77 crore could be reported. (Para 4.2)
The Committee apprehends that the present allocation of funds to the Hospital might
adversely affect its services and in the process, the large number of patients. While
cautioning the Hospital to utilize its allocated funds judiciously and optimally, the
Committee recommends that it should be granted adequate funds to meet its functional
requirements. (Para 4.3)
The Committee observes that procedures and rules are made to streamline,
strengthen and facilitate a process and not create hurdles and bottlenecks. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that effective coordination between the Department and the Hospital
authorities is required in this regard. If required, suitable steps for improvement in
the procedural aspect may be initiated so as to provide better health care delivery system.
(Para 4.4)
The Committee is happy to note that scheme of redevelopments of hospitals
including redevelopment of Safdarjung Hospital with the proposal to increase its bed
strength from 1531 to 3000 has finally been included in the approved schemes for the
Eleventh Plan. HSCC has submitted a final report on ‘Redevelopment Plan of Safdarjung
Hospital’ to the Department for consideration. The Department has started work for
engaging consultants for preparation of DPR for the detailed redevelopment plan. The
Committee would like to point out that ‘in principle’ approval by the Planning Commission
has already taken considerable time. The Committee therefore, urges the Department to
make wholehearted efforts to expedite the procedural formalities at the earliest. The
redevelopment plan is required to be started without any further delay, keeping in view the
ever-increasing patient load on the Safdarjung Hospital. The Committee recommends
that scarcity of funds and lack of coordination should not come in the way of its
timely completion and the Department should make every conceivable effort in this regard.
(Para 4.5)
The Committee expresses its serious concern on the slow progress made with regard
to setting up of Renal Transplantation Unit. Status of the project for IVF unit is more
discouraging as ‘in principle’ approval is yet to come. The Committee can only emphasize
that the Renal Transplantation Unit should be made functional by the year end by closely
monitoring the progress of the same. Procedural formalities with regard to IVF unit also
need to be completed at the earliest. (Para 4.7)

77
The Committee’s attention has been drawn by a large number of vacancies in
different categories of posts in Safdarjung Hospital. Out of the total sanctioned staff
strength of 4781, there were 1054 vacant posts in different categories as on July, 2007. The
Committee has been given to understand that workload of the Hospital has progressively
increased manifold in the past few years. The doctor patient ratio has inversely grown,
there is an acute need of more doctors per patient and related infrastructure including
sub-staff. In such a scenario, with the redevelopment project of Safdarjung Hospital likely
to take off at the earliest, additional staff strength of all the categories would be required.
The Committee, accordingly, recommends that the Department in co-ordination with
hospital authorities should chalk out an action-plan for acquiring the required manpower.
(Para 4.8)
V. DR. RAM MANOHAR LOHIA HOSPITAL, NEW DELHI
The Committee is constrained to note that inspite of an assurance that each Central
Institute will have a separate monitoring Committee, given by the Secretary, H&FW before
the Committee last year, no action seems to have been taken. The Committee, therefore,
reiterates that a proper monitoring mechanism needs to be put in place so as to arrest this
trend of sub-optimal utilization of the funds. (Para 5.2)
The Committee has been observing that a number of projects-big and small
envisaged for strengthening and augmenting the existing services in the premier hospital
continue to remain in the implementation status with very little progress being made. The
Committee has been constrained to point out that the year 2007-08 was also no exception.
Funds allocated remained under-utilised with the following three major projects running
behind schedule:—
• Strengthening of Accidents and Emergency Department and setting up of Trauma
Care Centre.
• Setting up of PGIMER at Dr. Ram Manohar Lohia Hospital.
• Upgradation of School of Nursing into College of Nursing.
All these projects were to be completed in 2007-08 only. The Committee notes that
academic session for PG Courses in Medicine, Paediatrics and Anesthesia is to begin in
2008-09. While welcoming the starting of PGIMER at Dr. RML Hospital, the Committee
would appreciate if the PGI becomes fully operational running all the courses with the
required infrastructure and regular staff in place. The Committee apprehends that there is
little chance of Trauma Care Centre becoming operational in 2008-09 with appointment of
178 additional staff yet to be made and process of purchase of equipment and consumable
going on. The Committee also finds that not much progress seems to have been made in
the upgradation of School of Nursing into College of Nursing. The target remains the same
in 2008-09 also as in the previous year. (Para 5.3)
VI. ALL INDIA INSTITUTE OF MEDICAL SCIENCES (AIIMS)
The Committee was informed that the allocated funds would not be sufficient for
maintaining the infrastructure and patient care services of the Institute. The Committee
feels that the decrease in non-plan from Rs.310.00 crores in 2007-08 to Rs.290.00 crores is
surely going to affect the patient care services offered by the Institute. The Committee
apprehends return of the ‘user charges regime’ in AIIMS because consumables are the only
negotiable component of the non-plan budget as salary and bills have to be paid any way.
(Para 6.2)

78
The Committee is constrained to observe that enhanced outlay for the Eleventh
Plan period does not seem to have any visible impact. Plan provision of Rs.200.00 crore for
2007-08 not only remains at the same level as in the previous plan period but has also been
brought down to Rs.160.00 crore at the RE stage with actual expenditure reported up to
29.02.2008 being only Rs.113.33 crore. The Committee is not able to comprehend the
reasons for under-utilization of funds duly allocated for specific purposes. Failure on the
part of a premier institute like AIIMS to utilize the funds as targeted indicates that
problem areas continue to persist both in the co-ordination between the administrative
Ministry and the Institute and its functioning. (Para 6.4)
The Committee hopes that position would improve now. (Para 6.5)
The Committee would emphasize that procedural formalities for the centre should be
expedited so as to complete it by the targeted date. (Para 6.6)
The Committee also takes note of major new initiatives for which plans were under
preparation during 2007-08 as listed below:—
➢➢➢➢➢ Construction of new PC Block
➢➢➢➢➢ Advance facilities for Paediatrics (Medical) and (Surgery)
➢➢➢➢➢ Advance facilities for Geriatrics
➢➢➢➢➢ Facility for Family Medicine and Public Health (Para 6.7)
The Committee finds that another set of new projects has been listed to be taken
during 2008-09. The Committee strongly feels that new initiatives should be taken up with
priority being fixed for the most needed ones. The Committee would appreciate if these
initiatives do not continue to be on paper during 2008-09. The Committee recommends that
funds provided for the AIIMS in the Eleventh Plan show both optimum and judicious
utilization as per the action plan with additional provision as and when required. The
Committee is of the view that an effective monitoring mechanism to be effected by all
concerned both at the institute and the Ministry level needs to be in place for the purpose
at the earliest. (Para 6.8)
The Committee expresses deep concern that in the premier institute of the country
like AIIMS so many posts are lying vacant. In the opinion of the Committee, this is
definitely bound to affect the quality of services rendered by the Institute. The Committee,
therefore, recommends immediate action to fill up the vacant posts. (Para 6.9)
The Committee strongly feels that position is bound to aggravate further specially in
view of increasing number of doctors and nurses leaving the institute in the recent years.
The rate of exodus of doctors and nurses from the Institute is a cause of serious concern.
The Department needs to devise a strategy immediately to arrest this trend. The Committee
would like to be informed of the remedial steps taken in this regard. (Para 6.10)
The Committee is deeply concerned about the matter as the Institute is one of the
best training grounds for the doctors and that too at highly subsidized rates involving
precious tax payers’ money. The Committee is of the view that this brain drain is on two
counts-higher studies and lucrative assignments. At the same time, the Committee is also
of the opinion that some policy or enactment should be made so that tendency of leaving
the Institute by doctors/nurses can be minimized. This could be in the form of a monetary
bond or post qualification compulsory service. The Committee strongly feels that urgent
steps are required to be taken so as to ensure an ideal working environment for our young
talented doctors along with all the incentives comparable to those enjoyed by private sector

79
doctors to the extent possible. The Committee would like to be apprised of the steps taken
in this regard which should not be only AIIMS specific but should also cover all the
Government medical institutions. (Para 6.11)
The Committee is given to understand that the Valiathan Committee had submitted
its report on the functioning of AIIMS more than a year ago. The Committee is surprised
to note that only follow up action taken so far is a meeting held under the Chairmanship
of Secretary (Health and Family Welfare) with Director, AIIMS on the 1st March, 2008. The
Committee was informed that the matter was now under Government’ s consideration. The
Committee is not happy with the undue delay in the implementation of Valiathan
Committee recommendations. Any further delay would simply negate the very purpose for
setting up such a Committee, that too at the directive of the Prime Minister. The
Committee, therefore, urges upon the Department to expedite the implementation of the
Valiathan Committee Report. (Para 6.12)
The Committee can only hope that the Burns Unit duly approved will be made
operational by the targeted date. (Para 6.13)

VIII. NORTH EASTERN INDIRA GANDHI REGIONAL INSTITUTE OF HEALTH AND
MEDICAL SCIENCES (NEIGRIHMS), SHILLONG
The Committee is happy to note that considerable progress has been made in
operationalization of NEIGRIHMS during 2007-08. The Committee is, however, perturbed to
note that no improvement could be made so far as manpower required for the Institute is
concerned. Like 2006-07, position remained unchanged during 2007-08 also. (Para 8.5)
The Committee would like to point out that efforts made by the Department for
getting the teaching/specialists faculty posted/deputed fr om Armed Forces Medical Services
have not been successful due to shortage of senior faculty in the AFMS cadre also. The
Committee would again emphasize that it does not have much faith in the collaboration
measures reported to be made with Institutions like NIMHANS and Dr. Cherian’s Frontier
Lifeline. The Committee is not aware how far the efforts for clinching similar agreements
with CMC-Vellore, CMC-Ludhiana, Amrita Institute of Medical Sciences, Kochi, AIIMS and

Departments of Neurology, Neuro-Surgery and Cardiology could be made operational at the

other corner of the country. Same would be the position with the proposed tie-up with other
Institutes. The Committee would also like to point out that the Department must be fully
aware about the shortage of faculty at these premier Institutes also. The Committee
strongly feels that such stop-gap arrangements, even if made cannot make the Institute
fully functional. Target of making 500 bedded hospital and teaching Institute at Shillong is
thus likely to remain on paper only for considerable time. The Committee reiterates that
the Department has to make all conservable efforts for having permanent faculty at the
Institute. Special incentives and extra facilities have to be worked out for attracting the
required manpower to the Institute. Collaboration with leading Institutes/public private
partnership can be feasible for limited number of posts and period only. The Committee

81
would also like to be apprised about the present status of phase-I of filling up of 725 posts

The Committee notes that against a provision of Rs.10.00 crore in 2007-08 only an

provision of Rs.62.20 crore, utilization of only Rs.30.17 crore could be reported by the end
of the Plan period. (Para 9.2)

manpower requirement, construction of OPD, Neurology Block, Casualty and Service Blocks,

finds that the High Court of Jharkhand is monitoring the development of the Institute on
the pattern of NIMHANS. The very fact that the High Court is monitoring the development

Committee would like to be informed about the progress made w.r.t. the proposed re-
development plan and the circumstances leading to the monitoring of the development of
the Institute by the Jharkhand High Court. (Para 9.3)

The Committee is not aware about the details of developmental projects -both
ongoing and proposed, to be taken up during the Eleventh Plan period. The Committee
would like to be informed of the activities along with the developmental plans of the
Institute for which the funds have been proposed for the Eleventh Plan. (Para 10.2)
The Committee observes that the reply seeking for the details of the short-term
training courses/workshops in respiratory diseases for faculty members and medical
