The Committee in its 22nd Report on the Demands for Grants (2007-08) presented
on 3rd May, 2007 had expressed its apprehension that it would take at least another plan
period before the six AIIMS like Institutions would start functioning in the real sense. The
Committee is constrained to modify its assessment. From the details made available to the
Committee, construction work on the six AIIMS like Institutions is expected to start by
August-September, 2008 and would be completed in 24 months. Thus, it is more than clear
now that only buildings would be ready by the end of Eleventh Plan. The real target of
making available best health care services to public through these institutions seems to be
a distant dream even now. The Committee finds that tendering process for procurement of
medical equipments is at an initial stage. Process for other allied infrastructure facilities
and manpower-both highly qualified/technical as well as non-technical is yet to start. With
regard to upgradation of 13 Medical College Institutions, the Committee can only hope that
work would be completed within the targeted date of 20 months. The Committee is,
however, worried about the fate of upgradation of Grants Medical College and JJ hospital,

82
Mumbai due to a court case pending in Nagpur High Court in the matter. The Committee
is of the view that the Department should take up other linked activities like arranging for
the faculty and the other requisite infrastructure simultaneously so that no delay takes
place in operationalization of the Institutions once the construction activity is completed.
(Para 11.6)
The Committee also recommends that funds as and when required should be made
available to the Department. The Committee would however like to point out that though
funds have never been a problem for this ambitious project of national importance,
utilization thereof has been far from satisfactory level. The Committee, accordingly,
recommends setting up of a joint mechanism of Centre and the concerned States so that
greater coordination is achieved and effective monitoring of the ongoing projects is done.
The Committee also calls for greater emphasis on adhering to the time lines so that the
overall cost of the project is not escalated further. (Para 11.7)
The Committee, during the oral evidence of the Secretary had taken a serious view
of the delay in implementation of the project. The Committee, therefore, desires the
Department to apprise it of the progress made in implementation of the project, after every
two months. (Para 11.8)
XII. IMPROVEMENT OF NURSING SERVICES
However, the Committee is surprised to observe unsatisfactory level of achievement
under the quantifiable deliverables/physical outputs set for 2007-08. The first target set was
training of 8000 nursing personnel through 48 identified Nursing Institutions. By the end
of the year, no progress seems to have been made from the details made available to the
Committee. Proposal for conducting 78 courses for training of 2340 nurses was under
process. Training of additional 1600 nurses depended upon proposals to be received from the
Institutions. The Committee has been informed that out of 30 institutions, funds could be
released for strengthening of 23 institutions. Status of these institutions is, however, not-
known. The Committee would also like to point out that projects like upgradation of RAK
College of Nursing into Centre of Excellence, upgradation of School of Nursing into College
of Nursing at Dr. RML Hospital, Safdarjung Hospital and Lady Harding Medical College and
establishing a College of Nursing in JIPMER, Puducherry have been there for the last few
years with no evidence of progress being made. Only exception is College of Nursing
at Lady Harding Medical College reported to have started functioning in 2007. The
Committee hopes that required manpower and infrastructure has been made available there.
(Para 12.2)
The Committee is not very hopeful as upgradation of School of Nursing at Dr. RML
Hospital has also been listed as one of the targets to be achieved during 2008-09. The
Committee would like to reiterate that all these projects need to be closely monitored so
as to ensure their completion within the time schedule without any cost escalation in the
original estimate. The Department should not be a mere spectator, it should devise some
mechanism for proper utilization of the funds and its repeated contention that the
utilization/grants of funds depends upon receipt of SOE/UCs is not acceptable to the
Committee. The Department has to play a more proactive roles in co-ordination with the
hospital/college authorities. The problem areas wherever noticed need to be removed at the
earliest. (Para 12.3)
The Committee is not aware about the existence of any Monitoring Committee for
such projects. The Committee is of the view that such a mechanism will prove to be very
useful, especially in view of Rs.198.00 crore allocated for strengthening/upgradation of

83
Nursing Services. The Committee welcomes the enhancement in the assistance to be
provided to Nursing Institutions from Rs.10.00 lakhs to Rs.25.00 lakhs. Such a move was
over due. The Committee, however, wonders whether any exercise has been initiated for
identification of locations of all the proposed Centres/Schools/Colleges so far. The
Committee would appreciate if implementation of all these projects is carried out in a time-
bund manner. The Committee is not aware about any assessment/review made recently
about the (training both pre and in-service) programmes for Nurses and also functioning of
Training Institutions for Nurses. The Committee is of the view that such an exercise is
necessary for strengthening the Nursing Services which is a very crucial component of
health care. (Para 12.4)
The Committee is happy to note that the National Awards for Nurses, given as a
mark of highest recognition for the meritorious services of the nurses and nursing
profession in the country, that continued up to 1989, have been revived and named as the
National Florence Nightingale Award from 2007 with the consent of the President of India.
17 Nursing personnel have been awarded with this prestigious award during the year 2007.
(Para 12.5)
The Committee recommends that a suitable mechanism should be evolved for
maintaining a live register of nurses so as to enable the Department for formulating
appropriate policy pertaining to nurses. (Para 12.6)
The Committee recommends that the Department should make all out efforts
including effective co-ordination and close monitoring so that all the proposals for
strengthening of nursing education are implemented properly and desired results
are achieved for getting adequate number of qualified and trained nursing personnel.
(Para 12.7)
While appreciating the initiatives, the Committee would like to point out that out of
total nursing strength of 3015 in Central Government Hospitals in Delhi, only 795 nursing
personnel have been provided with accommodation. If such unsatisfactory conditions are in
Delhi, the Committee can well imagine the conditions in State Government Hospitals. The
Committee strongly feels that residential facilities for Nurses need to be augmented at the
earliest. The Committee recommends the Department to formulate a comprehensive policy
to stop exodus of nurses as also to offer more incentives so as to make the profession more
attractive for arresting this trend. (Para 12.9)
XIII. UPGRADATION OF DIS TRICT HOSPITALS
The Committee welcomes the initiative of the Department for upgradation of the
District Hospitals. While recommending priority to the remote and rural area hospitals and
those States where MMR and IMR are high and where maternity facilities are not up to the
mark, the Committee would recommend formulating a mechanism so as to facilitate early
selection, granting and overseeing proper utilization of funds. The Committee would also
emphasize that all efforts should be made to fully utilize the approved outlay of Rs. 1500.00
crores for the Eleventh Plan. For this, targets need to be set and all hurdles in
implementation need to be removed. The Committee has in the past witnessed that funds
could not be utilized optimally and many schemes could not achieve desired success for want
of proposals, submission of utilization certificates from State Governments etc. The
Committee, therefore, recommends to the Department to expedite scrutiny of the proposals
received from the State Governments from the beginning of financial year 2008-09 itself.
(Para 13.2)

84
XIV . RASHTRIYA AROGYA NIDHI
The Committee observes that even after more than a decade of setting up of the
fund with 50% of the contribution made by the State/UT to be provided by Central
Government, there are still several States/UTs which have not set up the State Illness
Assistance Fund. Every State/UTs should have such a fund. The Committee would appreciate
if this matter is taken up at the highest level in all such State/UTs. (Para 14.3)
The Committee feels that in order to facilitate easy access to quality health care to
the poor and downtrodden strata of our society, the limit of Rs. 50,000 under immediate
financial assistance funds, per case, for which funds are placed at the disposal of Medical
Superintendents of above hospitals, need to be enhanced realistically for treatment of
dreaded diseases like AIDS, Cancer etc. Some of the major States like U.P., Assam,
Karnataka, Kerala and Jammu & Kashmir do not have such a fund. With only a very few
major hospitals located in metros having extended facility under the fund, people of such
States/UTs are being deprived of medical care for no fault of theirs. From the details of
funds released to States/UTs during 2005-08, it is very clear that such States are having
negligible funds at their disposal. The Committee wonders about the adequacy of such State
funds. The Committee is of the view that with the increasing rate of inflation and also
increasing number of patients suffering from major diseases, an assessment of the
Rashtriya Arogya Nidhi should be made at the earliest. Necessary changes may be made
thereafter. The facility of financial assistance should be extended in more hospitals so as
to cover the geographical limits of the country. The Committee also recommends to the
Department to give wide publicity to the scheme specially in the hospital campuses
to generate awareness so that the same can be utilized by the needy and poor patients.
(Para 14.4)
XV. NATIONAL URBAN HEALTH MISSION (NUHM)
The Committee observes that NUHM is one of the most ambitious Projects after
National Rural Health Mission (NRHM). Objectives of the Mission are laudable and are
according to the requirements of the present scenario. The Committee cautions the
Department to take all necessary steps so that the problems afflicting the implementation
of NRHM like those related to ground level healthcare functionaries, availability of doctors,
paramedics and infrastructure do not recur and interfere in the implementation of parallel
scheme meant for urban areas. For achieving the targets proposed under mission the
Department should do proper homework and work out modalities for their implementation.
The Department should start coordinating with the States right from the beginning of the
project. The Committee would like to be apprised about the progress made in this regard.
(Para 15.4)
XVI. NATIONAL AIDS CONTROL PROGRAMME (NACP)
The Committee is constrained to note that against a Plan provision of
Rs.815.00 crore which was increased to Rs.953.89 crore at the RE stage during 2007-08 for
NACP, expenditure reported upto 13th Mar ch, 2008 was only Rs.767.34 crore. The
Committee observes that optimum utilization has not been achieved in any of the
components of NACO. The Committee notes that the Department has not been able to
achieve optimum utilization of funds during 2006-07 also. The Committee  was given to
understand that procedural delays in the procurement of equipment and non-utilization of
funds placed at the disposal of other Ministries like Ministry of Social Justice and
Empowerment and Information and Broadcasting were the main factors for under-

85
utilization of allocated funds during 2006-07. The Committee is afraid that similar reasons
would be given for 2007-08 also. It seems that weekly monitoring meetings at NACO level
and quarterly monitoring meetings with the State SACs followed by visits of teams of
officers to the States to ascertain the progress of work and level of expenditure have failed
to make any noticeable improvement. In view of enhanced allocation of Rs. 1100.00 crore
made for 2008-09, the Committee recommends to the Department to take immediate
corrective measures and make every conceivable effort so as to ensure optimum and
judicious utilization of funds. (Para 16.5)
The Committee is dismayed to note that progress made under several components of
the programme is abysmal and the trend has been continuing irrespective of the issue being
raised again and again. The Committee has been viewing with serious concern the trend of
targets remaining under-achieved in the past few years. Last year, the Committee was given
to understand that non-procurement of blood bank equipment seriously hampered the
modernization of District Level Blood Banks. Non-availability of STD specialists and
specialized STD services were held responsible for target set for STD clinics. The Committee
has been given to understand that instead of the previous emphasis on opening of STD
facilities, now targets are being set for the number of STD cases treated. The Committee
would, however, like to point out that readjustments of targets will not result in having the
required STD specialists and services. The Committee reiterates its earlier recommendation
of formulating a comprehensive plan for the training of doctors in handling AIDS cases. The
Committee recommends to the Department to inform it about the major problem areas in
the implementation of National AIDS Control Programme and the corrective measures
taken/ proposed by the Department to overcome the same. (Para 16.6)
The Committee would recommend to the Department to continue its consultations
with the States that have either suspended or banned the programme and achieve consensus
in implementing the scheme. (Para 16.7)
The Committee appreciates these priorities of the Department and recommends the
Department to inform it about the specific steps to be taken by it for achievement of the
same. (Para 16.8)
The Committee is happy to note that though delayed, the Department has taken the
desired step towards starting the second line of treatment to lessen the sufferings of drug
resistant patients. The Committee would like to recommend to the Department to put in
place an effective mechanism so that no patient in need of second line ART is deprived of
it. (Para 16.10)
The Committee is not fully inclined to agree with the contention of the Ministry.
Some of the corrective measures in centralized procurement as mentioned below clearly
indicate that besides deficiencies at the State level, implementation at the Central level was
also not upto the mark:—
➢➢➢➢➢ Procurement responsibility shifted from Procurement Support Agencies to the
United Nations Office for Project Services for Bank supported operations.
➢➢➢➢➢ Creation of Financial Management Group at the Health Ministry.
➢➢➢➢➢ Development of detailed guidelines and operational manuals for procurement of
NGOs and Public Private Partnerships.
➢➢➢➢➢ Introduction of evaluation of NGO performance by Committee having one
external evaluator.

86
➢➢➢➢➢ Termination of contracts of about 25% NGOs.
➢➢➢➢➢ Pre-award validation/certification of WHO GMP made mandatory in all cases.
(Para 16.12)
From the information available with the Committee, it notes that services of as
many as 177 NGOs have been discontinued. Besides that 48 Community Care Centres being
run by NGOs have been discontinued after on site evaluation. The Committee is dismayed
at the fact that an alarming percentage of NGOs were blacklisted and had to be removed.
The Committee is not inclined to admit that the whole problem was at the district level of
officials. The Committee opines that either this is a case of poor monitoring mechanism at
the Department level or there is more to the matter than what is visible. The Committee
would like to have a Status Note on the performance of NGOs, unspent balances available
with the blacklisted NGOs and action taken for the recovery of the same. Details of all
similar cases/discrepancies related to NACO and the action taken by the Department/CBI
in that regard may also be furnished to the Committee. (Para 16.13)
XVII. NATIONAL CANCER CONTROL PROGRAMME (NCCP)
Against a Tenth Plan allocation of Rs.333.00 crore, enhanced provision of
Rs.2871.92 crore including a provision of Rs.471.92 crore for tobacco control has been made
for the Eleventh Plan. While welcoming this initiative of the Government, the Committee
is constrained to point out that level of utilization has to keep pace with the enhanced
provision. The Committee has been persistently highlighting the need for better
management and co-ordination of all concerned. However, the position remains unchanged.
Against the Tenth Plan allocation of Rs. 333.00 crore, utilization reported at the end of the
year was only Rs.252.95 crore. The Committee finds that year 2007-08, which is the
first year of the Eleventh Plan failed to bring any improvement. Plan allocation of
Rs.140.00 crores for 2007-08 for the NCCP was reduced to Rs.70.00 crores at the RE stage.
The expenditure reported up to 29.02.08 is only Rs.40.31 crores. Similarly, plan provision of
Rs.40.00 crore for tobacco control had to be brought down to Rs.29.00 crore with utilization
of only Rs.7.63 crore by 29.02.2008. (Para 17.3)
The Committee takes a serious view of total lack of initiative on the part of the
Department so far as implementation of National Cancer Control Programme is concerned.
The Committee strongly feels that its following observations made in the 25th report have
failed to make any impact on the Department:—
“The Committee is not satisfied with the citing of a number of procedural formalities
as the major factor for undue delay in the release of funds by the Department. It
is for the Department to take a pro-active role by pursuing with State Governments
for sending viable proposals. As admitted by the Department, the proposal for up-
gradation of nine existing RCCs into Centre of Excellence was considered only during
the last quarter of the year and five institutions were approved for funding. However,
due to non-availability of required funds, only four institutions could be funded.
What is more disturbing is that the entire allocation of Rs. 8.70 crore earmarked for
NE Region remained unutilised for want of complete proposals. Keeping in view the
experience of 2006-07, the Committee recommends to the Department to put in place
an effective monitoring mechanism for implementation of Cancer Control
Programme.”
It is a sorry state of affairs that at the end of the year, a large number of proposals
received for different components were at a ripe stage but due to paucity of time and some

87
technical deficiency found in the proposals, the same could not be materialized. It is high
time that an effective monitoring mechanism in co-ordination with all the implementing
agencies is put in place without any further delay. (Para 17.5)
The Committee observes that achievement of these targets will depend to a large
extent on the finalization, of EFC for the Eleventh Plan which proposes substantial increase
in the grant-in-aid. The Committee, accordingly, recommends that efforts may be made to
obtain the EFC approval at the earliest. It has also been proposed to enter into new phase
of Public Private Partnership which also required enhanced grant-in-aid. The Committee
would like to be apprised about the details of this new component. As commented in the
previous para, the Committee once again enjoins upon the Department to enhance its
efforts from the beginning of this financial year and take suitable corrective measures
including strict monitoring so that the approved outlay for NCCP is properly and optimally
utilized. (Para 17.6)
The Committee recommends to the Department to take up its case more vigorously
and with sound reasoning with the State Government of West Bengal for early handing over
the piece of land for early construction of the campus of CNCI, Kolkata. (Para 17.7)
Committee feels that some corrective measures need to be taken by the Department
for submission of UCs by the State Governments under NCCP. Depar tment being a nodal
agency, should make all efforts so that funds allocated are in no way allowed to go
unutilized for want of proposals and submission of UCs. As far as non submission of
utilization certificates is concerned, the Committee feels that there could be possibilities of
diversion of the funds. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department has to
ensure timely submission of UCs. The Committee would appreciate if a Status Note on
pending UCs (State/NGO-wise) is submitted to it. (Para 17.8)
The Committee recommends to the Department to give utmost priority to evaluation
of the National Cancer Control Programme by a premier agency having experience of
work in such Disease Control Programmes. Proper evaluation would help in identifying
weak links and result in effective implementation of various components of the programme.
(Para 17.9)
XVIII. NATIONAL TOBACCO CONTROL PROGRAMME (NTCP)
The Committee was informed last year that the ‘in principle’ approval of the
Planning Commission for setting up of the National Regulatory Authority and Referral Labs
for testing Tar and Nicotine content in various tobacco products has been obtained. Process
for seeking approval of the competent authority had already begun at that time. The
Committee, however, notes that no progress seems to have been made in this regard
thereafter. Keeping in view the prolonged process of getting the approval of the competent
authority, the Committee does not have much hope about the same being obtained by June,
2008. The Department has to make concerted efforts so that approval of the competent
authority for setting up of the National Regulatory Authority, backbone of the entire
programme is obtained at the earliest. (Para 18.4)
More than one million people are dying due to consumption of tobacco in the country.
The Committee, therefore, strongly feels that the Ministry needs to bring up sustained
Mass Media/IEC campaign regarding the adverse and harmful effects of tobacco
consumption immediately, as also when NTCP is launched. Sufficient funds should be made
available for the same. (Para 18.5)

XIX. NATIONAL MENTAL HEALTH PROGRAMME (NMHP)
The Committee is constrained to note that in spite of approved outlay being
drastically reduced to nearly half for the National Mental Health Programme, the
expenditure reported upto 29th February, 2008 is a meager Rs.14.13 crores. A proposal for
releasing funds to the extent of Rs.22.165 crore (including Rs.4.71 crore for NE) was stated
to be under consideration. The Committee takes a serious view of the continuing trend of
poor utilization of funds earmarked for the programme. (Para 19.4)
The Committee is dismayed at the fact that the expansion of the National Mental

recommends the Department to present its case strongly and effectively so as to get
necessary approval without further delay. Further, the Department can not simply shy away
from its responsibility by stating that progress of the events in these schemes depends on
the active cooperation of the State Governments and other stake holders. The Committee,
accordingly, recommends the Department to approach and have regular interactions with the
State Governments concerned and identify the problem areas which need to be addressed.

in the programme actively and furnish proposals with all requisite information to enable
release and utilization of the funds optimally. The Committee would like to be informed of

CARDIOV ASCULAR DISEASES STROKE (NPDCS)
The Committee is happy to note that the pilot phase of the programme has finally

XXI. MEDICAL EDUCATION
The Committee is aware that keeping in view the shortage of doctors and existing
medical institutions not being adequate enough, MCI norms for opening of colleges/increase
of seats need to be reviewed. The Committee, however, feels that this exercise should be
undertaken with extreme caution and objective of imparting quality medical education
remaining intact. Relaxing norms by allowing private promoters to have land in two pieces

89
within 10 Kms. of each other and allowing corporate entities to setup medical colleges are
initiatives which should be implemented after examining all pros and cons. The Committee
is of the opinion that in the exercise of relaxation of existing norms, assessment of those
experts having the experience of this field should be given due weightage. (Para 21.4)
The Committee also takes note of the suggestion of the Department to MCI for
relaxing the age of retirement of staff of private medical educational institutes from 65 to
70 years, subject to their physical ability, in order to fill-up the acute shortage of teaching
staff in that sector. Secretary, Department of Health and Family Welfare has also informed
the Committee that a Cabinet Note has been prepared for increasing the age of retirement
to 65 years in Government Medical Educational Institutes. Committee is also given to
understand that PG degrees of USA, UK, Australia, New Zealand and Canada have been
recognized and for other countries like Germany and France the matter is under
consideration. The idea is that they can come and settle here or they can come as visiting
faculties. The Committee welcomes these steps. (Para 21.5)
On being asked as to whether any mechanism was in place to check this, the
Secretary, Department of Health and Family Welfare stated that at present there is no
mechanism to prevent Indian students from going abroad to study. The Committee is of the
view that the Department needs to devise an effective mechanism, which could include a
legislation, so that Indian medical students can be prevented from going to such places
whose educational system does not match with ours. The Committee would like to be
informed about the steps taken by the Department in this regard. (Para 21.6)
The Committee is anguished to note that the fate of so many students of the
remaining 18 medical colleges, who have already appeared in their final examination,
remains undecided. The Committee is of the view that the students should not suffer due
to such technicalities and bureaucratic hurdles. A decision without any further delay may
be taken in the matter. A Status Note on such colleges may also be submitted to the
Committee. (Para 21.7)
The Committee opines that if implemented, the recommendations of the Commission
would be a milestone in improving the standards and quality of medical education in India.
The Committee recommends action may be initiated in this regard and Committee apprised
accordingly. (Para 21.9)
XXII. V ACANCIES IN CGHS CADRE
The Committee is constrained to observe that the Department was able to achieve
little progress in filling up the vacant posts during the last one year. As informed to this
Committee the joining rate of the GDMOs is very less. The Committee, therefore,
recommends the Department to enhance its efforts in the right direction by identifying the
problem areas and devising a strategy to counter such problems in all sub-cadre posts at the
earliest. The Committee would like to be informed about the steps taken by it to fill up
vacancies in the different sub-cadres. (Para 22.2)
Now that the Sixth Pay Commission has submitted its recommendations, the
Committee would recommend to the Department to expedite the implementation of the
Javed Chaudhary Committee recommendations. The Committee would like to be informed
of the progress made in this regard. (Para 22.3)
The Committee views with serious concern the grave injustice done to the GDMO
cadre for no fault of theirs. Inspite of their being eligible for specialist post, continuance
of such doctors in GDMO cadre is indeed against all principles of natural justice. Non-

90
implementation of Fifth Pay Commission recommendation of SAG level positions in All
India Service to be 17% of total cadre has created another hurdle in their career
progression. The Committee finds that Sixth Pay Commission recommendation of filling up
the additional posts to be created for fulfilling any gap by direct recruitment will make the
position of GDMOs very vulnerable. The Committee is of the firm opinion that the
Department should take up this issue immediately with the Ministry of Finance. Every
attempt should be made to remove the grave injustice done to the GDMO cadre so that this
sub-cadre of professionals gets due recognition and morale boost like others in All India
services. (Para 22.5)
XXIII. NEW SCHEMES
The Committee is dismayed to note that every year the Department announces new
schemes/programmes, many of which are without finalizing the modalities and proper
ground work, thereby resulting in under or no utilization of funds. The Committee
recommends to the Department to enhance its efforts to complete all necessary formalities
and launch the programmes at the earliest so that funds do not get blocked in such
schemes. (Para 23.2)
XXIV. MISCELLANEOUS
The Committee recommends the Department to take care of the eco-friendly part of
the whole exercise. (Para 24.1)
The Committee recommends the Department to work out modalities for establishing
specialized kidney centres immediately and in the meantime approach the Planning
Commission for funds with a proposal to improve dialysis facility in the country. In view
of increasing gap in demand and supply, at least the well known Institutes across India
should be provided with the dialysis machines during the current financial year. The
Committee would like to be informed about the steps taken by the Department in this
regard. (Para 24.2)

requirement of health infrastructure in the country. In a vast country like ours, rigid
norms based on population only and made uniformly applicable were perhaps not proving to
be justified and not based on ground realities. The Committee is also of the view that
change in the norms for health infrastructure proposed by the Planning Commission was
called for. The Committee is, however, not aware whether any preparatory exercise has been
initiated for conducting surveys as per the revised norms. The Committee is afraid that if
this issue is allowed to linger on for long, the very objective of NRHM of bridging gaps in
the health care will continue to be a distant dream. The Committee, accordingly, impresses
upon the Department to initiate action at the earliest. (Para 3.2)

The Committee has its apprehensions regarding the effectivity of ASHA as a
multipurpose social health activist, as envisaged under the NRHM. The Committee observes
that job responsibilities of ASHA are manifold as indicated below:—
– awareness generation-Health, RCH, HIV/AIDS.
– advising newly married couples for their special needs.
– guiding pregnant women for availing of institutional facilities for Anti-Natal,
Natal and Post-Natal needs.
– counselling on nutrition, pregnancy, breast-feeding, immunization and family
planning.
– establishing link with PHCs, private providers and others for service requirement
of beneficiaries.
– mobilising parents for child survival interventions.
– promoting basic sanitization.
– provision of non-clinical spacing contraceptives.
– surveillance of communicable diseases. (Para 3.12)

95
ASHA is also the primary provider for National Health Programme. She is the Depot
Holder for health commodities like Vitamin A, Impregnated bed nets, ORS etc. She is also
supposed to handle treatment of minor ailments. Another  major task assigned to ASHA is
to provide escort services for women seeking delivery services at institutions, requiring
emergency care and MTP services, women and men for clinical contraception services and
VCTC. The Committee has been given to understand that States have also taken up the
training of ASHAs on diagnosis of malaria cases. For being eligible for ASHA, a woman has
to be 25 to 35 years of age, married, resident of the village, acceptable to the village and
community and proficient in reading and writing. The Committee fails to understand as to
how a single woman, who is a simple villager can take care of one thousand population by
performing such wide-ranging tasks. Situation becomes more complex and well away from
ground realities when one finds that only remuneration payable to  ASHA is for pr oviding
Escort Services. Instances of Escort Services may not be very frequent some times.
The Committee strongly feels that ASHA is supposed to  play a very challenging role.
(Para 3.13)
The Committee is of the view that with the passage of time, the number of
responsibilities of ASHA will itself become a challenge for her to cope up with. This will not
only reflect in the quality of her work and performance but ultimately fail in fulfilling the
very objectives with which the initiative was initially conceptualized. As the initiative is still
in the early stages, the Committee suggests that the Department should review the
responsibilities entrusted to  the ASHA. As the initiative is still in the early stages, the
Committee suggests that the Department should review the responsibilities entrusted to  the
ASHA. Committee’s attention has been drawn by the findings of Common Review Mission
which conducted appraisal of NRHM in November, 2007, 16 months after NRHM got final
Cabinet approval in July, 2006. Appraisal was based on one-two districts in A.P., Assam,
Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Orissa, M.P., Gujarat, J&K, Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu, Tripura, U.P.  and
West Bengal. The Committee notes that performance assessment of ASHA has led to  mixed
findings in different States. Non-payment against activities/conflicts regarding compensation
money and lack of role clarity between ASHAs and AWWs are two major problem areas
identified. The Committee apprehends that situation may worsen with more complexities
arising in future. The Committee is, therefore, of the view that role of ASHA needs to  be
reassessed and reformulated. (Para 3.14)
Rural Health functionaries
The Committee observes that the recommendations of Task Force like local
preference, contractual appointments for filling short-term gaps, convergence with AYUSH
for overcoming the constraints of shortage of health manpower programme do not seem to
have made much impact. The Committee finds that the appraisal of Common Review
Mission conducted in November, 2007 has highlighted the shortage of manpower at all levels
in Sub-Centres/PHCs/CHCs in Andhra Pradesh, Assam, Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Gujarat, J&K,
M.P., Orissa, Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu, Tripura, U.P.  and West Bengal. The Committee is of
the view that it is high time that this critical appraisal is followed by an action plan for
making available the required manpower in these States. The Department has to  play a pro-
active role without any further delay. One must not forget that the very objective of NRHM
of strengthening of primary health infrastructure rests on the availability of key health
functionaries at the right places. (Para 3.15)
Mobile Medical Units (MMUs)
Against such a backdrop, chances of improvement do not seem to be possible in the
near future. The Committee understands that many States are having their own set-up of

96
ambulances which seem to be functioning well. There are also States where NGOs are
involved in providing this service. The Committee feels that based on the findings of
Common Review Mission in respect of some States, steps may be taken for strengthening
the facility of MMUs.
The Committee had the opportunity to apprise itself about the key findings of the
appraisal conducted by the Common Review Mission in November, 2007. The study is based
on team visits made to one or two districts in Andhra Pradesh, Assam, Bihar, Chhattisgarh,
Orissa, M.P., Gujarat, J&K, Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu, Tripura, U.P. and West Bengal. The
Committee finds that assessment of NRHM on 24 parameters has been made through this
appraisal. The Committee takes note of the constraints being faced by these States in the
implementation of NRHM and the recommendations on the areas that need strengthening
and course correction. While appreciating this initiative, the Committee is of the view that
such an appraisal needs to be followed by intensive interaction with all the implementing
agencies in the States at the earliest. Otherwise the very purpose of undertaking such an
exercise will be defeated. The Committee also strongly feels that such Common Review
Missions should be conducted in all the States, with one region being taken at a time. It
would also be a good idea if two-three performing and non-performing districts in each State
are taken together for making an comparative analysis. Incorporation of surprise visits will
make the assessment more realistic. (Para 3.16)
IV. NATIONAL VECTOR BORNE DISEASE CONTROL PROGRAMME (NVBDCP)
The Committee notes that like in the previous years, funds provided in 2007-08
remained under-utilised. Expenditure reported upto 29.02.08 is Rs.283.74 crore. Secretary,
while deposing before the Committee had mentioned that by 31.03.2008, expenditure figures
stood at Rs.385.38 crore, indicating 96.46% utilisation of allocated funds of Rs.399.50 crore.
The Committee is constrained to point out that instead of there being an improvement,
position has worsened in 2007-08. An amount of Rs.102.00 crore being spent in the last
month of the financial year calls for serious introspection. The Committee has been
repeatedly impressing upon the Department for initiating corrective measures in this
regard. Reasons like delay in procurement process, submission of SOE/UCs by States/UTs
and non-recruitment of required staff seem to have persisted in 2007-08 also. (Para 4.2)
The Committee strongly feels that mere chalking out an elaborate Action Plan and
allocation of funds for control of a major disease does not seem to make any sense if year
after year same constraints seem to persist. The Committee once again tries to impress
upon the Department to take immediate steps for removal of bottlenecks in the successful
implementation of Malaria Control Programme. The Committee would like to mention
that under the National Vector Borne Disease Control Programme, major component is
Malaria Control having the maximum allocation of Rs.351.68 crore out of a provision of
Rs.440.03 crores for the entire programme in 2008-09. Therefore, it is in the fitness of
things that concerted efforts are also made for optimum and judicious utilisation of
allocated funds. (Para 4.3)
The Committee is alarmed by the trend of Pf cases reported from these States.
Committee’s attention has also been drawn to quantum jump of number of malaria deaths
reported in the country. In 2006,1639 deaths were reported against 963 deaths occurring in
2005. By November, 2007, this figure has already reached 807. The Committee has every
reason to apprehend that actual figures of deaths may be higher than what is officially
recorded. Reason being there is no mechanism at present to independently verify the field
level figures for any State. (Para 4.5)

97
The Committee has been persistently drawing the attention of the Department to the
urgent need for implementation of all malaria control measures in Malaria endemic States
of NE Region, Orissa and West Bengal. The Committee is well aware that NE States
together contribute 4% of the country’s population, 12% of malaria cases, 18% of Pf cases
and 54% of the total malaria related deaths reported in the country during 2006. Figures
must have remained unchanged in 2007 also. Another  cause of concern is increasing trend
of resistance to conventional anti-malarial drug Chloroquine noticed in NE States. The
Committee notes that Global Fund supported Intensified Malaria Control Project in NE
States being implemented since July, 2005 with a contribution of US $ 30 million for
the first two years of the project also seems to have failed to have the desired impact.
(Para 4.6)
The Committee notes that increased supervision and monitoring is one of the main
strategies adopted for effective control of malaria. The latest figures made available to the
Committee reveal continuance of shortage of surveillance and supervisory staff in NE States.
In Assam, the biggest State of NE Region, against the sanctioned posts of 694 Health
Supervisor (Male) only 570 were in position, against 343 Health Supervisor (Female), there
were 316 and only 1647 MPW(M) against 3080 sanctioned posts. What is more disturbing is
that while Tripura failed to furnish the data, Meghalaya and Nagaland have provided
incomplete information. The primary role of MPW (M) and MPW (F) is door to door
surveillance and detection of communicable diseases and it’s reporting. The fact that these
functionaries play a vital role in disease detection and surveillance cannot be ignored. By not
appointing these functionaries, the States leave a big gap at the field-level disease
surveillance, detection and treatment. This vital issue needs to be pursued at the highest level
in the concerned States. The other strategy adopted is use of Rapid Diagnostic Kits by ASHAs.
The Committee does not have high expectation from this initiative as firstly required number
of ASHAs have to be in place in malaria endemic States and even if they are there, they
would be over-burdened with the various tasks already assigned to them. The Committee fails
to comprehend the continuance of such a discouraging situation inspite of special dispensation
for NE States. The Committee can only reiterate that there is need for drastic measures and
extensive monitoring under the supervision of State Nodal Officers. (Para 4.7)
Kala-azar
The Committee strongly feels that effective surveillance, timely treatment and
compliance of treatment regimens in all PHCs would lead to better reports in 2008. The
Committee is of the view that only if intensive monitoring at all levels is carried out, the
goal of elimination of Kala-azar by 2010 can be made achievable. Situation so far has not
been very encouraging. All the quantifiable objectives listed in the Action Plan for 2008-09
need to be closely monitored on monthly basis. (Para 4.9)
Japanese Encephalitis
The Committee is dismayed to note that despite various methods adopted by the
Department over the past year to contain the disease, the number of cases reported to be
suffering from JE/AES has shown an increase over the previous year figures. The fact is
even more disturbing that though the Department claims to have completed 99.97%
immunization in the past year in 7 worst affected districts in Uttar Pradesh, the situation
there has worsened with 2675 cases and 577 deaths in 2007 (till December) over the 2006
figures of 2320 cases and 528 deaths. The Committee fails to comprehend as to why inspite
of a number of preventive measures taken by the Central Government in co-ordination with
the State Government of Uttar Pradesh, the JE/AES related cases and deaths continue to

98
be high in the State. The Committee apprehends that the actual figures would increase the
tally much further. The Committee would like to take the opportunity to State that though
the data for Assam has not been made available by the Department, going by the fact sheet
of 2006, it is apprehensive that the situation in Assam would also show a similar trend as
that of U.P. (Para 4.10)
The Committee would like to draw the attention of the Department to the fact that
the year 2006 had reported a visible impact of preventive measures initiated by registering
a declining trend when compared with 2005 figures. Quantum jump in the first three
quarter of 2007 calls for a serious review with special focus on Assam and U.P., the two
main endemic States. The Committee would impress upon the Department that analysis of
epidemiological and entomological data for epidemic outbreak prediction and timely remedial
measures is required to be carried out on an urgent basis.
The Committee feels that perhaps the precautionary methods adopted by the
Department have not percolated properly to the affected population because of which the
disease has once again registered an increase. The Committee adds that lax monitoring of
the disease by the central as well as the State Government could aggravate the situation
further unless it is dealt with a sense of urgency. It suggests the Department to undertake
on-the-spot review of the situation as to the possible causes for upsurge in the reported
cases. The Committee urges the Department to step-up the ongoing IEC activities in the
endemic States so that the desired objective is reached soon. (Para 4.11)
Dengue/Dengue Haemorrhagic Fever/Chikungunya
Incidence of Chikungunya cases in the country during 2006 and 2007 has led the
Committee to the conclusion that various initiatives taken by the Department have so far
failed to yield any desired results. The Committee strongly feels that with the enhanced
allocation of Rs.14.59 crore in 2008-09 for Dengue and Chikungunya, effective measures are
required to be undertaken in the affected States. Mere circulation of detailed guidelines and
advisories for prevention and control of these diseases to all affected States would not serve
any purpose. What is required is to identify the affected districts and go for regular fever
surveillance in such endemic areas to detect an unusual trend. The Committee is of the
view that if this analysis of ground reality is followed by IEC activities and strengthening
of apex Referral Institutions for diagnosis and treatment, number of Dengue/Chikungunya
cases would show a declining trend. The Committee apprehends that unless adequate
remedial measures are taken, sporadic outburst of these diseases would continue to be
reported from different States every year. (Para 4.17)
V. NATIONAL T. B. CONTROL PROGRAMME
The Committee appreciates the successful implementation of RNTCP Phase-I and
ongoing Phase-II. Several initiatives/interventions taken at different levels and variety of
implementing agencies have contributed to the increasing population coverage and 85% cure
rate. However, India still contributes 20% of TB cases reported in the world. Out of 8.8
million cases per annum, 1.8 million cases are from India alone. New complex off shoots of
TB also keep on emerging, the most visible being worsening HIV epidemic increasing the
number of TB cases. The Committee notes that HIV is the most potent risk factor for
progression of TB infection to disease form. HIV-TB patients detected in 2005 were 12,062,
13,614 in 2006 and 18,559 in 2007. The Committee is aware that increase in number of
co-infected (HIV-TB) patients being detected over the last three years is a result of innovative
and co-ordinated measures taken by the Department. But the other dimension of this trend

99
is increasing complexities involved in the treatment of such cases. The Committee hopes that
the National Framework formulated by RNTCP and NACP for joint TB/HIV collaborative
activities will lead to better and effective control of this emerging problem area. (Para 5.4)
The Committee observes that the other major challenge to TB control in the country
is increasing number of MDR- TB cases. The Committee is aware that such cases are bound
to increase the magnitude and severity of TB epidemic and pose a major threat to TB
control. The Committee in its earlier Report has pointed out that 7% defaulters in a year
is quite a significant number of cases remaining untreated or half-treated. With a single
TB patient infecting 10-15 persons in a year, rate of infection is bound to increase. The
Committee would like to point out that formulation of guidelines for management of MDR
TB cases and publication thereof will not prove to be sufficient enough. The Committee had
given a simple suggestion for identifying the defaulter TB patients from the records being
maintained at centres/hospitals with the help of NGOs/Social Workers and Private
Practitioners. Intention of the Committee was to identify such cases at the first default
stage itself. The Committee finds that under a new initiative a total of 50 MDR- TB patients
were to be registered for treatment in Gujarat and Maharashtra during 2007-08 to be
doubled every year subsequently and ultimately in the entire country. While welcoming this
initiative, the Committee would also like to point out that cost of MDR- TB treatment is
300 times more than non-MDR TB. The Committee can only say that preventive measures
will be both cost-effective and helpful for the patients. The Committee is of the firm
opinion that through effective IEC activities and alertness of health workers regular intake
of medicines can be easily monitored. The Committee, therefore, suggests that monitoring
of TB patients—the most vital aspect, should not be ignored at any cost. (Para 5.5)
The Committee is disappointed to note that in spite of repeated cautioning by it
regarding the issue of unspent balances being carried forward to the next year there has
been no improvement in the situation. Despite various measures like training of

the Department, the expenditure figures in respect of many of the States reveal that huge

seen little change over the past year. From the information provided by the Department to
a specific query regarding allocation and utilization of funds for the year 2007-08 a very

VI. NATIONAL LEPROSY ERADICATION PROGRAMME (NLEP)
The Committee in its 22nd Report, had voiced its serious concern for
under-utilisation of allocated funds in 2006-07 due to unspent balances in majority of
the States. The Committee takes note of detailed analysis of actual expenditure pattern in
2006-07 carried out by the Department. The Committee is surprised to observe that even
this detailed analysis indicates provisional figures of 77.59% of utilisation of allocated funds
by the States. The Committee’s concern is further deepened by the fact that the two major
States Bihar and Jharkhand could utilize only 33.9% and 30% of the allocated funds during
the year 2006-07. Creation of confusion due to merger of the leprosy society with the State
Health Society under NRHM has been cited as the main reason for this position. The
Committee has been given to understand that a number of measures like review of
programme performance and expenditure pattern in the quarterly review meetings of
district Leprosy Officers streamlining of procurement procedure and monitoring at the
central level were initiated during 2007-08. The Committee also notes that more focus was

101
given on implementation of Action Plan during annual meeting and quarterly review
meetings of State Programme Officers. Not only this the States were also instructed to
prepare a month-wise Action Plan of IEC and Training from July, 2007 onwards and
submitting the monthly implementation reports of these activities. The Committee is
however, constrained to observe that these elaborate measures initiated by the Department
failed to make any visible impact as the ground realities continue to remain unchanged.
Drastic reduction of allocated funds had to be made at RE stage in 2007-08 with even that
provision remaining under-utilised upto 29.02.08. (Para 6.2)
The Committee is apprehensive that an enhanced allocation during 2008-09 may also
face similar outcomes. The Committee feels that though the plan of action under the
programme is well prepared, monitoring the timely and proper utilization of funds needs to
be taken on a more serious note. Mere advisories to State Implementing Agencies will not
serve the purpose. It, therefore, recommends that the Department take up the issue with
the State Programme Officers especially of Bihar and Jharkhand in an emphatic manner
during its quarterly review meetings. (Para 6.3)
The Committee welcomes the initiatives taken by the Department to provide
reconstruction treatment to leprosy disabled persons. The Committee would appreciate if
modalities for implementing this new scheme are finalised at the earliest. The Committee
would appreciate if this scheme takes off at the earliest. The Committee would, however,
emphasize that strict monitoring should be ensured so that really needy persons are
benefited. Adequate publicity also needs to be given. All the stake-holders both
implementing agencies and targeted beneficiaries, need to be made aware of this new
initiative proposed under the programme. (Para 6.5)
VII. NATIONAL PROGRAMME FOR CONTROL OF BLINDNESS
The Committee, is, however, surprised to find that implementation of new initiatives
depends on the approval of EFC Memo by the Ministry of Finance and CCEA. Till then, the
funds allocated for 2008-09 will continue to be utilized as per the existing scheme approved
for the Tenth Plan. The Committee is not happy with this state of affairs. Second year of
Eleventh Plan has already started and by the time approval of the competent authority is
finally received, the year 2008-09 would be nearing its end. The Committee would like to
point out that some of the new initiatives like construction of dedicated Eye Wings/Eye
OTs in District Hospitals, appointment of manpower, development of mobile Ophthalmic
Units in NE States will have to undergo a number of procedural formalities before their
actually taking off. The Committee accordingly recommends that concerted efforts need to
be made for getting the formal approval at the earliest. The Committee would appreciate
if simultaneously preparatory activities are also started. (Para 7.4)
The Committee has been taking note of instances of malfunctioning of Eye Camps
reported in the Media in the different States. The Committee feels that monitoring of Eye
Camps is being exclusively done by the District Blindness Control Societies. Department’s
role starts as and when reports regarding malfunctioning of Eye Camps held in States are
brought to the notice of the Ministry. Corrective measures are accordingly taken by the
Ministry. The Committee, however, feels that the Department needs to be more pro-active
in such cases. One corrective measure which can be initiated by the Department without
any special efforts involved is to review the performance of such Eye Camps in the State
level meetings, with required follow-up action taken on the reported incidents of
malfunctioning of Eye Camps. The Committee is also of the view that follow-up treatment
after Eye Camps should be made mandatory and strictly enforced. District hospital

102
authorities also need to be involved in the conducting of such Eye Camps by introduction
of compulsory, pre-checks in Eye Camps before start of Eye surgery and other treatment.
The Committee would like to add here that the Department should also devise some method
of surprise inspection of such eye camps organized by the NGOs to facilitate cataract
operations. This, the Committee feels, would ensure stricter compliance by all the concerned
entities and help reduce eyes mishaps. The Committee notes that the process for
independent evaluation of NPCB including evaluation of work being done by NGOs has been
initiated. The Committee would appreciate if this exercise is expedited so that corrective
measures are taken at the earliest. (Para 7.5)
The Committee is not convinced that the IEC activities are being carried out as
intensely as is stated by the Department. The Committee has been given to understand that
out of the total allocated budget under National Programme for Control of Blindness,
around 7% has been spent on IEC, which according to the Committee, is quite a sizable
amount. The Committee strongly feels that public awareness about the noble cause of eye
donation for blind persons continues to be very low. The Committee is of the view that a
review of IEC activities on this aspect need to be made in consultation with all the stake
holders, specially reputed Eye Hospitals/NGOs doing commendable work in this area and
also both Government and private ad agencies. The Committee would also like to emphasise
that the functioning of Eye Banks in the country requires to be reviewed in view of reported
lack of logistic support for timely collection of eyes by the Eye Banks. Steps also to need
to be taken for increasing the number of Eye Banks in the country. (Para. 7.7)
The Committee notes with disappointment that the target to bring prevalence of
blindness to 0.8% by 2007 has not been reached. The Department has informed that as per
the report of Rapid Survey on Avoidable Blindness (2007), the prevalence of blindness has
come down to 1% and that Cataract remains the single largest cause of blindness, low
vision and one eye blindness in India. The Committee also infers from the above study that
the prevalence of blindness due to Trachoma also continues to be there. It is a well known
fact that blindness is a bane of nature. The Committee believes that most of the people in
smaller towns and rural areas are not aware of the symptoms of the above ailments, and
the methods to manage eye care, their eye-care service seeking behavior pattern do not
change. The Committee exhorts the Department to take all possible necessary steps to
devise IEC activities in local media and television channels so that awareness among the
people is increased. The Committee believes a lot of cases of blindness can be checked by
such a measure and would in the long run help to achieve the targeted goals under the
programme. (Para 7.9)

Maharasthra, Andhra Pradesh, Kerala and Gujarat are reported to be performing well
during 2007-08. The Committee however notes that 25% of Rs. 793 crores utilized under
Mission Flexipool were used for other activities under NRHM. The Committee would like to
have an idea about the details of such activities. (Para 9.11)
Reports are being received from various sources that there is a lot more to the
compensation received from under the programme than is visible to the naked eye. There
are instances when institutional deliveries are being falsely reported and the entire
compensation package is being misused/misappropriated. (Para 9.12)
The Committee feels that monitoring mechanism for such Schemes needs to be very
effective so that no grey areas are there to be misused by unscrupulous persons. The
Committee would like to have a Status Note on the procedure of verification of claims and
release of compensation package under the programme. The Committee also strongly feels
that community participation is encouraged so as to keep a watchful eye on the activities
of Implementing agencies under the Scheme. The Committee would also appreciate if an
assessment is made about the impact of JSY on the lowering of Maternal Mortality Rate
in the crucial States. (Para 9.13)
ROUTINE IMMUNISATION PROGRAMME
The Committee has been observing that State specific problems specially in the low
performing States continue to persist. Shortage of Health Workers, lack of awareness and
laxity in monitoring and supervision of the programme are some of the problems being
noticed in such States. Reported coverage of different vaccines under the Routine
Immunization Programme confirms the Committee’s apprehensions that in some of the
States like Arunachal Pradesh, Bihar, Jharkhand, Manipur, position is very unsatisfactory.
The Committee would like to point out that the steps taken for strengthening the Routine
Immunization Programme like recruitment of health workers, regular reviews at all levels
and catch up rounds in poor performing States do not seem to have yielded the desired
results. The Committee can only say that catch-up rounds in poor performance States with
the districts identified before hand is the most important step for effective reduction in the
number of un-immunized and partially immunized children. Entire focus of the
Implementing agencies should be on this alone. (Para 9.15)
The Committee understands that the three pioneer Institutes namely Central
Research Institute (CRI), Kasauli in Himachal Pradesh, Pasteur Institute of India (PTI),
Koonoor, Tamil Nadu and the BCG Vaccine Laboratory (BCGVL) in Chennai, Tamil Nadu
have been directed to stop vaccine production. The Committee strongly feels that these
vaccine production units should not be converted to only testing laboratories. The
Committee accordingly, recommends that the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare should
withdraw the order without delay. (Para 9.16)
