State facilitators have been deputed in Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, Orissa, Uttarakhand and
NE States to facilitate the training programme.
ASHAs are performing various tasks. National Health System Resource Centre (NHSRC) is
reviewing the ‘job responsib ilities’ and “Role clarity of ASHA”.
Recommendations/Observations
3.13 ASHA is also the primary provider for National Health Programme. She is the Depot Holder
for health commodities like Vitamin A. Impregnated bed nets. ORS etc. She is also supposed to
handle treatment of minor ailments. Another major task assigned to ASHA is to provide escort
services for women seeking delivery services at institutions, requiring emergency care and MTP
services, women and men for clinical contraception services and VCTC. The Committee has been

91
given to understand that States have also taken up the training of ASHAs on diagnosis of malaria
cases. For being eligible for ASHA. a woman has to be 25 to 35 years of age, married, resident
of the village, acceptable to the village and community and proficient in reading and writing. The
Committee fails to understand as to how a single woman, who is a simple villager, can take care
of one thousand population by performing such wide-ranging tasks. Situation becomes more
complex and well away from ground realities when one finds that only remuneration payable to

Action Taken
ASHA is already performing wide ranging tasks for which incentives are being given. The
list of remuneration and activities is at Annexure-V.
Recommendations/Observations
3.14 The Committee is of the view that with the passage of time, the number of responsibilities
of ASHA will itself become a challenge for her to cope up with. This will not only reflect in the
quality of her work and performance but ultimately fail in fulfilling the very objectives with which
the initiative was initially conceptualized. As the initiative is still in the early stages, the Committee

We agree with the observations. Accordingly, NHSRC has agreed to review the
responsibilities of ASHA, AWW and ANM.
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE
The Committee notes with a sense of relief that the Department has at last come to
concur with the observations of the Committee regarding its apprehensions on the role clarity
and feasibility of discharging the duties assigned to ASHA. The Committee would like to state
here that these apprehensions were voiced by it in earlier reports so that the objective with

Department has stated in its Action Taken Note that National Health System Resource Centre
(NHSRC) is reviewing the ‘job r esponsibilities’ and “Role clarity of ASHA” as well as that of
AWW and ANM. The Committee observes that the Department has not specified any
timeframe, within which NHSRC would be completing its review. In the meantime, these
Social Health Activists would continue discharging their duties originally mandated with the
likelihood of new ones adding to their responsibilities. The NHSRC has to complete its review
in a time bound manner so that such an important health initiative does not become
redundant. The Committee, therefore, urges upon the Department to ensure the timely
submission of the Report by NHSRC, followed by expeditious implementation of the same.

NATIONAL VECTOR BORNE DISEASE CONTROL  PROGRAMME
Recommendations/Observations
4.7 The Committee notes that increased supervision and monitoring is one of the main strategies
adopted for effective control of malaria. The latest figures made available to the Committee reveal

NE Region, Assam against sanctioned posts of 694 Health Supervisor (Male) only 570 were in

The fact that these functionaries play a vital role in disease detection and surveillance cannot be

the concerned States. The other strategy adopted is use of Rapid Diagnostic Kits by ASHAs. The
Committee does not have high expectation from this initiative as firstly, required numbers of ASHAs
have to be in place in malaria endemic States and even if they are there, they would be over-
burdened with the various tasks already assigned to them. The Committee fails to comprehend the
continuance of such a discouraging situation inspite of special dispensation for NE States. The
Committee can only reiterate that there is need for drastic measures and extensive monitoring under
the supervision of State Nodal Officers.

JAPANESE ENCEPHALITIS
Recommendations/Observations
4.10 Japanese Encephalitis (JE) is a viral disease with a tendency of seasonal outbreaks. JE has
been reported repeatedly from 15 States out of which, Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Haryana, Karnataka,
Kerala, Maharashtra, Manipur, Tamil Nadu, Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal have been reporting
repeated outbreaks. There is no specific anti viral drug for JE and cases are managed
symptomatically. Efforts have been directed to provide technical support and strengthen capabilities
of States through training to tackle this disease. A vaccination programme for children between 1
and 15 years of age under the Universal Immunization Programme, using single dose live attenuated
SA-14-14-2 vaccine has been launched in 2006. In 2006, 11 districts in 4 States were covered
which was expanded to 28 districts in 10 States during 2007. A total of 93.08 lakh children were
vaccinated against the target of 105.31 lakh children achieving 88.39% coverage. As per the Annual

95
Report, 2007-08, the vaccination campaign has so far been completed in Assam (89%), Haryana
(86%), West Bengal (61 %) and in 7 districts of Uttar Pradesh (99.7%).
The Committee is dismayed to note that despite various methods adopted by the Department
over the past year, to contain the disease, the number of cases reported to be suffering from JE/
AES has shown an increase over the previous year figures. The fact is even more disturbing that
though the Department claims to have completed 99.97% immunization in the past year in 7 worst
affected districts in Uttar Pradesh, the situation there has worsened with 2675 cases and 577
deaths in 2007 (till December) over the 2006 figures of 2320 cases and 528 deaths. The Committee
fails to comprehend as to why inspite of a number of preventive measures taken by the Central
Government in co-ordination with the State Government of Uttar Pradesh, the JE/AES related cases
and deaths continue to be high in the State. The Committee apprehends that the actual figures
would increase the tally much further. The Committee would like to take the opportunity to State
that though the data for Assam has not been made available by the Department, going by the fact
sheet of 2006, it is apprehensive that the situation in Assam would also show a similar trend as
that of U.P.
Action Taken
About 88% was covered during 2007 in 27 districts. 4022 cases and 963 deaths were
reported.
Infection with JE virus may be asymptomatic or may cause febrile illness, meningitis,
myelitis or encephalitis. Encephalitis is the most commonly recognized presentation of JE and is
clinically indistinguishable from other causes of acute encephalitis syndrome (AES) which may
include meningococcal meningitis, TB meningo encephalitis, viral encephalitis, JE, Cerebrospinal
meningitis and even cerebral malaria, hence since 2006 Dte. of NVBDCP issued guidelines to report
JE under AES. The CSF/sera samples collected for AES cases are subjected to serological testing
and for the past three years, JE positivity has fallen from 39% in 2005 to 14.2% and 13% in 2006
and 2007 respectively. Though 51 Sentinel sites with manpower and equipment for serological
testing have been identified in 12 JE endemic States by Dte. NVBDCP, all the samples are not
tested due to constraints in laboratory testing. Secondly, in Eastern Uttar Pradesh, apart from JE
other viruses like enterovirus (EV76&89 strains) are circulating in the community which was
established by NIV, Pune during 2006 as out of 306 CSF and 179 sera samples, only 36% and
18% JE positivity was reported from these samples. In addition, 21.56% (EV76&89 strains) and
1.96% Coxsackie ‘B’ was detected in 6 CSF samples. It is pertinent to note that vaccination is
given against JE only.
Recommendations/Observations
4.11 The Committee would like to draw the attention of the Department to the fact that the
year 2006 had reported a visible impact of preventive measures initiated by registering a declining
trend when compared with 2005 figures. Quantum jump in the first three quarter of 2007 calls for
a serious review with special focus on Assam and U.P. the two main endemic States. The
Committee would impress upon the Department that analysis of epidemiological and entomological
data for epidemic outbreak prediction and timely remedial measures is required to be carried out
on an urgent basis.
The Committee feels that perhaps the precautionary methods adopted by the Department
have not percolated properly to the affected population because of which the disease has once
again registered an increase. The Committee adds that lax monitoring of the disease by the Central
as well as the State Governments could aggravate the situation further unless it is dealt with a
sense of urgency. It suggests the Department to undertake on-the-spot review of the situation as

96
to the possible causes for upsurge in the reported cases. The Committee urges the Department to
step up the ongoing mc activities in the endemic States so that the desired objective is reached
soon.
Action Taken
The JE situation in Eastern UP is reviewed at regular intervals by Additional DG and
Director, NICD. The last meeting was held on 12.05.08. Apart from above, Dte. of NVBDCP set
up JE sub-office and Vector Borne Disease Control unit (VBDCU) in Gorakhpur in February and
April, 2007 respectively. The main task assigned to the sub-office of VBDCU is to closely monitor
JE situation by making field visits, collecting entomological/epidemiological data, analyzing and
interpreting the same in consultation with Dte. of NVBDCP and sharing it with district authorities
for immediate remedial measures. During 2007, two multidisciplinary Central Teams were deputed
to Gorakhpur and Saharanpur districts (30.7.07 to 6.8.07) and 25-31 October respectively.
Recommendations of both these teams were discussed with concerned State/district officials for
immediate corrective measures. The States are also supported by providing funds for various JE
components. JE kits are also supplied to all JE endemic States by Dte. NVBDCP. During 2008, all
the States were sent advisories for preparing Action Plan on Prevention and Control of AES/JE on
5.02.08. It was followed by sending a check list indicating month wise activities on 25.02.08. On
19.03.08 a one day workshop was organized at BRD Medical College, Gorakhpur on
clinical manifestations and case management. Experts from NVBDCP helped the States/district
authorities to draw up a field oriented Action Plan in a meeting held under the Chairpersonship of
Principal Secretary (Health) and F.W., Government of Uttar Pradesh on 20.03.08. A central multi
disciplinary team of 6 experts also visited the State and BRD, Medical College, Gorakhpur w.e.f.
13-15 May, 2008 for making an on the spot assessment on the requirement of manpower, civil
works and equipment for establishing AES treatment unit as desired by HFM, Government of India.
Dte. NVBDCP organized 2 days workshop cum training at Lucknow on surveillance and
case management on 30-31 July, 2008 which was attended by 40 participants including 35 officials
from 11 endemic districts and 5 State officials.
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE
The Committee observes that a number of measures have been initiated by the
Department in co-ordination with the State authorities with regard to control of Japanese
Encephalitis (JE) in eastern U.P., the most endemic area. The Committee also takes note
of two problem areas - one of constraints in lab-testing and prevalence of other viruses,
apart from JE with vaccination being available only against JE. The Committee fails to
understand why, inspite of adequate funds being provided under the Programme, proper
sample testing facilities have been lacking. The Committee would like to State here that
lack of proper serological testing facilities would result in improper detection of infected
cases and could aggravate the situation further. The Committee suggests that mobile labs
for conducting the required test may be introduced so as to supplement the existing
facilities and to overcome the constraints faced in lab testing. The Committee would
appreciate if such an initiative is implemented at the earliest by the Directorate of NVBDCP
after due consultation with the State and district authorities in the JE infested Areas in
Assam and U.P.
The Committee would like to point out that problem of other viruses, apart from JE
in eastern UP was deteted by NIV , Pune in 2006. By now, strategy for tackling these viruses
including vaccination should have been in place and being implemented. The Committee,
therefore, impresses upon the Department to take the required action on an urgent basis.

CHIKUNGUNYA
Recommendations/Observations
4.16 State-wise analysis of suspected Chikungunya cases and number of confirmed cases during
2006 and 2007 reveals a very disturbing trend about the spread of this disease. In 2006, maximum
number of confirmed cases were reported from Maharashtra (804) followed by Karnataka (298)
and Gujarat (225). In contrast, Kerala reported the highest number of confirmed cases of 909 while
there are 347 confirmed cases occurring in West Bengal in 2007 up till November. Another cause
of serious concern is overall increase in total number of confirmed Chikungunya cases from 2001
in 2006 to 1876 in 2007 (upto November).
Recommendations/Observations
4.17 Incidence of Chikungunya cases in the country during 2006 and 2007 has led the
Committee to the conclusion that various initiatives taken by the Department have so far failed to
yield any desired results. The Committee strongly feels that with the enhanced allocation of
Rs.14.59 crore in 2008-09 for Dengue and Chikungunya, effective measures are required to be
undertaken in the affected States. Mere circulation of detailed guidelines and advisories for
prevention and control of these diseases to all affected States would not serve any purpose. What
is required is to identify the affected districts and go for regular fever surveillance in such endemic
areas to detect an unusual trend. The Committee is of the view that if this analysis of ground
reality is followed by IEC activities and strengthening of apex Referral Institutions for diagnosis and
treatment, number of Dengue/Chikungunya cases would show a declining trend. The Committee
apprehends that unless adequate remedial measures are taken, sporadic outburst of these diseases
would continue to be reported from different States every year.
Action Taken
During 2007,59535 cases for Chikungunya were reported. Total 7850 samples tested out of
which 1826 was confirmed for Chikungunya virus.
During 2006-07, Rs.21.60 crores was released as emergency package to the affected States
for items like Fogging Machines, Pyrethrum Extract, Temephos and Insecticide-treated bed nets
and IEC activity. Subsequently in 2007-08, Rs.8.75 crores was released as emergency package to
the affected States for items like Pyrethrum Extract, Temephos and IEC activities including social
mobilization of the community.
During 2006, Chikungunya disease appeared in the country after acquiescence of almost
three decades. The community did not have immunity against this disease and 1390322 suspected
cases of Chikungunya were reported by 16 States/UTs respectively. Only 15961 samples (1.15%
of suspected cases) were tested, of which 2001 were confirmed for Chikungunya virus (12.5%
of the samples tested).
In 2007, due to the intensification of implementation of the strategic action plan for
prevention and control of Dengue and Chikungunya in the country including community based
vector control and intensification of focused IEC activities, the number of suspected cases were
only 59535 i.e. 95.72% less than 2006 from 14 States. Besides, in 2007 Government of India had
established 110 Sentinel Surveillance hospitals in the affected States for proactive surveillance and
diagnosis. In addition, 13 Apex Referral Laboratories were also identified and linked with these 110
Sentinel Surveillance Hospitals for providing advanced diagnostic facility and back up support.
Therefore, due to better facility in 2007 more samples could be tested and confirmed, total 7850
samples tested (13.2% of suspected cases) and 1826 confirmed for Chikungunya virus (23.3% of
the samples tested).

98
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE
The Committee appreciates the efforts made by the Department in intensifying multi
pronged approaches to contain the incidence of Dengue and Chikungunya cases. The
Committee feels that results of such measures would surely reflect in the numbers of cases
detected for the year 2008. The Committee would like to be apprised about the IEC
interventions undertaken in this regard.
Committee’s attention is, however, drawn to the number of samples tested against
the suspected cases. The Committee notes that out of 59,535 suspected cases in 2007 only
13.2% were tested and of these 13.2% cases (7,850 samples tested), 23.3% of the samples
turned out to be confirmed cases. The Committee feels that 13.2% samples tested is a
fairly low number compared to the suspected cases figures and given the fact that more
than 23% turned out to be confirmed cases of the 7,850 tested samples, the figures could
be much more if the number of samples tested were increased.
The Committee apprehends that in such a situation, there are chances of there being
a large number of confirmed yet undetected cases. The Committee, therefore, suggests that
the Department should concentrate its efforts towards strengthening the testing lab
facilities so that maximum number of samples are tested.

BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
The Committee has been drawing the attention of the Department to the uneven
pace of utilisation of funds allocated under NRHM. Year 2007-08 was also no exception. As
on the 29th February, 2008, utilisation figures stood at Rs. 8800.88 crore which reached to
Rs. 10,310.16 crore by the 31st March, 2008, clearly indicating release of Rs. 1509.28 crore
during the last month of the financial year. The Department has not come up with any
clarification on this pertinent issue. The Committee is also not happy with the attempt
made by the Department in projecting a satisfactory utilization status of allocated funds by
drawing a comparison between RE allocation and utilization thereof. The fact remains that
inspite of increased allocation at the beginning of the year, the same had to be brought
down at the Revised Estimate Stage. Crucial programmes like Routine Immunisation, Pulse
Polio Immunisation, Intergrated Disease Survelliance Project showing this trend is a cause
of serious concern for the Committee.
The Committee is not prepared to accept the argument put forth by the Department
that balance remaining at the end of the year is mainly due to curtailed releases owing to
low absorptive capacity in the NE region. The Committee is constrained to observe that the
Department, instead of devising means to break through the obstacles to ensure proper
utilization of funds in the region, seems to pose a picture of resignation in the matter. The
Committee is of the firm belief that under the above circumstances, major healthcare
interventions in the NE region would not be reaching the targeted beneficiaries, thereby
depriving them of the healthcare initiatives. The Committee strongly feels that the
Department, being the apex nodal body in the country for healthcare initiatives, has to
strive harder so as to ensure their reach to the NE region in the real sense. The
Committee, therefore, recommends to the Department to take up this issue with the Chief
Secretaries of all the NE States as well as the Department of Development of NE Region.
(Para 2.5)
The Committee is disappointed to note that the Department has chosen to remain
silent on the reasons of steadily decreasing allocation of funds to such an important
healthcare programme like the Routine Immunisation Programme. The Committee is also
not convinced by the justification given by the Department with regard to Integrated
Diseases Surveillance Project. The Department has also, not indicated in its reply as to what

equipments. Similarly, it is also not clear as to what is the exact number of units that were

that funds for networking could not be released to NIC since UCs and SOEs could not be
timely obtained from it. The Committee is aware that National Informatics Centre (NIC) is

were delays in submission of UCs and SOEs by the latter. The Committee, under the
circumstances, can only conclude that the Department’s attempts in the matter have been
lackadaisical, and as a result of which, achieving targeted landmarks in fully
operationalising critical initiatives like that of the IDSP have been put on the backfoot. The
Committee observes that the Department should actively pursue the project of making IDSP
fully operational and should be extra vigilant towards achieving the targets set for such
critical health initiatives. (Para 2.6)

therefore, once again emphasizes that the Department has to evolve a mechanism

to be informed about the outcomes of the evaluation studies at the earliest and furnish the
relevant reports for its perusal. (Para 7.7)

set under the National Iodine Deficiency Disorders Control Programme for 2007-08 very

the target of analysis of 20,000 salt samples @ 500 samples per district from 40 districts
could not be undertaken due to non-availability of programme vechicle by administration.

point out that proper planning means achievement of targeted goals within the prescribed
apprehensions about undue delay in their actual initation. More than one year has passed
since then and third year of the Eleventh Plan period is also reaching its end. However, the
EFC Memo for the proposed projects remains under active consideration in consultation with
the Integrated Finance Division. The Committee has been drawing the attention of the
Department to the trend of undue delay in getting the formal approval for the proposed
projects from all the authorities. However, no serious introspection on such a vital aspect

2(c) : Procurement of sub-standard bed nets worth Rs.12.91 crore
Directorate General of Health Services, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, New Delhi
has given contract for procurement of 10 lakh bed nets (2 lakh double size+8 lakh single size) to
Hospital Services Consultancy Corporation (1) Limited (HSCC) for distribution in North Eastern
States under the National Anti Malaria Programme (renamed National Vector Disease Control
Programme in 2003). The Ministry accorded expenditure sanction for Rs.18.52 crore in
December, 2000 and an advance of Rs.4.32 crare was released to the HSCC during the year 2001.
HSCC placed the supply order in October, 2000 to three suppliers i.e. M/s R.S. Industries,
M/s ISSA Industries and Superior Industries. The supply of bed nets was to be completed within
90 days from the date of issue of order. The suppliers supplied 7,17,500 bed nets (double size
74,500 and single size 6,43,000) during February–April, 2001.
On receipt of a complaint of the supply of sub-standard bed nets, the Ministry issued
instructions in April, 2001 to the Government of Assam to withheld the distribution of bed
nets and deputed an officer of the rank of Deputy Secretary to investigate the matter.  By
the time, 1,63,000 bed nets (double size; 60,000 and single size 1,03,000) out of the above supply
had already been distributed by the concerned Stat Government. The samples lifted by the Deputy
Secretary from the State Government stores in Assam were tested at Indian Institute of
Technology, Delhi (IIT)  that showed that 3 out of 4 samples were inferior. Subsequently, more
samples were lifted in January, 2003 by an inspection team constituted with representatives of
various departments and IIT from the sealed stores in the presence of the representatives of HSCC
and supplier. These samples were also tested (March, 2003) at Indian Institute of Technology, Delhi
(IIT). The report received from the IIT revealed that the bed nets have failed to meet the Bureau
of Indian Standards (BIS) specifications, which was required as per the contract, in a number of
areas like bursting strength, GSM, number of holes etc. In addition, these bed nets did not carry
any label or marking to indicate the manufactures nor was the marking  “NAMP” supply not
for sale’ found on bed nets. An Expert Committee  constituted by the Ministry, further,
observed (June, 2003) that test results of the sample indicate a huge variation from the BIS
standards and large size of holes made these nets almost unfit for use.
Based on the above report, notices were issued (March, 2003) by HSCC to above firms to
lift the sub-standard bed nets lying in the godown at Guwahati. However, the concerned firms have
refused to lift the material stating that they should have been informed within four months of
supply. 14,500 double size and 5,20,000 single size bed nets totally 5,34,500 valuing at
Rs.9.45 crores were lying in the godown which was hired by the Department at Rs.89,000/- per
month. The avoidable expenditure on rent of godown alone amounted to Rs.51.67 lakh as on
November, 2005.

143
Audit Review Findings
Failure on the part of the Dte. of NVBDCP to ensure quality of bed nets as per BID
specification not only defeated the very objective of providing relief from severe malaria in

sanction of Action Plan to the end of user. Time involved in the present processing system is more

Para:- 3 Non initiation of action against faculty member Dr. R.S. Dhaliwal
Dr. R.S. Dhaliwal was Additional Professor, Cardiovascular and Thoracic Surgery
department. He carried out a number of open heart operations at PGI during the period 1994 to
2001. He used to purchase interior quality heart valves and accessories at very high rates on behalf
of patients under his treatment. He was asking them to deposit cash with unathorized agent who
supplied the material directly to Dr. Dhaliwal thereby ensuring that the patients could not check the
quality and quantity of  material supplied. The agent who was supplying the material was
Shri Surinder Singh Uppal owner of M/s Hitech Surgical Company 9/60, Rajouri Garden, New
Delhi allegedly having office in Sector 47, Chandigarh. M/s Northern Remedias (P) Ltd., SCO
No. 98, Sector 47, Chandigarh and M/s Paul Medical Hall. Sector 11, Chandigarh. Shri Uppal issued
bills for the sale of their heart valves in the these two firms which were found to be non existent
at the given address at Delhi.
The CBI registered Preliminary enquiry on 12.6.01 against Dr. R.S. Dhaliwal and others. After
investigation the CBI registered an FIR/RC on against Dr. R.S. Dhaliwal and others.
Dr. Dhaliwal performed 324 Tharacic Sargery during the period January, 1994 to July, 2001 of which
39 cases investigated by the CBI. The method adopted by Dr. Dhaliwala as by CBI was that he used
to personally take cash or drafts from patients for the valves at higher rates and passed on the
payments to Shri Uppal and Shri Singla. He also referred certain patients to Shri Uppal for supplying
valves who used to receive payments and supply the valves directly is Dr. R.S. Dhaliwal charging
higher rates. In certain cases the payments were taken for different brands of valves at a higher rate
and wrongful implantation was done. The investigation of CBI also mentions the personal diary of
Shri Uppal indicating the details of such cases, patients, profit and share given to Dr. Dhaliwal, which
is corroborated by GEQD and confessional statement of Shri Uppal. In the report it is mentioned that
Shri Uppal admitted before the  Magistrate that he has paid Rs.15 lakh to Dr. Dhaliwal for 160 such
patients out of the profits in addition to his own profits up to Rs.11 lakh.
The copy of the investigation report dated 22.3.2005 was sent the Secretary (Health) to
sanction prosecution under section 120B (Criminal conspiracy), 420 (cheating), 467, 468, 471
(forgery) of IPC and Section 13 of Prevention of Corruption Act. The Ministry asked the PGIMER
to send its comments on the case and to place the matter before the Governing Body for action.
The Governing Body discussed the matter in its meeting held on 31.8.05 vide Agenda Item
No. 14 and it was decided that the matter of sanction of prosecution against Dr. R.S. Dhaliwal
may be referred to the Ministry for taking decision in consultation with the Law Department. As
per decision of the Governing Body on the issue, the matter was referred to the Secretary, Health
and Family Welfare, Government of India, New Delhi vide letter Vig cell/PGI/F-545 dated 2.9.05.
The Government of India intimated that the Governing Body of the Institute is competent to grant
prosecution sanction against Dr. R.S. Dhaliwal now Professor and Head, Department of Cardic
vasscular and Thoracic Surgery, PGIMER, Chandigarh. Finally the matter was placed before the
Governing Body in its meeting no. 110 dated vide agenda item No. 17 where the Governing Body
authorized Director the PGIMER, Chandigarh who is a Member Secretary of the Governing sign
and convey the prosecution sanction on behalf of the Governing Body..

I. Augmentation of Patient Care Facilities
Cardio Pulmonary Rehabilitation
This is a new Unit which has been approved by the Governing Body of this Institute and is to
be developed during Eleventh Plan to provide comprehensive medical rehabilitation to patients
suffering from chronic respiratory diseases. A medical doctor and a physiotherapist have already
been trained in Cardio Pulmonary rehabilitation from Canada and they have initiated the work.
Expansion of 24 hours Emergency Facility
The existing 24 hours respiratory emergency section requires expansion due to increase in load of
emergency patients attending the hospital. The existing services that are provided to the patients
are insufficient to provide state-of-the-art facilities. Additionally, life-saving equipments have to be
upgraded in this section.
National Allergy, Asthma AND Clinical Immunology Centre
V .P Chest Institute is a well known for its patient care and research activities in the field of Allergy
Asthma and Clinical Immunology in the last 50 years. As the specialty of Allergy and Immunology
has made tremendous advancement during the last decade, Governing Body has approved the
establishment of a National Allergy, Asthma and Clinical Immunology Centre with subsidiary units
located in various parts of the Country.
Clinical Pharmacology
This is a new unit which has been approved by the Governing Body of this Institute to study the
respiratory pharmacology in relation to patient management.
Radio-diagnosis
This is an expansion to the existing facilities, which require upgradation and replacement of
obsolete radio imaging equipment. In addition, the new equipment is also proposed to be added for
more advanced diagnostics facilities for patient care.
Augmentation of diagnostic facilities
Due to the increase in patient care and related increase in the diagnostic investigations, the existing
facilities are inadequate and require up gradation and replacement, which is essential for patient care
management.
Running cost
This forms an important component to maintain optimal patient care services along with
management of the various diagnostic facilities provided. It inter alia  includes annual maintenance
of equipment, consumables, chemicals and related materials, testing kits etc. as required for
efficient patient care.
II. Renovation/Infrastructure development
Clinical Research Centre (Renamed as Viswanathan Chest Hospital)
This is the hospital wing of the Institute, which has been renamed as “Viswanathan Chest Hospital”
by the Governing Body of this Institute. The current hospital facilities housed in this wing had been

209
in place since last 50 years and there is an urgent need to upgrade the hospital building for
enhancement of patient bed strength and handling increasing patient load.
Resident hostel for Postgraduate students
The existing residential hostel for postgraduate (PG) students is insufficient to accommodate all the
resident doctors admitted to various postgraduate courses. In addition, due to the implementation
of the Oversight Committee Report with regard to enhanced seats in the reservation category in
postgraduate admission, the number of postgraduate resident will increase considerably (54%) and
there is an urgent need to increase the hotel facilities.
III. Augmentation of facilities of the Laboratories
The following laboratories of the Institute (Biochemistry, Physiology, Pharmacology, Microbiology,
Pathology, Mycology and Respiratory Virology) are in a dilapidated condition. These laboratories are
in existence since last 50 years without modernization and are not maintained as per the standards
required for running the facilities efficiently. These laboratories require adequate up-gradation and
renovation including life saving diagnostic facilities.
IV. Implementation of Oversight Committee Report
As per the implementation of the Oversight Committee Report, the number of Post Graduate seats
has to be increased by 54% from the existing level of seats. This requires creation of additional
infrastructure in terms of patient beds, other diagnostic and patient care management facilities,
augmentation of manpower especially in area of resident doctors (junior and senior), nursing and
other technical staff and augmentation of library and information sciences. Residential quarters are
to be provided to the additional nursing and other technical staff.
V. Introduction of New Courses and Induction of Junior/Senior Resident Students
V .P Chest Institute being a post graduate medical educational Institute, it is proposed to introduce
new post graduate medical courses in order to strengthen the specialty of Respiratory Medicine and
related sub-specialties.
VI Others
In order to augment the research facilities of this Institute, the existing Animal House has to be
upgraded to improve the research capabilities of the Institute.

BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
Recommendations/Observations
2.1 Against a projection of Rs.4102.00 crores by the Department of AYUSH for implementation
of existing schemes and launching of new schemes during the Eleventh Plan, a plan outlay of
Rs.3988.00 crores has been allocated by the Planning Commission. The Committee welcomes the
enhanced allocation for AYUSH Sector in the Eleventh Plan. The Committee, however, observes that
Tenth Plan provision of Rs.1194.60 crores although less than one-third of Eleventh Plan allocation
remained under-utilised with an expenditure of only Rs.1030.15 crores reported at the end of the
plan period. BE allocation in the last three years of the Tenth Plan had to be brought down at the
RE stage, with the reduced allocation too remaining under-utilised. The Committee views with
serious concern the continuance of this trend in the Eleventh Plan also.
Action Taken
The initial Tenth Plan approval outlay of the Department was Rs.775 crore which was
revised upward to Rs.1194.60 crore through Annual Plan allocation. The shortfall in expenditure
during the last three years of the Tenth Plan vis-a-vis the BE allocation is mainly attributable to
less expenditure incurred under setting up of All India Institute of Ayurveda, North Eastern Institute
of Folk Medicine and North Eastern Institute of Ayurveda and Homoeopathy which have been
sanctioned by the Government towards the end of financial year 2007-08. A high level monitoring
committee under the Secretary (AYUSH) is overseeing the implementation of the schemes i.e. All

Recommendations/Observations
3.3 The Committee notes from the Outcome Budget that construction of an auditorium was
planned during 2006-07. However, the work on the project is yet to start. The Department has
attributed the delay to non finalization of construction works by CPWD. The Committee would like
the Department to apprise it of the stumbling blocks in the way of finalizing the construction works
of the auditorium, explain the shortfall in achievement of the SC/ST medical mobile camps and
specify the contributory factors for the reduced number of the patients. The Committee would also
like to be intimated about the corrective measures taken by the Department to address the above
issues.
Action Taken
Construction of Auditorium: The proposal for construction of an Auditorium was planed
during 2006-07 and the CPWD was paid Rs.1.84 crores as advance for this deposit work. It was
decided to construct the new Auditorium at the spot where the old Assembly Hall stood by
dismantling and demolishing it. Accordingly the CPWD prepared the Estimate, Drawings etc. in
consultation with the Central Design Bureau of the Ministry and the CPWD could not start the
work due to the difficulty in appointing a Consultant for Interior Decoration etc. prior to finalization
of final Drawing, Estimate etc. The estimated cost was worked out to Rs.2.45 crores.
In the meantime, the Institute as well as the Department felt that the proposed new
Auditorium should be planned keeping in view the national status of the Institute and also
considering the increased activities of Workshops, Seminars, Conferences of national and
international level. Therefore, constructing the Auditorium at the present site, which is very small,
will not help this purpose and it was felt that the Auditorium should come up with modern look
and with all facilities suiting not only to the present day needs but also keeping in mind the future
requirements of the fast developing Institute. This will also benefit in increasing the seating capacity
as well as adding more amenities.
Accordingly, the Central Design Bureau and the CPWD prepared a revised Plan and Estimate
and the estimated cost raised to Rs.4.50 crores. This was approved by the Standing Finance
Committee in December, 2006.
The CPWD was accordingly conveyed the sanction but due to some legal proceedings, the
CPWD was not able to spend money on constructions, they could not take up the work on time.
The matter was taken up with CPWD and they were apprised of the concern of the Hon’ble
Parliamentary Committee on the delay in starting the work.
The CPWD has now promised that they are in the process of issuing the Tenders for the
work and it was also assured that construction of the Auditorium will start very soon.
Shortfall in SC/ST Mobile Camps: The initial provision for SC/ST Mobile Camps for 2006-07
and 2007-08  was Rs.3.00 lakhs each respectively, which was raised to Rs.10 lakhs each
respectively in the RE. The Institute organized 32 Medical Camps benefiting 24,467 patients in
2006-07 and 33 Medical Camps benefiting 25,703 patients in 2007-08.  Actually there is no shortfall
in the Medical Camps as the Institute has organized the possible number of Camps and utilized the
allocated provision to the maximum extend possible. The Institute was running with shortfall in the
number of teachers and it was not possible to spare teachers to undertake the Camps as they were
hectically engaged in various teaching, patient care, research activities etc. and also that for each
Camp, at least one teacher has to be spared and deputed for a minimum 8 days. Therefore, the
maximum possible number of Camps was organized.

13
The allocation proposed for 2008-09  is Rs.6 lakhs and accordingly, the Institute will organize
maximum Camps for the benefit of SC/ST Population and will ensure to increase the number of
Camps. During 2008-09  (up to 20-5-2008) 2 Camps have already been organized.

YOGA AND NATUROPATHY
Recommendations/Observations
6.7 The Committee is happy to note that the MDNIY and CCRYN, which are premier
institutions of the country operating in the field of Yoga and Naturopathy, have started research
projects in collaboration with the private sector for the benefit of the common people. However,
taking into account the fact that private firms are largely driven by profit motive, the Committee
has a word of caution for the Department. The Committee is of the view that since these research
projects are being financed by taxpayer’s money, it should ensure that the health benefits ensuing
from them percolate down to the lowest rung of the society in terms of cheaper and viable health
care alternatives. The Committee also recommends that MDNIY should make more sincere efforts
for undertaking more research projects on various aspects of Health Care so that the infrastructure
available with the institution and the funds allocated to it could be utilized optimally.
Action Taken
Most of the research projects undertaken by the MDNIY and the CCRYN have been taken
up with government institutions. Only a few research projects have been taken up with reputed
private institutions.
Research projects are taken up on the basis of their relevance to public health objectives
and they are not taken up only for the purposes of intellectual or scientific interest. The intention
is that the research projects should yield outcomes which should directly impact public health in
the country.
As regards the recommendation that the MDNIY should take up more projects relating to
health care, it may be pointed out that the two major initiatives taken up by the MDNIY involve
the setting up of full-fledged research centres in NIMHANS, Bangalore and JIPMER, Puduchery.
The research outcomes from both these centres are bound to be significant.
In addition to this MDNIY also intends to set up an Advanced Yoga Education and Research
Centre at the Defence Institute of Physiology and Allied Sciences, Delhi (DIPAS). The collaboration
with DIPAS. which has played a pioneering role in conducting scientific research into various
aspects of Yoga, is bound to be very fruitful.
Recommendations/Observations
6.12 The Committee reiterates its earlier recommendation, of taking steps for regulating the Yoga
and Naturopathy courses and accreditation of Institutions in these two areas. The Department also
needs to explore the possibility of setting up of a Regulation Council for Yoga and Naturopathy.
The Committee notes that some initiatives have been taken by the Department which need to be
pursued by the Department with all concerned. Only then, the real objective of extending the
benefits of these two therapies to the needy would be achieved.
Action Taken
The Department has examined the issue of the regulation of Naturopathy courses and the
accreditation of Naturopathy institutions in depth and has come to the conclusion that the optimal

17
course of action would be for the State Governments to enact suitable legislation for the purpose.
The Department has already advised the State Governments accordingly. There has not been much
response from the States. However, the Department of AYUSH will continue to try to persuade the
State Governments to initiate action in the matter.
Recommendations/Observations
6.13 The Committee is happy to note that some headway has been made in the direction of
regulation of Yoga and Naturopathy, though a lot still remains to be done. The Committee
recommends to the Department to continue to pursue with the State Governments the
implementation of all the model guidelines for regulation and standardization of naturopathy courses
that have been circulated to them.
The Committee was informed that a naturopathy centre at V aidyanath Dham, Deoghar,
which was started by Gandhi ji, is presently not operational. The Committee recommends the
Department to get the above centre revived in consultation with its management and with the local
authorities. The Committee would like to be informed of the progress made in the matter.
Action Taken
Given the small number of colleges offering courses in Naturopathy and which are located
in a handful of States, there does not appear to be any need for Central Regulation in the matter.
Given the limited number of these institutions, a Central Regulatory Council would be both
unnecessary and unviable. As far as Yoga is concerned, it is felt that a self-regulatory association
consisting of the premier Yoga institutions in the country would be a far better proposition for the
regulation of Yoga in the country. After extensive consultations with all the major Yoga schools in
the country, a consensus has been evolved about standardized syllabi for Yoga education, therapy
and training courses.
The Director, CCRYN has been in touch with the erstwhile management of the Naturopathy
centre at Vaidyanath Dham, Deoghar. It is learnt that the institution is in receivership and is now
under the control of the District Collector. The Director, CCRYN will visit Deoghar to contact the
District Collector to find out the status of the institution. Any assistance required for re-starting
the institution will be provided.

Recommendations/Observations
3.13 The Committee expresses its concern over such a large number of vacant posts both in
teaching and non-teaching cadres. Not only this, percentage of Guest-Faculty and contract
appointments is also quite high. The Committee observes that the shortfall would be further
accentuated as a result of the latest Supreme Court judgment upholding 27% reservation for Other
Backward Classes (OBCs). The Committee feels that the steps taken to tide over the problem of

27
shortfall in the teaching and the non-teaching cadre posts by way of engaging guest faculty,
outsourcing etc. is a short-term measure which can never be a substitute for filling up the posts
on a permanent basis. Since the amended Recruitment Rules have been submitted to the Minister
of H&FW for his approval, the Committee is hopeful that these will be notified shortly. However,
the Committee would like to observe that the NIH is an autonomous organization of national
importance and all care needs to be exercised to ensure that its autonomy does not get eroded in
any way by the revised Recruitment Rules. The Committee would also like to recommend that the
Department set in motion the process of completing other remaining formalities so that the
recruitment does not only get started immediately after notification of the Recruitment Rules but
is also taken to its logical conclusion within a specified time-frame.

The amendments in the Recruitment Rules have been approved. The advertisement for filling
posts in being given. As and when the regular posts are filled up, the guest faculty/visiting faculty

Recommendations/Observations

diseases and also mental health/disorder. The Committee is aware that findings of these Research

mechanism in place for ensuring timely completion of such projects. The Committee also strongly
feels that there is a need for a centralized cell working in co-ordination with all the Research
Councils for propagating the positive impact of such research studies. The Committee also
recommends that adequate financial allocation be extended to the four Research Councils to equip
their research labs and if need be, more funds be allotted to them at RE 2008-09 stage.

Mural Project Screening Committee comprising the experts and Scientists from different streams
so that evaluation of the projects is done on their merits. Besides there should be a close
monitoring of the progress of all the sanctioned projects for getting the desired results as well as
to avoid misuse of funds.

The Department has constituted a centralized cell consisting of Adviser (Ay.), Adviser
(Homoeo.), Deputy Adviser (Unani) and Director (MN) for the purpose of effective monitoring of
EMR projects and dissemination of research findings.

councils to not only monitor the progress of EMR projects but also to propagate the positive

The Committee welcomes the setting up of a centralized cell for the purpose of
effective monitoring of EMR projects and dissemination of research findings. The
Committee hopes that this cell has become fully operational.

Yoga and Naturopathy particularly by the MDNIY . The Committee would like to be apprised of the
underlying causes for the under utilization. The Committee would also like to impress upon the
Department the imperative need for optimal and judicious utilization of funds allocated for a crucial
sector like health. The Committee has always been responsive to the genuine needs of the
Department and has been supporting its case for higher allocation in terms of the inherent powers
of the Committee. However, if the Department time and again defaults in ensuring optimal utilization
of the allocated funds, it will weaken its own case. The Committee would, therefore, even at the
cost of repetition, like to stress that the Department take necessary remedial measures to ensure
that the funds allocated in BE 2008-09 are utilized optimally and strictly as per the action plan.

expansion of the Institute’s activities would take place as envisaged. In particular, two research

centres were to be established – an Advanced Centre for Yoga Therapy and Research in Mental
Health and Neuro Sciences at NIMHANS, Bangalore and an Advanced Centre for Yoga Education,

Recommendations/Observations
9.24 The Committee observes that main streaming of AYUSH is of immense importance in the
sense it will help to deliver health care facilities to the most marginalized and impoverished
households in the rural areas of the country. Given the enormous shortfall in health facilities and
the pathetic condition of public health utilities in rural areas, this Scheme is a sterling initiative,
though it will only address a miniscule part of the health needs of the rural poor, leaving out large
swathes of India. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should draw an
action plan to ensure that the targets set for 2008-09 are achieved fully.
Action Taken
The integration of AYUSH medical and health services with mainstream modern medicine or
“mainstreaming” as it is generally known would result in good proportion of the presently
underserved population being able to obtain health services. The necessity for such mainstreaming
has been recognized and this is one of the objectives of the National Rural Health Mission (NRHM).
Under the NRHIM, AYUSH facilities are being co-located in allopathic health institutions. NRHM
also provides funds for the engagement of AYUSH physicians on contract basis to man these
facilities. Funds for the creation of infrastructure in these co-located AYUSH facilities, the
procurement of drugs, contingencies, etc. are provided from the Hospitals and Dispensaries
Centrally Sponsored Scheme of the Department of A YUSH. The convergence of funding from the
NRHM and the Hospitals and Dispensaries Centrally Sponsored Scheme ensures that AYUSH
facilities are created in allopathic health institutions and these facilities are properly set up and
manned. The achievements in the main streaming of AYUSH in the NRHM are given in the
Annexure-IV.

38
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE
The Committee notes that it has made a pointed recommendation to ensure that the
target set for 2008-09 under the scheme of mainstreaming of AYUSH in NRHM is achieved
fully. The Committee, therefore, reiterates its earlier recommendation that a action plan be
drawn to meet the targets set for 2008-09.
QUALITY CONTROL OF ASU&H DRUGS
Recommendations/Observations
10.14 The Committee is concerned over the fact that State Drug Testing Laboratories have not
become functional in many major States as pointed out by the Secretary. The Committee observes
that drugs are used for saving valuable human lives and if adequate mechanism is not available with
the State Governments to regulate quality of ASU&H drugs, then it is a very serious situation. The
Committee has been given to understand that the Central Council of Health and Family Welfare
comprising Chief Ministers of all the States and chaired by the Health and Family Welfare Minister,
has passed a Resolution on the need for the States to utilize the assistance given by the Central
Government for upgradation of State Drug Testing Laboratories and strengthening of the drug
enforcement machinery. The Committee, therefore, desires the Department, to once again take up
the matter with all the Chief Secretaries of the States apprising them of the Committee’s concern
in the matter.
Action Taken
The matter has been taken up with the State Chief Secretaries.
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE
The Committee would however like to be apprised of the outcome of talks with State
Chief Secretaries and whether the talks remained fruitful in revival of some of SDT
laboratories.
Recommendations/Observations
10.16 The Committee supports the budgetary provisions made for the Scheme. However, the
Committee has no idea whether any monitoring mechanism is in place to ensure that the funds
placed at the disposal of the States and the ASU&H manufacturing units will be spent for the
specified purposes. The Committee would, therefore, recommend the Department to devise an
effective monitoring mechanism to ensure proper utilization of funds allocated for the purpose. The
Committee would also like to be apprised of the number of UCs pending under this Scheme and
the amount involved therein.
Action Taken
As far as assistance to ASU&H manufacturing units in the revised schemes is concerned,
there is an in-built monitoring mechanism as the subsidy of 30% on expenditure (subject to a
maximum of Rs.30.00 lakhs) is a back-ended subsidy and the money would be released through
the bank from which the unit has availed loan facility. The release of further funds is subject to
certification by PLIM/PHARMEXCIL that the stated unit has indeed upgraded itself as envisaged
under the scheme. As far as funding to the State Governments is concerned, funds would be
released only as a reimbursement of the expenditure already incurred on testing in NABL accredited
laboratories and this is subject to States having functional DTL and support enforcement
mechanism in place. The No. of pending UCs is 105 under the scheme.

COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE

involved in pending Utilization Certificates (UCs). The Committee, therefore, recommends

under reference be intimated to it.
DEVELOPMENT OF COMMON FACILITIES FOR AYUSH INDUSTRY CLUSTERS
Recommendations/Observations
10.19 The Committee observes that as per the Department’s own admission, development of
common facilities for AYUSH industry clusters is of immense importance as it is envisaged to fill
in the critical gaps in the AYUSH Sector , especially raw material standardization, quality control and
productivity improvement compliances etc. However, the progress made in the matter is not
commensurate with the expected results. The Committee is pained to observe that due to languid
pace of approval of the Scheme, budgetary provisions made in BE 2007-08 could not be utilized,
which has resulted in reduced allocation in BE 2008-09.
Action Taken
The Centrally Sponsored Scheme for ‘Development of AYUSH Industry Clusters’ has been
launched with the approval of the Competent Authority. Since, this is new and innovative Scheme,
it took some time to put the component of the Scheme across the industry. The Department
conducted number of stakeholders consultations in different parts of the country to explain the
Scheme. As a result of the concerted ef forts of the Department, three proposals were granted ‘in
principle’ approval in the financial year 2007-08. One Detailed Project Report (DPR) for Thrissur
Cluster is likely to be put before the Scheme Monitoring Committee by August, 2008. M/s IL&FS
CDI Ltd. has been appointed as Project Management Consultant for implementation of the Scheme.
It may be mentioned here that the Department has already received five new Concept Notes from
different parts of the country for setting up of the common facilities for AYUSH industry. So far
as the implementation of the Scheme is concerned, because of the concerted efforts of the
Department, eight proposals have already been received against a target of ten fixed by the Planning
Commission for first 2-3 years. The expenditure will pick-up once the DPRs are received and
approved in the Department in a time-bound manner.
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE
Though the Committee is happy to note that a good number of proposals have been
received by the Department, it is not sure as to how many DPRs would materialize. The
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department thrash out the appropriate policy
matrix for the purpose of facilitating speedy submission of the DPRs.

Recommendations/Observations
14.1 The Committee notes that a panel of Experts under the Chairmanship of Director, Institute
of High Tibetan Studies, Sarnath, V aranasi has been constituted for examination of the status,
strength and association of Tibetan system of Medicine with Ayurveda. The expert panel has also
been requested to examine the contribution of different institutions under the Tibetan system of
Medicines in the country and the necessity of funding them for their further development. The
Committee would appreciate if the Report is expedited and follow-up action taken thereon.
Action Taken
The Department of AYUSH has constituted a Committee under the chairmanship of
Prof. G.N. Samten, Institute of Higher Tibetan Studies, Varanasi to assess the status, strength and
association of Sowa Rigpa with Ayurveda and its reorganization. The Committee has extremely
reviewed the issue and submitted a detailed report with the following summary of
recommendations. The Department of AYUSH has initiated the action.
• Considering the status, strength and association with Ayurveda, Sowa-Rigpa system
deserves to be recognized as a traditional health care system like other existing
systems in India.
• In Sowa-Rigpa practicing regions. Amchis may be considered for appointment in all
local health scheme and Government hospitals.
• The status of existing Sowa-Rigpa colleges is very poor, they may be brought at par
with Ayurveda and Siddha colleges applying all norms of CCIM.
• A separate committee may be constituted to redraft the Sowa-Rigpa graduate’s syllabus
to make it comprehensive like that of Ayurveda to produce professionally competent
graduates.
• Good Manufacturing Practice may be made compulsory for all Sowa-Rigpa
Manufacturing Units.
• A separate cell may be created in C.C.R.A.S. for translation of Sowa-Rigpa Tibetan
medical literature into Hindi and English.
• Sowa-Rigpa representative may be accommodated in C.C.I.M. like that of Siddha and
Unani.

• The financial assistance may be provided to Sowa-Rigpa colleges to make them at par
with other traditional medicine colleges.
• Collaborative research in Sowa-Rigpa may be promoted. The Department of A YUSH
and CRAS has initiated action to promote the system.
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE

Tibetan System of Medicine – Sowa Rigpa but the Department has not indicated its reaction

ANNEXURE-III
The major findings of the Nityanand Committee are as follows:
1. Though CCRAS and its units have some significant contributions in the area of pharmacopoeial work and observatory clinical tr ials
for validating single and compound classical drugs and development of some new coded drugs, there is a need for restructuring
and consolidating of peripheral units of CCRAS.
2. CCRAS and its institutions as they are structured and functioning today leave much to be desired. In their present status and  set
up, these laboratories are not likely to be able contribute much to achieve their avowed objectives.
3. At this stage 10 to 12 of its better staffed and equipped research institutes be chosen and developed into National Institute s
in specialized areas, staffed adequately and equipped well with a focused R&D mandate. Research personnel spread over 37
peripheral units who are desirous of pursuing quality research work may be relocated to these 10 to 12 centres. The remaining
units may be allowed to continue with staff who do not wish to relocate providing OPD and IPD services in the area of their
operation and carrying out limited research work under the supervision of these 10 to 12 national research centre.
4. The Nityanand Review Committee Report has suggested the upgradation of 12 CRIs/RRIs to National Research Centres with a
specific mandate.
Process of implementation on the recommendations of the Committee has been initiated and consultation with the staff of the
Council has been initiated so as to remove the misgivings that certain units are being closed. The need based re-deployment of the staff
is being worked out and will be implemented in the phases.

ANNEXURE-V
Modalities of the Scheme for Grant-in-Aid to Non-Profit/Non-Governmental AYUSH Organizations/Institutions for
Revitalization of Local Health Traditions, Midwifery Practices etc.
The Scheme has mainly five core objectives viz.,
a. Systematic participatory documentation of Local Health Traditions (LHT) related to one or more of the following aspects
(i) Home remedies.
(ii) food and nutrition.
(iii) midwifery
(iv) bone setting
(v) other specialized local health practices
(vi) ethno veterinary practices.
b. Rapid assessment of selected health practices, prioritized by local communities, based on literature review.
c. Design and implementation of participatory clinical trials for high priority Local Health Practices (LHP) in the local commun ity.
d. Promotion via a participatory process, of sound LHPs, in the community, in order to enhance health security of rural communities.
The additional optional objectives may be one or more of the following:
■ Preparation of Inventory of Medicinal Plants, duly protected from misuse under the biodiversity act,
■ Undertaking pharmacological studies on high priority local health practices,
■ Supporting capacity building activities of folk healer associations,
■ Any other relevant objective conceived by the applicants.
Eligibility for application under the scheme:
1. The applicant should provide evidence of having previously interacted with local health traditions in any part of the country .
2. The applicant should have had previous organizational experience in executing an All India or regionally coordinated program related
to community health or a major community based research program in the health sector.

68
3. The applicant should possess adequate core staff including medical professionals experienced in community outreach.
4. Any institution that has obtained funding from any other Central Government Ministry/Department for the same purpose in the l ast
five years shall not be eligible for funding under this scheme.
5. Applicant shall have to make information available regarding any assistance taken from any State/Central Agency in the last 5  years.
Selection process :
1. The applicant should send a two page concept note containing information on
(a) Clear objectives as per the Scheme
(b) Geographical spread of the proposal
(c) Previous experience
(d) Potential partners and
(e) Broad budget estimate for a five year program.
The proposals are appraised by the Project Appraisal Committee and the proposals which are found suitable as per the provisions
of the scheme are placed before the Project Screening Committee chaired by Secretary (AYUSH) for approval.

PREFACE
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Health and
Family Welfare, having been authorized by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, do
hereby present this Thirty-seventh Report of the Committee on Action Taken by Government on
the Recommendations contained in the Twenty-ninth Report on Demands for Grants (Demand
No.48) of the Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare for the
year 2008-09.
2. The Twenty-ninth Report of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on
Health and Family Welfare was presented to Rajya Sabha and laid on the Table of Lok Sabha on
30th April, 2008. Replies of the Government on the recommendations contained in the Report,
received from the Department of Health Research were considered by the Committee at its meeting
held on the 12th November, 2009.
3. The Committee considered the draft Report and adopted the same at its meeting held on
the 12th November, 2009.
AMAR SINGH
N

November 12 , 2009 Department-related Parliamentary
Kartika  21, 1931 (Saka) Standing Committee on Health and Family Welfare.

1
REPORT
The Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Government on the
recommendations contained in its Twenty-ninth Report on Demands for Grants (Demand No. 48)
of the Department of Health Research for the year 2008-09.
2. Action Taken Notes have been received from the Government in respect of the
recommendations contained in the Report. They have been categorized as follows:
(i) Recommendations/Observations which have been accepted by the Government:
2.3, 2.5, 3.3, 3.4, 3.5, 7.2, 11.2, 11.3, Total–8 (Chapter-I)
(ii) Recommendations/Observations which the Committee does not desire to pursue in
view of the Government’s replies: 6.2, 8.2, 10.1, Total–3 (Chapter-II)
(iii) Recommendations/Observations in respect of which replies of the Government have
not been accepted by the Committee: 1.4, 1.5, 1.7, 3.7, 4.3, 5.2, 9.2, Total–7
(Chapter-III)
(iv) Recommendations/Observations in respect of which final replies of the Government
are still awaited: Total–Nil (Chapter-IV)

2
CHAPTER-I
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS WHICH
HA VE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE GOVERNMENT
BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
Recommendations/Observations
2.3 The Committee is not convinced with the clarification given by the representatives of the
Department. The Committee is unable to understand that in which manner the Department will
manage the expenditure on various activities out of meagre allocation of Rs.420 crores against the
projected demand of Rs.1613 crores. The Committee has all reasons to apprehend that the
proposed major infrastructure upgradations as well as the new activities proposed to be started by
the Department are going to be affected badly. The Committee desires that constraints of funds
should not come in the way of the infrastructure upgradation as well as the proposed new
activities. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should not hesitate in asking
for an enhanced allocation at R.E. stage so that the Research and Development activities are not
affected for want of funds.
Action Taken
The recommendation of the Committee will be kept in mind while preparing the Revised
Estimates for 2008-09 of the Council later this year.
Recommendations/Observations
2.5 The Committee observes that the allocation for 2007-08 under Plan will be fully utilized by
the Indian Council of Medical Research. The actual expenditure under Non-Plan is likely to exceed
the sanctioned Budget Grant. The additional expenditure will be met from the Council’s
Miscellaneous Receipts.
Action Taken
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare released an amount of Rs.144.15 crores (Plan),
Rs.90.00 crores (Non-Plan), and Rs.32.50 crores (NER) for the year 2007-08 which has been
completely utilized by ICMR during the year 2007-08. Besides, an additional (RE) amount of
Rs.90.00 crores (Plan) was also released to ICMR for the year 2007-08 which was also utilized
by the ICMR during the year 2007-08.
INDIAN COUNCIL OF MEDICAL RESEARCH (ICMR)
Recommendations/Observations
3.3 The Committee notes that management of communicable diseases, fertility control, maternal
and child health care, nutritional deficiencies and disorders, cancer, AIDS etc. have been a serious
cause of concern in the health sector. Some of the above problems have posed a serious threat
to a larger section of population of the country. This is the right time that the ICMR should gear
itself for a greater role in undertaking and coordinating the health research undertaken by the
2

3
different institutes/agencies as also it should take all out efforts for minimizing the causalities as
a result of the diseases referred to above particularly due to the non-communicable diseases,
nutritional deficiencies, maternal and child mortality etc. The Committee, therefore, recommends
that the ICMR should not leave any stone unturned in the matter of management and control of
the above diseases.
Action Taken
The recommendations of the Committee have been circulated to all the Divisions of ICMR
for information and compliance.
3.4 The Committee takes note of the following activities proposed to be taken up during 2008-09.
(i) Intramural activities being undertaken by the 30 Institutes of the Council, including
works of a capital nature and infrastructural facilities such as equipment, consumables
etc.; and
(ii) Extramural research activities being undertaken at different medical colleges, hospitals
and research all over India with funds provided by the Council.
Action Taken
Matter of record.
Recommendations/Observations
3.5 The Committee is hopeful that the set targets would be achieved by ICMR and there would
be optimum and judicious utilization of funds allocated for the above mentioned purposes. The
Committee recommends that the additional funds, if any, required for achieving the set targets
should be made available to the Council at the R.E. stage.
Action Taken
The recommendations of the Committee have been noted for compliance.
ADV ANCED TRAINING IN RESEARCH IN MEDICINE AND HEALTH
Recommendations/Observations
7.2 The Committee notes that some very important activities are envisaged to be undertaken
under the above Scheme of Advanced Training in Research in Medicine and Health. However, only
Rs.5.50 crores has been earmarked for the purpose. The Committee impresses upon the
Department to ensure proper implementation of all the activities referred to above. The Committee
apprehends that this meager allocation of funds to the tune of Rs.5.50 crores would not be
sufficient to meet the requirement of this scheme and in that case the Department should go for
enhancement of the funds at R.E. stage.
Action Taken
Noted for compliance.
MISCELLANEOUS
Recommendations/Observations
11.2 Committee’s attention has been drawn by CAG Report No. 2 of 2007 which is a

4
Performance Audit on National Institute of Malaria Research functioning under the Indian Council
of Medical Research. Following are the main observations made by CAG in its Report:—
➢ NIMR did not Mosquito Fauna Surveys in the malaria endemic areas to know the
prevalence of different mosquito species and to develop cost effective strategies to
control malaria.
➢ Of the 74 projects with potential for technology development, NIMR developed only
tow technologies during 2001-02 to 2005-06 and could not transfer any of these two
technologies.
➢ Collaboration among NIMER, National Vector Borne Disease Control Programme and
State Programme Officer was inadequate.
➢ One third of the 51 scientists of NIMR were not involved in any project for a period
ranging from one to five years. Only 15 training programme for State Government
health officials were conducted over a period of five years. No annual action plan for
conducting training was prepared.
11.3 The Committee would like to be apprised about the reaction of ICMR on the
above-mentioned observations of CAG and follow-up action thereon.
Action Taken
The reactions of the ICMR to the observation of the CAG are, given below:—
(a) Mosquito Fauna Survey— Between 2001—06 NIMR conducted surveys in 27 districts
in 4 ecological zones. This was in excess of the target of 20 districts in the Tenth
Plan period.
(b) Malaria parasite Bank— The activity of the Malaria Parasite Bank is ongoing in nature.
It has so far accumulated 735 isolates of malaria parasite from different parts of the
country.
(c) Technology Development— A number of technologies developed by NIMR currently
form a part of the national efforts for malaria control. Some of these technologies are
described below:—
(i) Insecticide treated nets: MVBDCP is now using this technology in the
control of malaria in rural India. ITN is now a major intervention strategy
for malaria control in the country.
(ii) Larvivorous fishes: Guppy and Gumbusia fishes are used by the NVBDCP
all over the country in the control of malaria.
(iii) Based on multicentric trials, Biolavicides have been introduced in selected
urban areas for control of immature stages of mosquitoes.
(iv) The technology of bioenvironmental control of malaria was transferred to
Marmugao Port Trust in Goa.
(v) Alpha beta arteether: This is the best ant malarial drug used in the treatment
of drug resistant and p. falcuparum malaria cases. NIMR was partner with
CDRI in the development of this drug. The drug is exported to>30
countries (marketed by Themis Chemicals) It is widely used by NVBDCP
and private sector in malaria treatment.

5
(vi) Dip-stick: NIMR tested dip-sticks at many locations through its field
stations. This is the best non-microscopic method for the diagnosis of
malaria. Dip-stick is used by NVBDCP in malaria diagnosis for early
detection and prompt treatment.
(vii) Bulaquine an antimalaria drug developed by the CDRI (marketed by Primal
Co.) was tested to study replacing pattern of P. vivax.
It also needs to be stressed that development of any new technology requires to be
preceded by several studies on multiple locations and only after extensive testing and validation can
the technology be made part of the control programme. A period, of 5 years may not be adequate
to develop the technology and ensure its viable application.
(d) The activities of the Institutes of the ICMR can be classified into two broad headings,
namely Intramural and Extramural. There is no in-house requirement within ICMR that
requires each of its scientists to compulsorily undertake an Extramural project.
The current efforts of National Institute of Malaria Research at undertaking training
programmes will be increased substantially once its office functioning from different locations are
shifted to its own building at Dwarka.

6
CHAPTER-II
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS WHICH THE COMMITTEE DOES
NOT DESIRE TO PURSUE IN VIEW OF THE GOVERNMENT’S REPLIES
INTER-SECTORIAL CO-ORDINATION IN MEDICAL BIOMEDICAL AND HEALTH
RESEARCH
Recommendations/Reservations
6.2 The Committee hopes that all the activities falling under the Inter-sectoral coordination in
Medical, Biomedical and Health Research would be well taken care of by the Department. The
Department should ensure that any administrative/procedural formalities will not affect, in any way,
proper and optimum utilization of funds allocated for the purpose. The Committee would also like
to be apprised of the activities undertaken under this Scheme during 2008-09 and the extent of their
success vis-a.-vis  their envisaged targets.
Action Taken
A progress report on achievement of the targets set will be furnished after close of financial
year 2008-09.
INTERNATIONAL CO-OPERATION IN MEDICAL AND HEALTH RESEARCH
Recommendations/Observations
8.2 The Committee observes that International cooperation in Medical and Health Research is a
very important activity to be undertaken by the Department. Exchange of information and research
work at international level will boost health care services of the country as also help in tackling
health related problems. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should not
lose any opportunity in this direction. The Committee would like to be intimated about the activities
undertaken as well as the break-up of funds spent thereon under this Scheme during 2008-09.
Action Taken
A progress report on achievement of the targets set will be furnished after close of financial
year 2008-09.
COORDINATION IN THE FIELD OF HEALTH RESEARCH WITH GOVERNMENTS,
ORGANISATIONS AND INSTITUTIONS
Recommendations/Observations
10.1 The scheme seeks to coordinate between organizations and institutes under the Central/State
Governments in the areas of promotion of special studies in medicines and health. For this purpose
the Department will have to coordinate with a number of Departments like Department of Science
and Technology, Department of Bio-technology. Department of Agricultural Research and Education,

of health research is the most important activity entrusted to the Department. A number of
Government Department/agencies are engaged in research activities in the field of health care and
for getting better results and health care facilities, proper coordination and exchange of information
with the Government Departments/agencies is a must. The Department will have to make all out
efforts for effective coordination and monitoring with all the Government Departments/agencies
engaged in the field of health research. The Committee would like to be informed of the efforts
made by the Department in this regard as also the outcome of such efforts.
